docs.title: Check numbers and quotes
docs.text:
Ch. 3 · 3.1About 5 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Numbers, dates, and sentences inside quotation marks are where chatbots go wrong in ways that look right.
  • Check numbers against the original, a rough estimate, and a calculator.
  • Find each quote word for word in the original.

docs.title: Spot the difference
docs.text:
Have you played "spot the difference" with two pictures that look almost the same? The big shapes match, so you have to stare to find the small changes.

A wrong number from a chatbot looks just like that. It looks reasonable, so it's easy to miss. As Chapter 1 showed, a chatbot picks a likely next word. So it can give you a number that is likely-looking, not checked.

In 10-year-old words

Treat numbers and quotes like a spot-the-difference game. Compare them one more time.

docs.title: Where it goes wrong most
docs.text: Kind How it often goes wrong Numbers A close but different value, or a mixed-up unit (dollars and euros, millions and billions) Dates The year or day is off by a little Names Mixed up with a similar person or company Quotes The meaning is close, but the words aren't the original's Math A middle step in a long calculation is wrong

docs.title: Three ways to check
docs.text:
1. Match it with the original. Find the number in the original source and see if it's the same. If you pasted in your own material, ask the chatbot to put the original sentence next to each number.

2. Make a rough estimate. First see if it's in the right ballpark. Say a chatbot tells you 20% of 330 million people. That should be around 66 million. If it says 6 million or 660 million, you know right away something is off.

3. Use a calculator or a spreadsheet for math. For exact math, a calculator is surer than a chatbot. Have the chatbot write the formula, and get the value from the tool. Some chatbots connect to tools and do math with them. (Part IV covers this.)

docs.title: Checking quotes
docs.text:
Words inside quotation marks seem to promise "these are the exact words." But a chatbot may remember the meaning roughly and put different words inside the quotes. Checking is simple.

  1. Pick the key words from the quote.
  2. Search for them in the original with Ctrl+F (Cmd+F on a Mac).
  3. If you can't find them, the quote may not be exact. (A scanned page or odd spacing can also block a search, so glance at the page too.)

Anthropic's guide gives a tip for long documents. First have the chatbot pull out the relevant sentences word for word. Then have it answer based only on those sentences. The quotes stay in the answer as evidence, which makes checking easy.

★ Going deeper

  • One reason chatbots struggle with numbers: they read numbers as tokens too (Chapter 1). A long number gets chopped into chunks. With one public tokenizer we tried, 7006652 became 700 665 2. That's not how people line up digits to do math. Karpathy's tokenizer lecture links some trouble with simple math to tokenization. Newer models do much better, but they can still slip on long calculations.
  • Anthropic's guide also describes "best-of-N" checking: send the same question several times and compare the answers. If a number changes each time, that's a reason for doubt. The next page covers this.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
What is 1234 × 5678? Show your work.

Check it on a calculator. (The answer is 7,006,652.) Did it get it right? If not, look through its steps to find where it went wrong. Then try this:

Just write the formula for this calculation. I'll work out the value
on a calculator.

Which of the two ways makes you feel surer?

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Ask for "the source sentence too" with every number. With the original sentence next to each number, checking is easy.
  2. Make rough estimates a habit. If the size is off, you'll catch it right away.
  3. Leave math to tools. Let the chatbot write the formula, and get the value from a calculator or spreadsheet.
  4. Find quoted sentences in the original. If you can't find one, don't use it as a quote.
  5. Check units and the year a number refers to. The same number can mean different things in different units or years.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "The more detailed the number, the more accurate it is." A number with lots of decimal places can still be wrong. Detail is not proof.
  • "If it shows its work, the answer is right." The steps can look fine and still go wrong in the middle. Check the value on its own.
  • "If it's in quotation marks, those are the exact words." You don't know until you check.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Anthropic, Reduce hallucinations, Claude Platform Docs. "Use direct quotes for factual grounding" and "Best-of-N verification." Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Andrej Karpathy, Let's build the GPT Tokenizer, YouTube, 2024-02-20. In the intro, he links trouble with simple arithmetic to tokenization (checked through Rosetta's unofficial, auto-generated transcript).
  • OpenAI, tiktoken. We split 7006652 with the o200k_base tokenizer ourselves on 2026-11-09.
  • Our earlier page on tokens: It reads text in small pieces called tokens.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: The table of error types is our own summary. Other chatbots use other tokenizers and may split numbers differently.

docs.title: How to check sources
docs.text:
Ch. 3 · 3.1About 5 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Check a source the chatbot gives you in three steps: Is it real? Does it say that? Can you trust it?
  • Asking for sources is good. But a chatbot can make up the sources too.
  • Don't stop at one place. Check somewhere else as well.

docs.title: When a friend says "I saw it online"
docs.text:
A friend says, "I read online that eating potatoes makes you taller." What do you do? You ask, "Where did you see that? Send me the link." And even with the link, you open it to see if it really says that, and who wrote it.

Do the same when a chatbot says "according to a study..." As Chapter 1 showed, it continues text with likely words. So it can make up a study or a link that looks real but doesn't exist.

In 10-year-old words

Ask three questions: "Where did you see it?" "Did you open it?" "Does anyone else say so?"

docs.title: Three steps to check
docs.text:
Step 1: Is it real?

  • Does the link open? For a book or paper, search the title and see if it really exists.
  • Do the author, year, and title match what the chatbot said?

Step 2: Does it say that?

  • Is the chatbot's claim really written in that source? Open it and search for a key word (Ctrl+F, or Cmd+F on a Mac).
  • Have any numbers or quotes been changed a little?

Step 3: Can you trust it?

  • Who wrote it? A research group, a government office, a news outlet, or one person's blog?
  • When was it written? The information may be out of date.
  • Do other trustworthy places say the same thing?

docs.title: Read sideways
docs.text: Researchers at Stanford, Sam Wineburg and Sarah McGrew, watched how people judge websites. Professional fact checkers did something different from the others. When they landed on a site they didn't know, they didn't read it top to bottom. They quickly left it, opened new tabs, and looked up who was behind it. The researchers called this lateral reading, or reading sideways. You can do the same with a source a chatbot gives you. Before you read on, search in another tab: "Who runs this, and can I trust them?"

docs.title: Make the chatbot show its evidence
docs.text:
Anthropic's guide to reducing hallucinations suggests a way to make answers easy to check. Have the chatbot attach a quote and a source to each claim. If it can't find a quote that backs a claim, it should take that claim back.

Answer using only the material below. After each claim, add the exact
sentence from the material that supports it, in quotation marks.
If you can't find support in the material, don't make the claim.
Write "not in the material" instead.
<material>
(paste here)
</material>

When it answers from material you pasted in, the source is right in front of you. That makes checking easy.

★ Going deeper

  • When a chatbot uses web search, the pages it pulls in become its evidence. But it can still sum them up wrong or quote the wrong part. Use the same three steps on search-powered chatbots too. Part IV covers search and tools.
  • Anthropic's guide lists ways to reduce hallucinations. It also says these methods lower hallucinations a lot but don't get rid of them. Always check important information.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Ask a chatbot this:

Give me 3 trustworthy sources about the nutrition of potatoes,
with titles and links.

Open each link and run the three steps: Is it real? Does it say that? Can you trust it? Did any link fail to open, or say something different? Count how many pass. That gives you a feel for how much to trust a chatbot's sources.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Always open the source. If it won't open, it may be made up. If it opens, you still need to check that it says what the chatbot claims.
  2. Find the key sentence in the original. With Ctrl+F (or Cmd+F), it takes seconds.
  3. Read new sources sideways. For a site you don't know, search its name in a new tab and find out who runs it.
  4. The more it matters, the more you read the original yourself. Use the chatbot as a guide that points you to the original.
  5. Check the date. If you need up-to-date facts, see when it was written.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "It has a link, so it's true." Even if the link opens, it may say something different from what the chatbot said.
  • "If I ask for sources, it won't make things up." It can make up the sources too. That's why you open them.
  • "If it's a famous site, I can trust it all." Famous sites can be wrong or out of date too. Look at who wrote it and when.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Sam Wineburg and Sarah McGrew, Lateral Reading: Reading Less and Learning More When Evaluating Digital Information, Stanford History Education Group working paper, SSRN, 2017-10-25. A shorter version appeared in Teachers College Record in 2019.
  • Anthropic, Reduce hallucinations, Claude Platform Docs. "Verify with citations," and the reminder to always check critical information. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: We confirmed the paper's title, authors, and date in the DOI record. We could not open the full paper from our work environment. Our description of lateral reading comes from summaries of the study, so it still needs checking against the paper itself. The three-step check is our own practical summary.

docs.title: Copyright and plagiarism
docs.text:
Ch. 3 · 3.2About 5 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Before you use text or images a chatbot made, think about who owns it, and whether it looks like someone else's work.
  • There are things to watch both when you paste in other people's work and when you put out the result.
  • Schools and workplaces may have their own rules about using AI.

Please note

This page is general information, not legal advice. Laws and government guidance change, and they differ from country to country. For anything important, check with an expert or the right office.

docs.title: Copying a friend's homework
docs.text:
You shouldn't copy a friend's homework word for word. Handing it in as your own is even worse. And if your teacher says, "You can use other work for ideas, but list your sources," you follow that rule.

Writing from a chatbot is similar. A chatbot learned from huge amounts of text, so what it writes may end up looking like something already out there. And where you're allowed to use the result depends on laws and rules.

In 10-year-old words

Before you copy a chatbot's writing into your homework, check twice. Does it look like someone else's work? Are you allowed to use it there?

docs.title: Three situations
docs.text:
1. When you paste in someone else's work

  • Pasting in a whole book, article, or someone else's report may break the service's rules or copyright.
  • Quote only the part you need. When you can, ask it to explain in its own words instead.

2. When you use what the chatbot made

  • Check that the result doesn't look too much like an existing work. Be extra careful if it resembles famous song lyrics, lines from a novel, or a well-known character. (Looking alike isn't always illegal. Courts weigh many things.)
  • If you'll use the text or images to make money, read the service's terms about how you may use outputs.

3. When you put your name on it

  • School assignments, contests, and research papers often have rules about whether AI is allowed and how to say you used it. Check the rules first.
  • Hiding AI use can get you in trouble. And even when the rules allow it, checking the facts is still your job (remember hallucination).

docs.title: What the US Copyright Office says
docs.text:
In January 2025, the US Copyright Office released Part 2 of its report on copyright and AI. It covers whether things made with AI can be protected by copyright. Here are the points most useful to everyday users.

  • AI output can be protected only where a human author decided enough of the creative parts.
  • That can include human work you can see in the output, or creative choices a human made in arranging or changing it. Just typing a prompt is not enough.
  • Using AI as a helper doesn't, on its own, stop your work from being protected. Neither does adding AI-made parts to a larger work you wrote.

This is the view of one US office. Other countries may see it differently.

★ Going deeper

  • Whether it's legal for AI to learn from copyrighted work (for example, under US "fair use") is still being argued in many countries. Court rulings and policies keep changing. The US Copyright Office released a pre-publication version of Part 3 of its report, on training AI, in May 2025.
  • For you as a user, one thing is clear for now. Until the legal questions settle, the person who uses the output carries much of the job of checking it and answering for it.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Ask a chatbot for 5 short ad slogans.
  2. Pick one you like. Search for it with quotation marks around the whole slogan, like "your slogan here."
  3. See whether a similar slogan is already in use.
  4. Find the part of your chatbot's terms of service about rights to outputs, and read it.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Search a sentence before you use it. It's the easiest way to see if a similar line or ad already exists.
  2. Ask for an explanation, not a copy. "Sum up the main idea of this article in your own words" is safer than "Write it just like this article."
  3. Check your school's or workplace's AI rules first. Learn what's allowed and how to note that you used AI.
  4. Make a habit of saying when you used AI. If needed, add a line like "AI was used to help draft this."
  5. For business use, read the terms. Each service has its own rules about using outputs.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "AI made it, so nobody owns it." It depends on the country and the situation. A key question is how much creative work a human did.
  • "I only asked for it, so I'm not responsible." The person who puts out the result needs to check it.
  • "If I change a few words, it's not plagiarism." It depends on how close it is and on the rules. Copying something and tweaking it can still be a problem.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • US Copyright Office, Copyright Office Releases Part 2 of Artificial Intelligence Report, NewsNet Issue 1060, 2025-01-29.
  • US Copyright Office, Copyright and Artificial Intelligence (the report's main page, which lists Part 1 from 2024-07-31, Part 2 from 2025-01-29, and the Part 3 pre-publication version from 2025-05-09). Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: We read the Copyright Office's announcement and report page, not the full report. We didn't give specific legal judgments because the law in this area changes quickly and differs by country.

docs.title: Personal and sensitive information
docs.text:
Ch. 3 · 3.2About 5 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Typing into an online chatbot means sending what you type to the company that runs it. (A model that runs only on your own computer is different.)
  • Blank out personal details, like names, phone numbers, and account numbers, and keep work secrets out.
  • How your chats are used depends on the service and your settings, so you have to check.

Please note

This page is general information, not legal advice. Your workplace or school may have its own rules, and those come first.

docs.title: Writing on a postcard
docs.text:
Anyone who handles a postcard can read it, mail carriers included. To keep a message private, you put it in an envelope.

Typing into a chatbot is a bit like writing a postcard. If it's an online service, your words don't stay on your computer. They travel to the company's servers. (A model that runs only on your own computer is different.) How the company stores and uses them depends on the service and your settings.

In 10-year-old words

Typing into a chatbot is a lot like writing on a postcard. Before you write, cover up anything that would be a problem if someone else saw it.

docs.title: What to blank out
docs.text: Kind Examples Things that identify you Name, phone number, home address, Social Security number, bank account number, photos of your face Sensitive details Health conditions, medical history, religion, political views, sex life Other people's details Names and private situations of friends, customers, or coworkers Work information Plans that aren't public yet, customer lists, code, contracts Login details Passwords, verification codes, API keys

docs.title: How to blank things out
docs.text:
1. Change the names. "Jordan Smith" becomes "Person A." "123 Oak Street, Springfield" becomes "a house in a small town."
  2. Hide the numbers. Delete account numbers and ID numbers completely. Keep amounts only if the question needs them.
  3. Paste only what you need. Don't paste a whole document. Pick the paragraph your question is about.
  4. Ask about the general situation. Instead of "our customer Jordan at Acme Corp," try "a customer who complained about this."
In the text below, find personal details such as names, phone numbers,
addresses, and account numbers. Rewrite the text with them replaced by
[Name1], [Phone1], and so on. Don't list what you replaced.

(Be careful: if you ask a chatbot to do the blanking, you've already sent it the original. When you can, blank things out yourself.)

docs.title: Check how your chats are used
docs.text:
How a service handles what you type depends on the company, your plan, and your settings. Look in your app's settings and privacy policy for answers to these questions:

  • Are my chats used to improve the model? Can I turn that off?
  • How long are my chats kept?
  • What happens when I delete a chat?
  • If I use a work account, can my employer see my chats?

★ Going deeper

  • Regulators are paying attention. In September 2025, the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) opened an inquiry into seven companies whose chatbots act like companions. One thing it asked was how they use or share personal information from users' chats.
  • On the training side, researchers have shown that a model can sometimes repeat text from its training data word for word. A 2020 study by Nicholas Carlini and others pulled hundreds of exact pieces of text out of GPT-2, including some people's names and contact details. This is why "Does the service train on my chats?" is an important question. Policies differ from service to service, so it's hard to say one thing about all of them.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Pick one message you sent, or plan to send, to a chatbot. Check it like this:

  1. Use the table above. Does it contain any of those kinds of details?
  2. If it does, blank them out (change names, delete numbers) and rewrite it.
  3. Does the blanked version still get you the answer you want? Most of the time it does.
  4. Open your app's settings and find the option about how your chats are used.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Pause before you hit send. Ask yourself: "Would I be okay writing this on a postcard?"
  2. Ask with blanked text, then fill in the real details yourself. For example, write "Person A," and after you get the draft, swap in the real name.
  3. For work, check your workplace's rules first. If your workplace has an approved AI tool, use that one.
  4. Be extra careful with other people's details. You decide about your own information. Other people's information may need their permission.
  5. Never paste passwords or keys. When you paste code, make sure no keys are hiding in it.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "Only I can see my chats." How the company stores and uses them differs by service. Check the settings and the privacy policy.
  • "If I delete it, it's gone for good." Deletion rules differ by service. There may be a storage period or exceptions.
  • "If I blank things out, I can't really ask." Even with details hidden, you can get most of the help you need.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • US Federal Trade Commission, FTC Launches Inquiry into AI Chatbots Acting as Companions, press release, 2025-09-11.
  • Nicholas Carlini and others, Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models, arXiv, 2020-12-14.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: Privacy laws differ by country and state. We didn't list each service's storage and training policies because they keep changing. Check your own app's current settings.

docs.title: Get a second opinion
docs.text:
Ch. 3 · 3.1About 5 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • For answers that matter, don't trust a single try. Get a second opinion.
  • You can ask again, have it check its own answer, ask for the other side, or check somewhere else.
  • Two answers can agree and both be wrong. So the bigger the job, the more checking you do.

docs.title: Seeing a second doctor
docs.text:
When a doctor tells someone they have a serious illness, many people see a second doctor. The news is too important to rest on one person's word.

The same goes for chatbot answers. The more it matters, the more a second opinion helps. As Chapter 1 showed, a chatbot draws its answer from a score table, so the same question can get different answers. Where the answers differ is a clue.

In 10-year-old words

For anything important, check one more time, the way you'd see a second doctor. The bigger the deal, the more you check.

docs.title: Ways to get a second opinion
docs.text:
1. Ask the same question again. Ask the same question two or three times, each in a new chat, and compare. If the answers disagree on something, be extra careful about that part. Anthropic's guide calls this "best-of-N" checking. It says answers that don't match could be a sign of hallucination.

2. Have it check an answer. Paste the earlier answer back in and ask the chatbot to check it. The guide says that using an answer as the input for a follow-up question can catch things that don't add up.

In the answer below, find any facts that are wrong or weakly supported,
and list them. Mark anything you're not sure about as "needs checking."
<answer>
(paste the earlier answer)
</answer>

3. Ask for the other side. Try "Give me the three strongest arguments against this claim." It helps you notice an answer that leans one way.

4. Check somewhere else. Ask a different chatbot, search the web, read official pages or a book, or ask an expert.

docs.title: Match the checking to the size of the job
docs.text:
How big is the job? How to check Small (ideas, polishing tone) Read it once and use it Medium (work emails, report drafts) Ask again, and check a few key facts Important (money, contracts, schoolwork you hand in) Check the original sources and a second source Serious (health, law, safety) Always check with an expert in that field

★ Going deeper

  • Two answers can agree and both be wrong. Different chatbots may have learned from similar text, so they can be wrong in the same way. Getting the same answer several times doesn't make it right. Mix in a different kind of evidence, like the original source or an official page.
  • Telling you what you want to hear. In 2023, Anthropic researchers (Mrinank Sharma and others) tested five AI assistants trained with human feedback. All five tended to shape their answers to match what the user seemed to believe, instead of what was true. This is called sycophancy. The researchers found that people rating answers often preferred ones that agreed with them, which may be part of the cause. So if you ask "I'm right, aren't I?", it may just agree.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Try this with a chatbot.

1. (A claim you believe) is true, right? Tell me I'm right.

2. Give me 3 reasons (the same claim) is true and 3 reasons it might not be.
   At the end, tell me which side is more convincing, and why.

Compare the two answers. Did it agree with you easily in the first one? What changed in the second?

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Instead of "I'm right, aren't I?", ask for reasons on both sides. That kind of question makes it less likely to just agree.
  2. For answers that matter, ask again in a new chat. A fresh chat gives you a more independent second opinion than asking again in the same chat.
  3. Check only the parts that disagree. Don't try to check everything. Start where the answers differ.
  4. Decide the size of the job first. If you set your checking level ahead of time, like in the table above, you won't wear yourself out.
  5. For serious matters, check with a person. For health, law, and safety, use the chatbot's answer only as a starting point.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "Another chatbot said the same thing, so it's right." They can be wrong the same way. Check the original or an official source too.
  • "If I tell it to check itself, it'll catch everything." It helps, but it's not perfect. Use it to find the spots a person should check.
  • "Asking several times costs too much." Do it only for things that matter. Step up your checking as the job gets bigger.

docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Anthropic, Reduce hallucinations, Claude Platform Docs. "Best-of-N verification" and "Iterative refinement." Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Mrinank Sharma and others, Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models, arXiv, 2023-10-20 (revised 2025-05-10). Also on Anthropic's site: Towards understanding sycophancy in language models, 2023-10-23. We summarized the abstract.

docs.title: Ch. 4 Which AI Should You Pick?
docs.text:
There are so many AI tools it gets confusing. Sort them into kinds and pick the right one for your job.

4.1.1Chat, search, image, voice: the kinds of AI5 min read 4.1.2What changes between free and paid?5 min read 4.1.3Pick the AI that fits your work5 min read

docs.title: Pick the AI that fits your work
docs.text:
Ch. 4 · 4.1About 5 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • When choosing a tool, don't start with the brand name. Start with the job you want done.
  • Narrow down your choices with four questions: what kind of job, how exact, how sensitive, and how often.
  • Once you pick, test it on your real work, and check again now and then.

docs.title: Picking shoes
docs.text:
You wear different shoes for a walk, a run, or a hike. The best shoes aren't the most expensive ones. They're the ones that fit what you're about to do.

AI is the same. What you're going to do matters more than which service is famous.

In 10-year-old words

Before asking "Which one is best?", ask "What am I going to do with it?"

docs.title: Four questions
docs.text:
1. What kind of job is it? Writing, research, getting organized, pictures, or code? (See the table of kinds on the earlier page.)

2. How exact does it need to be? Ideas can be a bit off. Numbers, law, and medicine must be checked. The more accuracy matters, the more you need search, sources, and a human check.

3. How sensitive is it? If personal details or work secrets are involved, data settings and rules decide your choice. (See the privacy page in 3.2.)

4. How often will you do it? For a one-off, almost anything works. For a daily job, usage limits, reliability, and a way to save templates matter.

docs.title: Where to start, by job
docs.text: Job Look at first Polishing writing, first drafts A text chatbot. Paste in your own material Recent news, fact checks A tool with search, and open the sources Reading long documents A feature for uploading long files, and its limits Numbers and tables Check the math separately with a tool Pictures An image tool, and read its terms on copyright Work tasks The tools your workplace has approved, and data settings

docs.title: How to test
docs.text:
1. Give the same job to two tools. Use the job you do most often, so the test means something.
  2. Compare with a checklist. Note accuracy, tone, sources, speed, and anything annoying.
  3. Look for mistakes on purpose. Is anything wrong? When it's wrong, does it admit it?
  4. Once you decide, check again in about a month. (That's our suggestion.) Services change fast.
[Test job]
The job I do most often: ___
The result I expect: ___
What to check: Are the facts right? Is the tone right? How long did it take?

★ Going deeper

  • Anthropic's guide to choosing a model says to set your needs first, then confirm with real tests. It's written for developers, but it works for everyone. The needs are capabilities, speed, and cost. The tests should use examples that look like your real work.
  • Public score charts (benchmarks) are useful to glance at, but whether they match your work is another question. Part VI covers the limits of benchmarks.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Pick one job you do often and fill this in:

  1. Kind of job:
  2. How exact it needs to be (low / medium / high):
  3. Does it include sensitive information?
  4. How many times a week you do it:

Use your answers and the "Where to start, by job" table to pick a first choice. Then use that choice for the same job for a week.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Decide the job first, then the tool. If you do it the other way around, you end up bending your work to fit the tool.
  2. For jobs that must be exact, plan your checking too. Use the checking methods from Chapter 3.
  3. For work, start with approved tools. Privacy and secrets come first when you choose.
  4. Test with your real work. Someone else's examples may not look like your job.
  5. Check in once a month. A better tool may appear, or a feature you use may change.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "What everyone uses must be the best." What matters is whether it fits your work.
  • "Once I pick, I'm set for good." Services change, and so does your work. Check now and then.
  • "Number one on the score chart means number one for my job." Score charts measure different problems from yours.

docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Anthropic, Choosing the right model, Claude Platform Docs. Set your criteria first, then test with your own prompts and data. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09

docs.title: What changes between free and paid?
docs.text:
Ch. 4 · 4.1About 5 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Free and paid plans usually differ in how much you can use, which models you get, and which features. (Data settings differ by service and plan, so check those separately.)
  • Decide by asking whether your work actually needs what paid adds.
  • Prices and features change often, so check the service's own pages each time you decide.

Please note

We don't list prices or plan names on this page. Plans change so often that they'd be out of date the moment we printed them. Instead, here are ways to compare that won't go stale.

docs.title: An amusement park pass
docs.text:
At an amusement park, a basic ticket gets you on a few rides. A day pass lets you skip some lines and ride more. Some rides still cost extra, even with the pass.

Chatbots are similar. The free version is plenty for a lot of people. If you use it a lot, or for harder work, paying can help. But paid isn't always more accurate. Hallucinations and limits are still there when you pay.

In 10-year-old words

The difference between free and paid is how much you can do, and how big a job you can do. First ask whether your work needs that.

docs.title: Five things to compare
docs.text: Compare Questions to ask How much you can use How many messages per day or per few hours? What happens when I hit the limit? Models Can I use bigger, smarter models? How fast are they? Features Can it search the web, read uploaded files, make images, talk by voice, handle long documents? Data settings Can I stop my chats from being used for training? With a work account, can admins see my chats? Reliability Does it slow down or stop when lots of people are using it? Is there customer support?

docs.title: When paid makes sense, and when it doesn't
docs.text:
Times to think about paying

  • You use it a lot every day and keep hitting the free limit.
  • You need more than the free limit allows, like often uploading long documents to analyze.
  • Work depends on it, so speed and reliability matter.
  • You use it for work and need data protection settings. (A personal paid plan does not by itself protect company data. Check your workplace's approval and business plans first.)

Times free is enough

  • You ask questions now and then, or polish your writing.
  • You're still learning how to use it. (How you ask often makes a bigger difference.)
  • You'll check the results yourself anyway.

docs.title: How to decide
docs.text:
1. Use the free version for a week first. Write down which jobs hit the limit.
  2. Look at what got blocked. Were the jobs you couldn't finish actually important?
  3. Try paid for one month at a time. For a subscription, find out how to cancel before you start.
  4. Check that it helps. Give the same job to the free and paid versions, and compare.

★ Going deeper

  • Anthropic's guide to choosing a model says to balance capabilities, speed, and cost, and then to test your choice on your real work. It's written for developers, but the same idea works for everyone. The biggest model isn't always best. For simple jobs, a smaller, faster model can fit better.
  • Some services let you pick the model yourself. You can use a small model for easy questions and a big one for hard reasoning.
  • Developers who use a model through an API usually pay by the token. That's where the tokens from Chapter 1 turn into money.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Keep a use log for one week.

Date What you asked for Hit the limit? Happy with the result?

After a week, count the days when you hit the limit and the job mattered. That number is your reason to think about paying.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Decide about paying by looking at your log. If you decide by feel, you end up with subscriptions you don't use.
  2. Compare with the same question. Ask the free and paid versions (or two different services) the exact same thing and see the difference.
  3. For work, check your workplace's policy first. Using a personal plan with company material may break the rules.
  4. Read the data section of the terms. Different plans can have different data rules.
  5. Check the official pricing page yourself. Prices in blog posts and videos may be out of date.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "Paid means no hallucinations." Paid versions get things wrong too. You still need the checking habit.
  • "The expensive model is better at everything." For some jobs, a small, fast model is the better fit.
  • "Free is useless." Free is enough for many jobs. Learning how to ask comes first.

docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Anthropic, Choosing the right model, Claude Platform Docs. Balancing capabilities, speed, and cost, and testing with your own prompts and data. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: The five things to compare are our own list. We didn't write down any service's plans or limits. "Usually pay by the token" is a general statement, not true of every service.

docs.title: Chat, search, image, voice: the kinds of AI
docs.text:
Ch. 4 · 4.1About 5 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • You can sort the tools called "AI" by what goes in and what comes out.
  • Text chatbots, search chatbots, image and voice tools, and coding helpers are each good at different jobs.
  • Knowing the kinds makes it easier to pick the right tool, and to know what to doubt when it slips.

docs.title: A toolbox
docs.text:
A hammer, a screwdriver, and a tape measure are all "tools," but they do different jobs. You wouldn't use a screwdriver on a nail.

"AI" is one name for many tools that do different things. Look at what you put in (the input) and what comes out (the output), and it gets easier to tell them apart.

In 10-year-old words

AI is a toolbox. Look at what goes in and what comes out, and you can tell which tool it is.

docs.title: Sorting the kinds
docs.text:
Kind What goes in → what comes out Good for Watch out for Text chatbot Text → text Writing, explaining, ideas, translating Hallucination, missing recent news Chatbot with search Question → an answer from web results, with sources Recent news, questions where facts need checking It can sum up sources wrong Image maker Text (or a photo) → picture Illustrations, mock-ups, idea sketches Hands or lettering can look odd; copyright Voice Speech → speech Asking and listening out loud, interpreting, transcribing Hearing words wrong; privacy Coding helper A description or code → code Writing programs, finding bugs You must run the code to check it Agent A goal → it carries out several steps on its own Handing off multi-step jobs Small mistakes can pile up (Part IV)

This table is a rough way to sort things, to help you understand. These days, one service often offers several of these kinds together.

docs.title: Coming together
docs.text:
Karpathy's intro talk on large language models describes where they are heading. They handle more than text, like images and sound, and they use tools, like web browsing and a calculator. That's why you can now upload a photo, ask about it, get an answer from a web search, and get a table back, all in one chatbot.

But the same service can offer different features depending on your plan and the date. Check for yourself what the service you use can do right now.

★ Going deeper

  • A model that handles text, images, and sound together is called multimodal. One way it works: images get cut into pieces like tokens and read alongside the text. Once you learn about tokens and embeddings in Part III, this gets easier to follow.
  • Many image makers don't work by picking the next word. A common method starts from noise and cleans it up step by step until a picture appears. Researchers are also building models that make text and images together. This book focuses on text chatbots.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Write down 5 things you asked an AI to do in the past week. Then, for each one, decide which kind from the table you used.

  • Did you ask for something that needed a search, using a chatbot with no search?
  • Did you leave something that had to be exact to a chatbot alone?

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Ask about recent events with a tool that can search. A regular chatbot may not know what happened after it was trained.
  2. Treat AI pictures as drafts, and check any text or numbers in them yourself. Lettering inside images is easy to get wrong.
  3. Always run code before you trust it. Code from a coding helper can be wrong too.
  4. Read the feature list of the service you use, once. There may be features you've never tried because you didn't know about them.
  5. Don't try to do everything with one tool. Pick the right tool for each job.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "AI is all the same AI." Each kind is good at different things, and goes wrong in different ways.
  • "If it has search, it's always right." Search helps, but it can still sum up what it found the wrong way.
  • "Image AI guesses the next word, like a text chatbot." Different tools make things in different ways.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Andrej Karpathy, [1hr Talk] Intro to Large Language Models, YouTube, 2023-11-23. Chapters "Tool Use (Browser, Calculator, Interpreter, DALL-E)" (00:27:43) and "Multimodality (Vision, Audio)" (00:33:32), checked through Rosetta's unofficial, auto-generated chapter list and transcript. We could not watch the video ourselves.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: The table of kinds is our own. We left out product names and feature lists because they change fast. The note on how image makers work is a general overview without a specific source.

docs.title: II Put AI to Work
docs.text:
How to use AI for writing, research, and getting organized. Practical tips you can use right away.

Ch. 5AI for Writing3/3 written Ch. 6AI for Research and Study3/3 written Ch. 7AI for Notes and Numbers3/3 written Ch. 8Make It Part of How You Work3/3 written

docs.title: Ch. 5 AI for Writing
docs.text:
Using AI for first drafts, rewrites, and summaries.

5.1.1Get a first draft5 min read 5.1.2Rewrite and change the tone5 min read 5.1.3Summarize5 min read

docs.title: Get a first draft
docs.text:
Ch. 5 · 5.1About 5 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • When you're stuck staring at a blank page, AI is great for quickly making a rough first draft.
  • The order: decide your main points, get an outline, draft each paragraph, then fix it by hand.
  • A draft is just a draft. Checking facts and writing the final version are your job.

docs.title: Make the dough first
docs.text:
When you bake bread, you can't shape a pretty loaf right away. First you make the dough, and then you shape it. Writing works the same way. The first sentence on a blank page is the hardest one.

AI can make that dough fast. Don't expect a finished piece. Think of it as getting something to fix, quickly. That takes the pressure off.

One experiment backs this up. In a 2023 study in the journal Science, 453 college-educated professionals did writing tasks from their own kinds of jobs. Half of them got to use ChatGPT. For that half, the average time dropped by 40%, and the quality scores went up by 18%. But this was an online experiment with mid-level work writing. It doesn't promise the same results for your work.

In 10-year-old words

AI is a helper that makes the dough fast. You do the shaping.

docs.title: Four steps
docs.text:
Step 1: You decide the main points. You need to know what you want to say. Write down three main points yourself.

Step 2: Get the outline first. Don't ask for the full text right away. Ask for an outline.

[Goal] A weekly note to my team.
[Main points] 1) Friday's meeting moves to Monday 2) Next week's deadline
stays the same 3) Share your files by Thursday
[Readers] 8 coworkers on my team, all busy
First, suggest an outline of 3 paragraphs or fewer. Don't write it yet.

Step 3: Get a draft paragraph by paragraph. If you like the outline, have it write one paragraph at a time, or the whole draft.

Step 4: Fix it by hand. Change it to sound like you, check the facts, and write the last sentence yourself.

docs.title: Keep your own voice
docs.text:
AI drafts tend to sound like "anyone could have written this." To keep your voice, give it something you wrote as a sample (the "example" from Chapter 2).

Here's something I wrote before. Use its tone and sentence length
as a guide for the draft.
<my writing>
(paste here)
</my writing>

★ Going deeper

  • In the same study, the gap between workers also shrank: people who were weaker writers got more help. The researchers reported that inequality between workers went down. It's hard to say whether this lasts, or holds for other jobs.
  • When AI makes your draft, you may think less carefully about the content than when you write it yourself. This isn't a research finding. It's our own word of caution. For writing that matters, don't hand off the step of deciding your main points.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Pick one thing you need to write this week, like an email, an announcement, or a short bio.

  1. Write your three main points yourself.
  2. Use the template above to get an outline.
  3. Once you like the outline, get a draft.
  4. Change at least three spots to sound like you, and check the facts.

Compare how long it would have taken if you'd written it all yourself.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Decide the main points yourself. If AI picks them too, the result tends to fill up with ordinary ideas.
  2. Get the outline first. If the direction is wrong, you can fix it early.
  3. Paste in your own writing as a sample. The tone gets much closer to yours.
  4. Add "leave it blank if you don't know" to draft requests. Have it mark gaps like [number here]. That helps cut down on made-up numbers. (That's our tip.)
  5. Read the final version out loud. You'll hear the awkward sentences right away.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "I can send the AI draft as is." Skipping the fact check and the voice fix is risky.
  • "People can always tell AI wrote it." With a sample and clear context, it shows much less.
  • "Only people who can't write use AI." In the study, all kinds of people saved time. It's just a tool.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Shakked Noy and Whitney Zhang, Experimental evidence on the productivity effects of generative artificial intelligence, Science, 2023-07-14. The 453 people, 40% less time, and 18% higher quality come from the abstract.
  • Anthropic, Prompting best practices, Claude Platform Docs. Giving examples and context. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: We read only the abstract, not the full study. The tool in the study was ChatGPT as of 2023. The four steps are our own summary.

docs.title: Rewrite and change the tone
docs.text:
Ch. 5 · 5.1About 5 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • One of the jobs AI helps with most reliably is polishing something you already wrote.
  • Always say: "keep the meaning the same, and don't add facts."
  • Ask it to show what it changed, so checking is easy.

docs.title: A change of clothes
docs.text:
The same person wears different clothes to a job interview and to a picnic. In the same way, the same message needs different clothes for different readers. An apology to a client should be polite. A text to a friend can be casual.

Rewriting is safer than drafting, because the content already comes from you. That leaves less room for the hallucinations from Chapter 1. Still, while polishing, it can quietly change or add something.

In 10-year-old words

Keep the message the same and just change its clothes. The body inside shouldn't change while you're changing the outfit.

docs.title: Kinds of rewriting
docs.text: What you want What to say Spelling and grammar only "Fix only spelling and grammar. Don't change the sentences." Easier to read "Break up long sentences and use simpler words. Keep the meaning." A different tone "Make it polite and professional, with the same meaning." Shorter "Cut it in half without losing the meaning." A different mood "Make it warmer, not cold. Keep the facts the same."

docs.title: Two safety lines to always add
docs.text:
When you ask for a rewrite, make a habit of adding these two lines.

Don't change the meaning, and don't add any facts or numbers that aren't
in the original. List what you changed in the form [original → new].

With a list of changes, you can see at a glance what's different. That makes sneaky changes easy to catch.

docs.title: Keep your own voice
docs.text:
If you want a certain tone, a sample works faster than a description (Chapter 2).

Rewrite the "original" in the style of the "sample." Follow the sample's
sentence length, word choice, and mood. Don't change the content.
<sample>(something I wrote)</sample>
<original>(the text to fix)</original>

★ Going deeper

  • Why does AI sometimes shift the meaning while rewriting? Because rewriting is still "picking the next word." It looks at your sentences and picks new ones that mean about the same thing. Small differences can creep in. Numbers, negatives ("did not"), and words of degree ("almost," "always") are the easiest to change by accident.
  • So put the rewrite next to the original and check those three first: numbers, negatives, and words of degree.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Pick something you wrote lately, like one paragraph of an email or report.

  1. Ask it to make the text easier to read, and add the two safety lines.
  2. Use the list of changes to compare with the original.
  3. Check whether anything that shouldn't change did change, like numbers, promises, or negatives.

Did anything change? If so, what kind of thing was it?

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Add "keep the meaning, don't add facts" by default. That one line prevents a lot of trouble.
  2. Get a list of changes. Knowing what changed makes checking easy.
  3. Check numbers, negatives, and words of degree on their own. They can flip the meaning.
  4. Get versions for different readers. Ask for "a version for my boss" and "a version for a friend" at once, and compare.
  5. For writing that matters, read the final version yourself. Once you send it, it's yours.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "Rewriting is safe, so I don't need to check." It's on the safer side, but numbers or negatives can still change.
  • "If I describe the tone, it'll get it right." A sample is more precise.
  • "AI is perfect at spelling." It usually does well, but it can get names or technical terms wrong.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Anthropic, Prompting best practices, Claude Platform Docs. Specific instructions, and using examples as samples. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: "Numbers, negatives, and words of degree change easily" is common experience. We did not find a study that measures it directly. The table of rewriting kinds is our own.

docs.title: Summarize
docs.text:
Ch. 5 · 5.1About 5 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Summarizing is one of the most common AI jobs. But things that aren't in the original can slip in.
  • Set the reader, the length, and what to keep (numbers, dates), and you get a useful summary.
  • Check the summary against the original. For long text, summarize in parts, then combine.

docs.title: The blurb on the back of a book
docs.text:
Have you ever bought a book because of the blurb on the back, then found the book was about something else? A summary passes the content along to someone who hasn't read the original. If the summary is wrong, that person ends up believing something wrong.

AI summarizes fast. But as Chapter 1 showed, it continues text with likely words. So words that aren't in the original can slip in.

In 10-year-old words

A summary is like the blurb on the back of a book. It shouldn't say anything the book doesn't.

docs.title: What to set when you ask for a summary
docs.text:
Summarize the text below.
- Reader: my manager, who hasn't read it
- Goal: to see what we need to decide at the meeting
- Length: 5 sentences or fewer
- Must keep: numbers, dates, and the names of who's in charge
- Don't add anything that isn't in the original. If the original is
  unsure about something, say it's unsure.
<text>
(paste here)
</text>
What to set Why Reader Different readers care about different parts Goal A summary for making a decision differs from one for understanding Length If you don't set it, you get an in-between length What to keep Numbers and dates are easy to change while summarizing

docs.title: Summarizing long text
docs.text:
Very long text is hard to summarize in one go. Anthropic's guide gives tips for long documents (20,000 tokens or more). Put the long material at the top, and put your question and instructions at the end. The guide says that in its tests, putting the question at the end improved answers by up to 30%. It also suggests asking Claude to first pull out the relevant parts as exact quotes, then do the task. That helps it focus on what matters and ignore the rest.

You can also summarize in parts.

  1. Split the text by chapter or section.
  2. Summarize each part on its own.
  3. Put the part summaries together and make one overall summary.

docs.title: Checking a summary
docs.text:
What to check How Anything that isn't in the original? For each summary sentence, find the sentence in the original that backs it up Are numbers and dates right? Put them side by side with the original Anything important missing? Skim the original's headings and first sentences and compare Did the tone shift? Check that "might be" didn't turn into "is" 
For each sentence in the summary above, add the sentence from the
original that supports it, in quotation marks. If you can't find
support, mark that sentence "no support."

★ Going deeper

  • A 2023 study by Nelson Liu and others, called "Lost in the Middle," found that models did worst when the key information sat in the middle of a long input. They did best when it was at the beginning or end. Anthropic's docs also describe context rot: accuracy drops as text grows. So splitting long text into parts is often the safer choice.
  • Researchers also study hallucinations in summaries. A summary has one big advantage: the original is right there, so it's easy to check. Chapter 21 covers how hallucinations are measured.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Pick an article or report and ask for two summaries.

  1. "Summarize this in 3 lines."
  2. The template above (with reader, goal, length, and what to keep).

Check both against the original. Which one had more things that weren't in the original? Were the numbers right?

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Save a summary template. It has four slots: reader, goal, length, and what to keep.
  2. Add "don't add anything that isn't in the original." One line saves a lot of trouble.
  3. Put the long text on top and your question at the bottom. That's what the guide recommends.
  4. Check every summary against the original at least once. Especially numbers and dates.
  5. Check with "add the supporting sentence." Be suspicious of any sentence marked "no support."

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "The original is right there, so the summary can't be wrong." Even with the original, made-up words can slip in.
  • "The shorter the summary, the better." Too short, and key numbers and conditions drop out.
  • "I can paste in long text all at once." Accuracy can drop as text grows, so splitting it up often works better.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Anthropic, Prompting best practices, Claude Platform Docs. The section "Long context prompting": long data at the top, the question at the end, and pulling out quotes first. "Up to 30 percent" is the guide's own test result. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Nelson F. Liu and others, Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts, arXiv, 2023-07-06. We summarized the abstract.
  • Anthropic, Context windows, Claude Platform Docs. Context rot. Read on 2026-11-09.

docs.title: Ch. 6 AI for Research and Study
docs.text:
Using AI to get your bearings in a new field, read long documents, and study.

6.1.1Get to know a new field fast5 min read 6.1.2Read and sort out long documents5 min read 6.1.3Use it as a study buddy5 min read

docs.title: Read and sort out long documents
docs.text:
Ch. 6 · 6.1About 6 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • For long reports, papers, or contracts, decide your question first, and have it pull out the supporting sentences before it sums things up.
  • Put the material on top and your question at the bottom.
  • The longer the text, the more AI can miss in the middle. So split it up or check the evidence.

docs.title: Finding a book in a big library
docs.text:
If you walk into a library and say "Look into these books," you won't know where to start. If you say "Find the parts about the history of the potato," you can go straight to them.

Long documents work the same way. "Sort this out" is vague, so you get an ordinary summary. Once you decide what you want to know, you get something useful.

In 10-year-old words

When you hand it a long book, first tell it what to look for.

docs.title: Four steps
docs.text:
Step 1: Decide your question. Write down in a sentence or two what you want to learn from the material.

Step 2: Material on top, question at the bottom. Anthropic's guide says to put long material (20,000 tokens or more) near the top of your prompt and your question and instructions at the end. It says that in its tests, putting the question at the end improved answers by up to 30%.

Step 3: Pull out supporting sentences first. For long documents, the guide suggests having Claude first quote the relevant parts word for word. That helps it focus on what matters.

Step 4: Sum up. Have it answer using only the quotes it pulled out.

<material>
(the full report)
</material>

Read the material above and answer this question.
Question: What are the three biggest risks in this plan?
Steps: 1) First, quote the sentences from the material that relate to
the question, word for word, and number them.
2) Then answer using only those numbered quotes.
If a quote can't back something up, don't write it. Say "not in the material."

docs.title: Comparing several documents
docs.text:
When there are several documents, give each one a label so they don't get mixed up. Anthropic's guide shows wrapping each document in its own tag, along with where it came from.

<document index="1" source="2025 business plan">...</document>
<document index="2" source="2026 business plan">...</document>
Make a table of what changed between the two documents. Next to each item,
say which document and which sentence it comes from.

docs.title: The longer the text, the more care it needs
docs.text:
One 2023 study tested the models of that time. They did much worse when the key information sat in the middle of a long text. Today's models have likely improved, but it's hard to say the problem is completely gone. So for things that matter, check like this:

  • Ask in parts. Asking about each chapter on its own means less gets missed.
  • Check the supporting sentences. Find them in the original yourself.
  • Ask the same question with the documents in a different order. If the answer changes, it needs checking.

★ Going deeper

  • Another way to handle long documents is to cut them into chunks and pull in only the chunks you need. This is called retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Part IV covers it.
  • When you upload a file, it may be turned into text. A PDF may be handled as both page images and text. (This differs by service and file type.) Tables and charts can get scrambled along the way, so check the results against the original when tables matter.
  • Anthropic's docs say that even with a big context window, accuracy can drop as the text gets longer (context rot). Choosing what goes in matters more than stuffing in as much as you can.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Pick a long text, like a report of 10 pages or more, or a set of articles.

  1. First, ask "Summarize this" and get a summary.
  2. Then pick one question and use the "supporting sentences first" template above.
  3. Compare the two. Which one helped more with your question? Were the supporting sentences really in the original?

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Start by writing your question in one sentence. You'll likely get better results than with "sort this out."
  2. Material on top, question at the bottom. Just changing the order can make a difference.
  3. Get numbered supporting sentences. They make checking easy.
  4. For contracts and legal papers, use AI only to flag risks. Leave the final call to an expert, or read it yourself.
  5. Blank out personal and secret details before you upload. Chapter 3 covers this.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "If I upload a long document, it understands all of it." The longer it is, the more it can miss.
  • "Reading the summary is enough." For important decisions, read the relevant parts of the original.
  • "I gave it the document, so it won't make things up." Material helps, but it doesn't stop made-up answers completely. Check with the supporting sentences.

docs.text:

  • Anthropic, Prompting best practices, Claude Platform Docs. The section "Long context prompting": material on top, question at the end, quotes first, and structuring several documents. "Up to 30 percent" is the guide's own test result. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Nelson F. Liu and others, Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts, arXiv, 2023-07-06. We summarized the abstract.
  • Anthropic, Context windows, Claude Platform Docs. Context rot. Read on 2026-11-09.
