docs.title: Get to know a new field fast
docs.text:
Ch. 6 · 6.1About 5 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • To get the hang of a new field fast, start with a map of the big picture and a list of key words.
  • AI's beginner explanations are simplified and can be wrong. Use them as a map, and find evidence elsewhere.
  • Finish with a list of questions to ask next, so you keep learning on your own.

docs.title: A map of a new city
docs.text:
When you visit a new city, you look at a map first. Once you roughly know where things are, you won't get lost in the side streets.

A new field is the same. If you jump straight into expert material, it's full of words you don't know, and you get tired fast. AI is good at quickly drawing a map of the whole field and a list of key terms. But the map isn't always right, so check it as you go.

In 10-year-old words

Ask AI to draw you a map of the new city. Then walk around and check that the map is right.

docs.title: Five steps to get the lay of the land
docs.text:
Step 1: One easy paragraph. Ask for an explanation "in one paragraph, as if to a grade schooler." That gives you the big picture.

Step 2: Ten key words. Get the 10 terms that come up most in this field, each with a simple explanation.

Step 3: A map. Ask for the smaller areas inside the field and how they connect, laid out so you can see them at a glance.

Step 4: Mix-ups and debates. Ask what beginners often get wrong, and where experts disagree.

Step 5: Where to go next. Ask what kinds of material to read to go deeper, and which questions to ask.

I'm a [job / grade] and I'm brand new to [field]. Tell me, in this order:
1) A one-paragraph explanation a grade schooler could follow
2) The 10 most common terms, with a one-line explanation each
3) A map of the smaller areas in this field (a table or a list)
4) 3 common beginner mix-ups, and the questions experts disagree on
5) 5 questions to ask as I learn more
Mark anything you're not sure about as "not sure."

docs.title: Trust the map only so far
docs.text:
• Check the terms one by one. Look up each new term once in a trustworthy source.
  • Search for book and course titles yourself. Use the checks from Chapter 3 to see if the books or courses it names really exist.
  • Pay attention to the "debates" part. Where experts disagree, AI tends to give only one side, or to oversimplify.
  • Beginner explanations are simplified. Later, when you read expert material, you'll think, "Ah, the first explanation was too simple," and fix your picture.

★ Going deeper

  • AI knows well-known fields with lots of material fairly well. It gets more wrong in brand-new or very narrow fields (remember hallucination from Chapter 1). Ask yourself: "If I already knew this field, could I spot what's wrong?" The less you know, the harder it is to notice its mistakes.
  • So it's safer to pick one beginner book by an expert, or one official guide, as your anchor. Then compare what AI tells you with that anchor.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Pick a field you're curious about and use the template above. Then, with the answer:

  1. Pick 3 of the 10 terms, look them up, and see if the explanations hold up.
  2. If it named any books or materials, check that they really exist.
  3. Pick the most interesting question and look into it yourself.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Draw the map in a day. If you have a meeting about an unfamiliar topic, use this template the day before to get the big picture.
  2. Save the term list. You can pull it up when you get stuck reading.
  3. Ask it to mark what it's "not sure" about. That shows you where to check.
  4. Choose one anchor source. A beginner book, an official guide, or a trusted course.
  5. Make a list of questions for an expert. The questions from your map help a lot.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "When AI explains it, that's the same as an expert explaining it." Beginner explanations are simplified.
  • "If I read it once, I understand it." You only know you understand when you can explain it or solve a problem. Later pages cover this.
  • "I don't know this field, so I have no choice but to trust AI." The less you know, the more you need an anchor to check against.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Anthropic, Prompting best practices, Claude Platform Docs. Specific instructions and setting the format. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Anthropic, Reduce hallucinations, Claude Platform Docs. "Allow Claude to say I don't know." Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: The five steps and the "anchor" idea are our own practical tips. "It gets more wrong where there's less material" is a general pattern. We didn't find numbers that measure it.

docs.title: Use it as a study buddy
docs.text:
Ch. 6 · 6.1About 6 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • For studying, use AI as a practice partner that quizzes you, not as an answer machine. What you learn sticks better.
  • Research shows that trying to recall what you read sticks longer than reading it again.
  • Use three methods: ask for an explanation, get quizzed, and have your own explanation checked.

docs.title: Copying from the answer key
docs.text:
If you just copy from the answer key in a math workbook, it feels like you solved the problems. But on the test, you can't. Your brain does its work while you try to solve them.

If you keep asking AI "explain this," you get the feeling that you understand. But feeling that you understand is not the same as remembering.

In 10-year-old words

Don't just copy down AI's answers. Have AI give you questions, and you answer them.

docs.title: Recalling beats rereading
docs.text:
In a 2006 study in the journal Psychological Science, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke had students read a passage. Then some took a test where they tried to recall it, and others simply read it again. On a test five minutes later, the rereaders did better. But on tests two days and one week later, the students who had taken the recall test remembered much more. The rereaders also felt more sure of their memory, even though they did worse later. The researchers say tests aren't only for measuring what you know. They're a powerful way to learn.

So "quiz me" is closer to lasting learning than asking AI to "explain it again" over and over.

docs.title: Three ways to study
docs.text:
1. Get an explanation, then a quiz right away

Explain [topic] so a 6th grader could understand it.
When you're done, ask me 3 questions to check that I understood.
Don't give me the answers until I've answered.

2. Get quizzed

Give me 5 questions on [what I just studied], from easy to hard.
Ask one at a time. When I answer, tell me if I'm right.
If I'm wrong, give me a hint first.

3. Have your explanation checked

Here's how I understand [topic]. Tell me what's wrong or missing.
<my explanation>
(write it the way you understand it)
</my explanation>

The third one is especially good. Explaining something in your own words is studying all by itself.

docs.title: Limits of a study buddy
docs.text:
• AI's explanations can be wrong. If they differ from your textbook or your class, the textbook wins.
  • Its grading can be wrong too. For questions with set answers, check the answer key.
  • Watch out for the habit of getting answers right away. When you get one wrong, ask for a hint first. That's what makes your brain work.

★ Going deeper

  • In April 2025, Anthropic announced Claude for Education for universities, along with a learning mode. Instead of handing over answers, it guides the student's reasoning. The idea is that a helper that makes you think is better for learning than one that gives answers. Check whether the service you use has something similar.
  • The study tested reading a passage and recalling it. Whether the same works for other kinds of studying, like solving math or writing code, needs its own look.
  • The study also shows that for a test right away, like five minutes later, rereading can work better. Pick your method based on whether you want to cram for now or remember for a long time.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Pick one thing you studied this week.

  1. Use method 1 to get an explanation, and answer the 3 questions.
  2. A day later, solve 5 questions on the same topic with method 2.
  3. A week later, without AI, write down everything you remember on paper. Then use method 3 to have it checked.

How much do you remember after a week? Compare it with a topic you only reread.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. After "explain this," add "now quiz me." One line is all it takes.
  2. Ask it to hold the answer until you've answered. That's what turns it into recall practice.
  3. Space it out. Studying once today, again in two days, and again in a week is known to work better than all at once. (This spacing effect is a widely known learning principle, not a finding from the study above.)
  4. Explain it in your own words and get it checked. It's the easiest method of all.
  5. Compare AI's explanation with your textbook. For tests, your textbook and teacher set the standard.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "If AI explains it simply, I've learned it." Feeling that you understand is different from remembering.
  • "Rereading makes me feel confident, so it works." In the study, rereaders felt more confident, but a week later the recall group remembered more.
  • "If AI does my homework, it does my studying for me." Then nothing stays in your head.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Henry L. Roediger III and Jeffrey D. Karpicke, Test-Enhanced Learning: Taking Memory Tests Improves Long-Term Retention, Psychological Science, March 2006. The 5-minute, 2-day, and 1-week results and the confidence finding come from the abstract.
  • Anthropic, Introducing Claude for Education, 2025-04-02. The description of learning mode.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: We read only the abstract of the study. We marked the spacing effect as a widely known principle, but we did not check a separate source for it. Study features in each service keep changing.

docs.title: Ch. 7 AI for Notes and Numbers
docs.text:
Using AI for meeting notes, tables, and calculations.

7.1.1Meeting notes and emails5 min read 7.1.2Help with tables and spreadsheet formulas5 min read 7.1.3Be careful when it does math5 min read

docs.title: Be careful when it does math
docs.text:
Ch. 7 · 7.1About 5 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Chatbots write well, but in exact math with many steps, small mistakes can pile up.
  • Let AI set up the formula, and let a calculator work out the value.
  • For things where a mistake costs a lot, like money, taxes, or medicine doses, always check separately.

docs.title: Long multiplication in your head
docs.text:
Short addition is easy in your head. But try four-digit multiplication in your head. Get one middle step wrong, and the answer is wrong, because the bad number carries forward.

Something similar can happen when a chatbot does math. As Chapter 1 showed, it writes one piece at a time and never goes back to change a piece it already wrote.

In 10-year-old words

AI sets up the math problem. The calculator finds the answer. Don't ask a mental-math champ to do long multiplication in their head.

docs.title: What research says
docs.text:
A 2023 paper by Nouha Dziri and others, called "Faith and Fate," tested transformer language models on problems that must be solved in small steps. These included long multiplication, logic grid puzzles, and a classic planning problem. The models seemed to solve them by matching patterns they had seen before. They did not seem to have a real step-by-step method. They also argued something about writing one piece at a time. As problems get harder, accuracy can fall fast, because errors build up step by step.

Andrej Karpathy gives similar advice in his "Deep Dive" lecture. A model can only do a limited amount of computing for each token. So spread the work across many tokens, ask for in-between results, and use tools, like having it run code, whenever you can.

That paper tested 2023 models. Today's models do much better, since many use tools or think things through before answering. But you should still check for mistakes in complicated math.

docs.title: A guide by kind of math
docs.text: Math How to hand it off Short addition, simple ratios Fine to hand off, but check with a rough estimate Averages, totals, percentages Have it write the formula; get the value from a calculator or spreadsheet Dates (how many days until, which weekday) Check with a calendar or tool. These go wrong easily Exchange rates, unit conversions It may not know today's rates, so enter them yourself and ask only for the formula Loan interest, taxes, retirement savings Use it to understand the formula; get values from an official calculator or an expert Medicine doses, medical math Don't hand this to AI. Ask a doctor or pharmacist

docs.title: How to ask for the formula
docs.text:
Help me with this problem. Don't calculate the numbers yourself.
1) Write out the steps as formulas, one step at a time.
2) Explain what each number in each formula stands for.
I'll do the math on a calculator.
Problem: On weekdays, I spend $4.50 on coffee and $12 on lunch.
I don't spend anything on weekends. How much do I spend in 4 weeks?

With the formulas and explanations, you can check that you understand while you work out the values on a calculator. This catches math mistakes, and it also catches places where the problem was misunderstood.

★ Going deeper

  • When a chatbot is connected to a tool, like a calculator or code runner, the code works out exact values, which helps a lot (Part IV). But if the formula is wrong, an exact value still gives a wrong answer. A person needs to read and check the formula.
  • "Think step by step" often helps because writing out middle steps gives the model text to build its next pieces on. Today's reasoning models are trained to think at length on their own (Chapter 20). But steps can look right and still be wrong.
  • The study above looked at the limits of multi-step problems in general, not just math. Some people think long pieces of writing that contradict themselves share the same cause. The study didn't show that directly, though.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Try it two ways.

1. What is 3,847 × 2,916?

2. Break 3,847 × 2,916 into formulas, digit by digit, and write them out.
   I'll work out the values on a calculator.

Compare answer 1 with a calculator. (The right answer is 11,217,852.) If you follow the formulas from answer 2 on a calculator, do you get the right answer? If something went wrong, where was it?

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Ask for the formula instead of the value. You can read and understand a formula.
  2. Make a rough estimate. If you know 3,800 × 2,900 is about 11 million, you'll catch an answer that's way off.
  3. Check dates and units separately. Weekdays, leap years, and unit conversions are easy to get wrong.
  4. For money and health, use official calculators or experts. Use AI only to help you understand.
  5. Check the formula even when a tool is connected. An exact value is no use if the formula is wrong.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "If it shows its work, it's right." The steps can look fine and still go wrong in the middle.
  • "It's a computer, so its math is perfect." A chatbot is a machine that continues text, not a calculator.
  • "It got it right once, so it'll get it right again." Ask the same problem again and the answer can change (Chapter 1).

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Nouha Dziri and others, Faith and Fate: Limits of Transformers on Compositionality, arXiv, 2023-05-29. We summarized the abstract. It tested the transformer models of that time.
  • Andrej Karpathy, Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT, YouTube, 2025-02-05. Chapter "models need tokens to think" (01:46:56): spread computation across tokens, ask for intermediate results, and prefer tools such as code. Checked through Rosetta's unofficial, auto-generated transcript.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: We read only the abstract of the paper. This page doesn't measure how far today's models have moved past these limits. The guide table is our own. We checked the multiplication answer (11,217,852) ourselves.

docs.title: Meeting notes and emails
docs.text:
Ch. 7 · 7.1About 5 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • AI is good at sorting messy notes and long email threads into what's decided, what's still open, and who does what by when.
  • Set the format ahead of time. For anything it doesn't know, have it write "TBD" instead of making it up.
  • A person must always check who's in charge and the deadlines.

docs.title: Organizing a drawer
docs.text:
When a drawer is a mess, it's faster to put in dividers first and then sort things into them. Meeting notes are the same. Set up the dividers (the format) first, and sorting gets easy.

Even if your notes are jumbled, AI is good at splitting them into "decided," "still open," and "to do." But it has a habit of filling empty slots with likely-sounding guesses, so be careful.

In 10-year-old words

Put the dividers in first, and have it leave a slot empty when it doesn't know.

docs.title: A meeting notes template
docs.text:
Sort out the meeting notes below.
Format:
1) Decided (one line each)
2) Still open (one line each)
3) To-do table: task / who / by when
Rules:
- If the notes don't name who or when, don't make it up. Write "TBD."
- Don't change any numbers or dates in the notes.
- Mark anything that needs interpreting as "needs checking."
<notes>
(paste your meeting notes)
</notes>

Anthropic's guide to consistent output says to spell out the exact format you want, using JSON, XML, or your own template. Then Claude follows every part of the format more reliably. If you use the same template every time, your meeting notes come out in the same shape.

docs.title: Sorting out a long email thread
docs.text:
When 20 emails have gone back and forth, it's handy to have AI read them.

Read the email thread below and sort it out.
1) What has been agreed so far
2) Questions still waiting for an answer, and who asked them
3) What I need to do
4) A draft reply from me (polite, 5 sentences or fewer)
Don't add anything that isn't in the emails.
<emails>(paste here)</emails>

docs.title: What a person must always check
docs.text:
Check Why Names of who's in charge Similar names can get mixed up, or the wrong person assigned Deadlines Dates can shift, or "next week" can be read wrong Numbers Use the checks from Chapter 3 Decided or just suggested "Someone suggested we do it" is not "We agreed to do it" Missing points Make sure nothing important dropped out

★ Going deeper

  • You may use a service that turns a meeting recording into text (speech recognition). If it mishears, names and technical terms get written down wrong, and the AI sorts out that wrong text as is. Mistakes at the input stage carry through to the end. Check names and terms separately.
  • Meetings often include personal or secret information, so the checks from Chapter 3 matter a lot here. Use the tools your workplace has approved, and check the rules on whether attendees need to agree to recording.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Pick some rough notes (5 to 10 lines) you scribbled during a recent meeting or call.

  1. Use the template above to sort them out.
  2. Compare the to-do table with your original notes. Are the names and deadlines right?
  3. How many slots say "TBD"? Did it make up any?

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Save the meeting notes template. Use it as one of your question templates from Chapter 2.
  2. Include the "TBD if it's not in the notes" rule. It cuts down on made-up names and dates.
  3. Check right after sorting. While the meeting is fresh, it's easier to catch mistakes.
  4. Before you share, have each person confirm their tasks. Even if AI did the sorting, you're the one sending it.
  5. Blank out personal and secret details first. Notes still sort fine with names changed to A and B.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "If AI sorts it, it's right." Always check names and deadlines against the notes.
  • "If my notes are a mess, AI can't help." Turning messy notes into a clean structure is one of AI's strengths.
  • "I can just record the whole meeting and hand it over." Mistakes in the transcript can carry right through.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Anthropic, Increase output consistency, Claude Platform Docs. "Specify the output format you want." Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Anthropic, Prompting best practices, Claude Platform Docs. Specific instructions and structure. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: The meeting notes template and the checking table are our own practical tips. The point about speech recognition errors is general, and we didn't check a separate source for it.

docs.title: Help with tables and spreadsheet formulas
docs.text:
Ch. 7 · 7.1About 5 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • AI helps a lot with turning text into tables, explaining tables, and figuring out Excel or Google Sheets formulas.
  • When you ask about a formula, give the app, the column names, two or three example rows, and the result you want.
  • Test any formula on a small set of data first, and check in the app's help that the function really exists.

docs.title: A recipe and ingredients
docs.text:
If you tell a cook "Make something tasty," that's hard. If you tell them what's in your fridge and what flavor you want, they can give you a recipe. Formula questions work the same way. Tell AI what your table has (the ingredients) and the result you want (the flavor), and it can give you a formula (the recipe).

In 10-year-old words

Don't just say "Give me a formula." Say "I have this kind of table, and I want this result."

docs.title: Text to table, table to text
docs.text:
Text → table. Turn scattered information into a table.

From the text below, pull out each product name, price, and number
in stock, and make a table. If the text doesn't give a value, leave
the cell blank and write "none."
<text>(paste here)</text>

Table → text. Explain what a table shows in words. Make sure no numbers change.

docs.title: How to ask about a formula
docs.text:
A good question has four parts.

  1. The app. Excel or Google Sheets? (Functions differ a little.)
  2. Column names. What's in column A, column B, and so on.
  3. Two or three example rows. What your real data looks like (with personal details hidden).
  4. The result you want. Which cell, and what value should show up, with an example.
I'm using Google Sheets.
Column A: Name, Column B: Department, Column C: Sales (a number)
Example row: Alex / Sales / 120
I want the total sales for the Sales department in cell E2.
Give me one formula, and explain what each part means, one line each.

Test the formula on a small set of data first. Anthropic's guide on consistent output says to spell out the exact format you want and to use examples to guide the result. When you show an example of the result you want, you're more likely to get the right answer.

docs.title: When the formula doesn't work
docs.text:
• Copy the exact error message and share it, like "#NAME?" or "#VALUE!".
  • Share the values and the range in the cells the formula uses.
  • Check in the app's help or official guide that the function really exists. AI can make up functions that don't exist (hallucination).
  • Some functions only exist in some versions. Say which version you're using.

★ Going deeper

  • It usually works better to give the column names and a few example rows than to paste in a huge table. A long table takes up a lot of room in the context, and accuracy can drop (Chapters 2 and 6).
  • Some services let you upload a file, and the AI runs code to do the math itself (Part IV). Then the code does the math, but you still need to check which code ran on which columns.
  • For tables with personal details, blank them out using the methods from Chapter 3. Deleting the name column or swapping in fake data is enough for a formula question.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Pick a table you use (or make a 5-row practice table).

  1. Decide what you want to work out. (A total, a count of rows that match something, an average, and so on.)
  2. Ask using the four parts: app, column names, examples, and result.
  3. Put the formula into your small table and check that it matches what you get by hand.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Save a question template. It has four slots: app, column names, example rows, and result.
  2. Swap personal details for fake data. A formula question doesn't need real names.
  3. Check a few rows by hand. About three rows is enough to catch a pattern of mistakes.
  4. Ask for an explanation of the formula too. If you know what each part means, you can fix it yourself next time.
  5. If it fails, paste the error message as is. That's the fastest way to a fix.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "Every function AI gives me exists." It can give you a function that doesn't exist, or one from a different app.
  • "I have to paste the whole table for it to be accurate." Column names and a few example rows are often enough.
  • "AI can do the math, so I don't need formulas." Formulas and tools are surer for math. The next page goes into this.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Anthropic, Increase output consistency, Claude Platform Docs. "Specify the output format you want" and "Constrain with examples." Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: The four parts of a formula question are our own tip. "AI can make up functions" follows from how hallucination works in general. We didn't find a study about spreadsheets specifically.

docs.title: Ch. 8 Make It Part of How You Work
docs.text:
Don't use it once and stop. Turn it into a way of working for you and your team.

8.1.1Keep your favorite prompts5 min read 8.1.2A checklist before using it at work5 min read 8.1.3Rules your team agrees on5 min read

docs.title: Keep your favorite prompts
docs.text:
Ch. 8 · 8.1About 5 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Save prompts that worked well, give them names, and tweak them each time you use them. They become your own toolbox.
  • For each template, also write down when to use it, a good example, and what to watch for.
  • Don't just collect them. Test them now and then, and fix them.

docs.title: Making a cookbook
docs.text:
When a dish turns out great, writing down the recipe lets you make it again. Without it, you end up asking, "What did I put in that time?"

Prompts work the same way. If you collect the question templates from Chapter 2, you won't have to start from scratch each time. And as you use them, they keep getting better.

In 10-year-old words

Write your good prompts in a cookbook. Use them again, and make them a little better each time.

docs.title: What to write for each one
docs.text: Field What to write Example Name A name you'll recognize at a glance Weekly update draft When to use The situation it fits Every Friday, reporting to the team Template The prompt, with blanks (a question template from Chapter 2) A good example An input and result that worked well Last week's update Watch for Where this template goes wrong Check whether numbers changed Last updated When you last changed it 2026-11-09

docs.title: Where to keep them
docs.text:
• A notes app or a single document is plenty. You don't need a fancy tool to start.
  • Pick a naming rule. For example, "[Type] Kind: name," like "[Writing] Summary: for my manager."
  • Start with about ten. (That's our suggestion.) With too many, it gets hard to use them.
  • If your service has a feature like "custom instructions" or "projects," you may be able to save templates there. (It differs by service.)

docs.title: Test and improve
docs.text:
Anthropic's guide to building tests describes how to improve a prompt. Set success criteria. Write test cases, including tricky ones. Test the prompt. Fix it, and repeat. It says success criteria should be specific and measurable.

For personal use, you can make it lighter:

  1. One line of success criteria. For example: "Not a single number changes, and it's 5 sentences or fewer."
  2. Three test inputs. Keep two normal ones and one tricky one.
  3. Re-test with all three after each fix. See whether fixing one thing made another worse.

★ Going deeper

  • When the model changes, results can change too. If a template that used to work starts missing, check it again with your three test inputs. It's a common good practice to re-run your tests after a model update.
  • Sharing a collection of templates with your team helps a lot. Just don't put "good examples" with personal or secret details in it (Chapter 3).
  • There are tools that run tests like these automatically (evaluation tools). For personal templates, they may be more than you need.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Pick the 3 most useful question templates you've made from this book.
  2. Fill in every field from the table above and save them in your notes app.
  3. Use them for a week, and add what really happened to "A good example" and "Watch for."

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Save a prompt once you've used it three times. Write it by hand twice, then save it the third time.
  2. "Watch for" is the most important field. Your mistakes are what fill it in.
  3. Write your success criteria in one line. You need a standard for "it worked" before you can improve anything.
  4. Clean up once a month. Delete the ones you don't use, and improve the ones you use often.
  5. Remove personal details before sharing. Make sure no names are hiding in "A good example."

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "The more templates, the better." Too many are hard to find, so you won't use them. Start with ten or fewer.
  • "Once I make one, I'm done." Models and your work both change. Test now and then.
  • "I can just use someone else's templates." That's a fine start, but you'll need to adjust them to your work.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Anthropic, Define success criteria and build evaluations, Claude Platform Docs. Specific and measurable success criteria, tests that include edge cases, and the test-and-refine cycle. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: The light personal method (one line of criteria, three test inputs) is our own shortened version of the guide's developer method. "Re-test after a model update" is a general good practice, not a sentence we confirmed in the guide. Saving features differ by service.

docs.title: A checklist before using it at work
docs.text:
Ch. 8 · 8.1About 6 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • AI helps a lot with some jobs. With others, it can actually make you less likely to get the right answer.
  • Before you bring AI into your work, check the kind of job, whether you can check it, the risk, and how sensitive it is, with five questions.
  • Try it small, and measure before and after to decide.

docs.title: A road that isn't on the map
docs.text:
A bike is fast on a flat road. In front of a staircase, it just gets in the way. You need to know which paths you can ride on.

A large experiment in 2023 showed this. 758 consultants at the Boston Consulting Group worked on 18 realistic work tasks, some with AI (GPT-4) and some without. On tasks inside what AI could do, the AI users finished 12.2% more tasks on average and worked 25.1% faster. Their work was also rated more than 40% higher in quality than a control group's. But the researchers also picked a complex business task that they expected to be outside what AI could do. On that task, the AI users were 19 percentage points less likely to get the right answer. The researchers called this the jagged technological frontier. Two jobs that look about equally hard can fall on opposite sides: AI helps with one and hurts the other.

In 10-year-old words

On some paths AI is a bike. On others, it's a bike in front of a staircase. Find out which path you're on first.

docs.title: Five questions
docs.text:
Before you bring AI into a job, ask these five questions.

Question What to check Warning sign 1. Is it inside the frontier? Has AI handled similar jobs? Have you tried it small? A complex job you've never tried with AI 2. Can you check the result? Would you notice if it were wrong? Using results in a field you don't know 3. How bad is a mistake? Does it touch money, health, law, or reputation? One mistake costs a lot and is hard to undo 4. Is sensitive information involved? Personal details or secrets? (Chapter 3) Information you can't blank out 5. Does it follow the rules? Your workplace's, school's, or the law's? You don't know the rules

Scoring: If there are no warning signs, go ahead. If there's even one, first decide how to handle it: add a checking step, blank things out, or get approval. If question 3 is serious, use AI results only as a reference.

docs.title: Try it small
docs.text:
1. Pick just one job. Start with the one that repeats most and has the least risk.
  2. Measure "before." Write down how long the job takes without AI, and how good the result is. If you have no records, measure it once this week.
  3. Use AI for two weeks. Do the same job with AI, and write down the time, number of mistakes, and how happy you are with it.
  4. Compare. If it's faster but has more mistakes, that's not a win.

Anthropic's guide to testing says to set success criteria that are specific and measurable, and to check them with test cases. The same goes for your own work. Compare with numbers, not with "it feels better."

[Trial log]
Job: ___
Before: ___ minutes, ___ mistakes
After 2 weeks: ___ minutes, ___ mistakes
How I checked: ___
Keep using it? Yes / No / With conditions (conditions: ___)

★ Going deeper

  • In the study, the "outside" task was one the researchers chose on purpose to be hard for AI. So it doesn't mean "AI usually gets things wrong." The key point is that the edge is invisible and jagged.
  • The study used GPT-4 in 2023. Models and the ways people use them have changed a lot since then. You can't assume the same numbers hold today. A habit of testing each kind of job yourself lasts longer.
  • One problem the study points to: people may lean too hard on AI and accept wrong answers as is. That's why it matters to build checking into the job itself.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Pick one job you want to bring AI into, and fill in the five-question table above.

  1. Which questions show a warning sign?
  2. How will you handle each one? (A checking step, blanking things out, getting approval, and so on.)
  3. Make a two-week trial log and fill in the first line.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Decide the risk first. Question 3 is where every decision starts.
  2. Measure "before." Without a record, you can't tell what AI changed.
  3. Build a checking step into the job. Don't hand AI a job whose results you can't check.
  4. Grow from small jobs. Start where it works, and widen one step at a time.
  5. Review every couple of months. As models and services change, the edge moves too.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "AI always makes things faster." Depending on the job, it can make you faster, or make you more likely to be wrong.
  • "The harder the job, the more AI helps." In the study, a complex task outside AI's range got worse with AI.
  • "Testing takes too long, so I'll skip it." Measuring just one job for two weeks can show a big difference.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Fabrizio Dell'Acqua, Edward McFowland III, Ethan Mollick, and others, Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of Artificial Intelligence on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality, Harvard Business School working paper, SSRN, 2023. We checked the 758 consultants, 18 tasks, 12.2%, 25.1%, more than 40%, and 19 percentage points in the working paper's text.
  • Anthropic, Define success criteria and build evaluations, Claude Platform Docs. Specific, measurable success criteria. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: A later peer-reviewed version of the study reportedly gives a different quality number (over 30%). We used the working paper's numbers. The study looked at consultants and a 2023 model, so it can't be applied to every job or to today's models. The five-question table and the two-week trial are our own practical tips.

docs.title: Rules your team agrees on
docs.text:
Ch. 8 · 8.1About 5 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • For a team to use AI together, agree ahead of time on what can go in, who checks the results, and how to say AI was used.
  • Rules should be short and easy to follow. One page is enough.
  • When something goes wrong, focus on fixing it, not on blaming someone.

docs.title: Classroom rules
docs.text:
A classroom with no rules has arguments. A classroom with too many rules has rules nobody follows. Short, clear rules like "Walk in the hallway" are the ones people keep.

Teams using AI are the same. If everyone does it their own way, someone may paste in customer details, and someone else may hide that they used AI. Later, that turns into trouble.

In 10-year-old words

Make the rules short and clear, and fit them on one page.

docs.title: What goes on a one-page rule sheet
docs.text: Section What to decide Example OK uses What AI may be used for Drafts, summaries, ideas, sorting tables Not OK uses What it may not be used for Entering customer personal details, final legal judgments Data levels What may be typed in Public: OK. Internal: approved tools only. Sensitive: never Who checks Who reviews the results The writer checks first; the manager checks anything sent outside Saying so How to note AI use Outside documents say "AI helped draft this" Approved tools Which tools to use [The tool on your company account] If something goes wrong Who to tell A contact name and how to reach them

docs.title: Sorting data into levels
docs.text:
This is the most important part of the rules. It turns the privacy ideas from Chapter 3 into your team's own words.

  • Public: Material that's already public. Usually OK to type in, but check for personal details and copyright or sharing limits.
  • Internal: Company documents and plans that aren't public yet. Only in tools your workplace has approved.
  • Sensitive: Customer personal details, contracts, HR records, health information. Don't type it in, or only with details blanked out.

docs.title: Making the rules stick
docs.text:
1. Keep it to one page. If it's long, people won't read it.
  2. Add examples. "This is fine, this isn't" gets understood faster than rules alone.
  3. Decide together. Rules are more realistic when the people doing the work help make them.
  4. Say who to ask. When something's unclear, people need someone to ask.
  5. Update every three months. Services and laws change.
  6. Make it easy to report mistakes. Hidden mistakes grow into bigger problems.

★ Going deeper

  • On January 26, 2023, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) released its AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF). It helps organizations that build and use AI make it more trustworthy, and it's meant for voluntary use. On July 26, 2024, NIST added a Generative AI Profile (NIST-AI-600-1) that covers risks special to generative AI. If you want to build team rules in a more formal way, these are good references. For individuals and small teams, a one-page sheet like this one is more realistic.
  • This page is general information, not legal advice. Set your company's official policy together with your legal and security teams.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Draft a one-page rule sheet for your team (or club).

  1. Fill in the seven sections from the table above.
  2. Ask two teammates to read it and tell you, "What's unclear?"
  3. Fix the unclear parts and share it with the team.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Start with the three data levels. That alone prevents a lot of serious trouble.
  2. Name one person to ask when unsure. One name is enough.
  3. Have a person check anything that goes outside the team. Even if AI wrote it, the sender is responsible.
  4. Decide how to say AI was used. Hiding it is the riskiest choice.
  5. Show examples when you share the rules. They make the rules click faster.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "Rules make people use AI less." Knowing the safe zone actually lets people use it with confidence.
  • "Banning it keeps us safe." If you only ban it, some people may use it secretly. Show them a safe way instead.
  • "Once we set the rules, we're done." Services and laws change, so check every three months.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • NIST, AI Risk Management Framework. We confirmed on the page that it was released on 2023-01-26 for voluntary use, and that the Generative AI Profile (NIST-AI-600-1) came out on 2024-07-26. We did not read the full framework. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: The seven sections and the three data levels are our own practical template. We didn't describe the framework's inner structure because we didn't read it in full.

docs.title: III A Spoonful of How It Works
docs.text:
No hard math. Take a spoonful at a time of what happens inside a chatbot.

Ch. 9How Does AI Learn?3/3 written Ch. 10How Words Become Numbers3/3 written Ch. 11Attention3/3 written Ch. 12Building Sentences with Probability3/3 written

docs.title: Ch. 9 How Does AI Learn?
docs.text:
Reading and copying, learning from people, and why size matters.

9.1.1Read and imitate: pretraining6 min read 9.1.2Learn from people: fine-tuning and feedback6 min read 9.1.3Why size matters: parameters5 min read

docs.title: Read and imitate: pretraining
docs.text:
Ch. 9 · 9.1About 6 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • A chatbot's first round of school is reading a gigantic amount of text and practicing guessing what comes next.
  • The right answers are already in the text, so no person has to grade each guess.
  • A model that has only done this is not yet a helpful assistant. It's closer to a machine that continues text.

docs.title: A quiz where the answer is in the book
docs.text:
Picture a quiz where you cover up part of a sentence in a book and ask, "What word goes here?" The answer is already printed in the book, so you can grade yourself with no teacher.

That's a chatbot's first round of school. It takes huge amounts of text, hides what comes next, guesses the next token, and adjusts a little whenever it's wrong. It repeats this an enormous number of times. This is called pretraining.

In 10-year-old words

It reads tons of books and plays a "guess the next word" quiz by itself. The answers are in the books, so it doesn't need a teacher to grade it.

docs.title: One round of practice
docs.text:
1. Gather text. Lots of it: books, web pages, code.
  2. Cut it into tokens. The pieces from Chapter 1.
  3. Show the start and have it guess the next token.
  4. Compare its score table with the right answer. If it gave the right answer a low score, it adjusts by a lot.
  5. Nudge the numbers inside the model (the parameters). This is what "learning" means here.
  6. Back to step 1. Repeat a huge number of times.

After all that practice, its score table gets good. It can pick a pretty likely next word, even for sentences it has never seen.

docs.title: What does it end up learning?
docs.text:
To guess the next word well, it helps to pick up a lot about the text: grammar, tone, facts, how stories flow, the rules of code. All of these soak in along the way. Nobody decided "let's teach it grammar." It grew out of the practice.

The GPT-3 paper (2020) reported something surprising. A model this big, with pretraining alone, could do many tasks like translation and answering questions when given just a few examples or simple instructions in plain text. GPT-3 had 175 billion parameters, 10 times more than any earlier language model of its kind. The tip from Chapter 2, "give an example and it will follow," comes from this ability.

docs.title: The limits of this stage
docs.text:
• It also learns the wrong facts and prejudices in what it reads. That's the root of the bias from Chapter 3.
  • Its reading stops at some date. It doesn't know what happened after that. So recent news needs a search (Chapter 4, Part IV).
  • It's weak on things that rarely appear in text. Rare facts and less common languages get more mistakes (hallucination, Chapter 1).
  • It isn't a smooth "assistant" yet. It's a machine that continues text. Give it a question, and it may just keep writing what comes after the question. The next page shows how it becomes a helper.

★ Going deeper

  • More formally, the model compares the chances it gave each next token with the right answer. This gives a number called the cross-entropy loss. Training nudges the parameters a little at a time to make that number smaller, using a method called gradient descent. 3Blue1Brown's deep learning series explains this very well.
  • Research shows that when you scale up this "read and guess" training, the score table improves in a steady, predictable way. (See the page after next.)
  • The GPT-3 paper also pointed out datasets where the model still struggled, and problems that come from training on big piles of web text. It's good to read the weak spots, not just the strong ones.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Play "human pretraining." Show three friends or family members the same sentence and have each write the next word.

"On a rainy day, I love a warm cup of ____"

Did everyone write the same word? Think of the most common answer as the top choice on the score table from Chapter 1. The more people disagree, the flatter the score table for that sentence. Pretraining is this game played across millions of books.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Ask about recent news with a tool that can search. It doesn't know what happened after its reading stopped.
  2. Be extra careful in fields with little text. Local news and very specialized topics may have little training material.
  3. Ask "Up to what date do you know about?" It may not answer exactly, but it gives you a rough idea.
  4. Keep giving examples. That works well because it grew out of pretraining.
  5. Remember that wrong facts can come from what it read. That's why the checking habits from Chapter 3 matter.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "AI memorized the whole internet." It learns patterns more than it memorizes. It can sometimes repeat bits word for word, but that's not how it usually works.
  • "The more it reads, the fewer mistakes it makes." It reads wrong things too, so it can learn wrong things.
  • "Once pretraining is done, it's a chatbot." Not yet. There's another stage that turns it into a helper.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Tom B. Brown and others, Language Models are Few-Shot Learners, arXiv, 2020-05-28. The 175 billion parameters, "10x more than any previous non-sparse language model," doing tasks from a few examples or instructions, and the noted struggles and web-training issues all come from the abstract.
  • 3Blue1Brown (Grant Sanderson), Transformers, the tech behind LLMs, 2024-04-01. Recommended for going deeper.
  • Andrej Karpathy, Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT, YouTube, 2025-02-05. Chapters "pretraining data (internet)" (00:01:00), "tokenization" (00:07:47), and "neural network I/O" (00:14:27), and the point that a pretrained-only model is "a token autocomplete." Checked through Rosetta's unofficial, auto-generated transcript and chapters.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: We read only the paper's abstract. The six-step description is our own summary of the general idea. Public details about how today's models are trained are limited, so we didn't go into specifics.

docs.title: Why size matters: parameters
docs.text:
Ch. 9 · 9.1About 5 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Parameters are the numbers inside a model that get adjusted during training. A number like "70B" in a model's name is how many there are.
  • Research found that growing the model, the data, and the computing power improves results by a steady rule.
  • But size alone doesn't decide things. The amount of data and the way a model is tuned matter too.

docs.title: The knobs on a radio
docs.text:
Old radios had knobs to tune the station and the sound. With two or three knobs, you can't adjust much. With hundreds of billions of knobs, you could tune things very finely.

A chatbot has knobs like these, called parameters: billions to hundreds of billions of them. Training means turning each knob a tiny bit (page 9.1.1). In model names like "7B" or "70B," the B usually stands for billion, the number of parameters. 175B means 175 billion.

In 10-year-old words

Parameters are knobs the model turns while it learns. More knobs let it tune things more finely, but having lots of knobs doesn't make it good all by itself.

docs.title: Bigger gets better: scaling laws
docs.text:
In 2020, a paper by Jared Kaplan and others, Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models, found a pattern. Grow three things: the model's size, the amount of data, and the computing power used for training. As you do, a language model's error score drops in a steady way, following what's called a power law. Some of these trends held across a range of more than ten million times. Details of the design, like how wide or deep the network was, mattered little within a wide range.

Put simply: add more resources, and the score table improves by a rule you can predict. That's why companies kept investing in bigger models.

docs.title: But it's not just size
docs.text:
Data has to grow too. In 2022, a paper by Jordan Hoffmann and others looked at a fixed amount of computing. It argued that the most efficient choice is to grow the model and the training data at the same rate. If you double the model, double the training tokens too. They concluded that big models of the time had grown without enough extra data, so they were undertrained. To test this, they built Chinchilla, with 70 billion parameters and four times as much data, using the same computing budget as a bigger model. Chinchilla beat much larger models across many tests, including Gopher (280 billion), GPT-3 (175 billion), and Megatron-Turing NLG (530 billion).

How you tune it matters too. The InstructGPT model on the last page was 100 times smaller, and people still preferred it.

Please note

These studies are from 2020 and 2022, and AI has changed a lot since. Today, steps after training, the way models reason, and tool use all add a lot to how well they do. Don't read this as "size is everything." Read it as "size is one important factor."

docs.title: What comes with being big
docs.text:
• It's heavy. More parameters need more memory and more computer power to run. Here's a rough example. Say each parameter takes 2 bytes. Then 175 billion parameters take about 350 GB just for the numbers (175 × 10⁹ × 2 bytes). That's why big models usually run on a company's servers, not on a home computer.
  • It's slow and costly. Each question needs more computing (see free vs paid in Chapter 4).
  • For some jobs, a smaller model is better. For simple jobs, a small, fast model is often enough.

★ Going deeper

  • The 2020 scaling laws paper concluded that, for a fixed budget, it's efficient to train a very large model on a fairly modest amount of data and stop early. The Chinchilla paper corrected that: grow the model and the data together. This is research fixing earlier research, the way science moves forward.
  • Chinchilla reported an average accuracy of 67.5% on a test called MMLU, the best at the time. Chapter 21 covers what tests like this mean and where they fall short.
  • Researchers also work on helping small models catch up to big ones (for example, "distillation"), and on designs that use only part of the model for each input ("mixture of experts"). This book doesn't cover those.
  • Using more computing for "thinking time" is covered in Chapter 20.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Practice reading the numbers in model names.

  1. How many is 175B? (175 billion)
  2. How many times bigger is 175B than 70B? (2.5 times)
  3. If each parameter takes 2 bytes, about how much space do a 70B model's numbers need? (70 × 10⁹ × 2 = 140 × 10⁹ bytes, about 140 GB)

Then look on your service's help pages to see which model it uses. Does the name tell you its size? (Often it doesn't.)

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Don't assume a bigger model is always better. Look at how hard the job is, and at speed and cost too.
  2. Use a fast model for easy jobs and a big one for hard jobs. If your service lets you choose.
  3. Don't read the number in a model's name as a quality score. Parameter count is size, not quality.
  4. Be careful with old comparison articles. Model rankings change within months.
  5. Big models get things wrong too. Size doesn't make hallucinations go away.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "More parameters means smarter." Data, training methods, and tuning all play a part.
  • "The number of parameters is the amount of knowledge." It doesn't map that neatly. Parameters are knobs, not drawers.
  • "Make it bigger and hallucinations will disappear." Size alone doesn't fix that (Chapter 1).

docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Jared Kaplan and others, Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models, arXiv, 2020-01-23. Power laws, trends over more than seven orders of magnitude, and the small effect of width and depth come from the abstract.
  • Jordan Hoffmann and others, Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models, arXiv, 2022-03-29. Scaling model and tokens equally, Chinchilla (70B, 4 times the data) beating Gopher, GPT-3, Jurassic-1, and Megatron-Turing NLG, and 67.5% on MMLU come from the abstract.
  • Long Ouyang and others, Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback, arXiv, 2022-03-04.
  • Tom B. Brown and others, Language Models are Few-Shot Learners, arXiv, 2020-05-28.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
