  • Note: We read only the abstracts. These are older studies, so they may not apply directly to today's models. The 350 GB and 140 GB figures are our own rough math for storing the numbers only. Running a model takes more. "B" for billion in model names is a common habit, not a rule.

docs.title: Learn from people: fine-tuning and feedback
docs.text:
Ch. 9 · 9.1About 6 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • A pretrained model knows a lot, but it still has to learn how to answer questions helpfully.
  • People show it good answers and rank its answers, and that shapes it into a helper.
  • Because it learns from people's ratings, it can lean the way those ratings lean.

docs.title: A well-read student practices for an interview
docs.text:
Imagine a student who has read a huge number of books. They know a lot. But in an interview, when asked a question, they just ramble on as if continuing a story. Then a coach has them practice: "Answer the question, short and clear." Now they do much better.

A pretrained model is that student. It knows a lot, but it has to learn separately how to answer a question helpfully.

In 10-year-old words

A teacher shows the well-read student good answers and says "this answer is better," until the student becomes a good helper.

docs.title: How InstructGPT did it
docs.text:
In 2022, OpenAI researchers published the InstructGPT paper. They pointed out that making a model bigger doesn't, by itself, make it better at doing what users want. A big model can still say things that are untrue, harmful, or simply unhelpful. So they used feedback from people to shape it.

  1. Learn from good answers (supervised fine-tuning). People (called labelers) write the answers they'd want for a set of prompts. The model learns by imitating them.
  2. Rank answers. The model gives several answers to the same prompt, and people rank them from best to worst.
  3. Learn from the rankings (reinforcement learning from human feedback, or RLHF). The model is tuned again, so the kinds of answers people preferred come up more.

The result was striking. In people's ratings, answers from the 1.3-billion-parameter InstructGPT were preferred over answers from the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3, even though it was about 100 times smaller. It was also more truthful and gave fewer harmful outputs. Still, the researchers admitted it made simple mistakes.

docs.title: How this connects to the chatbots you use
docs.text:
• Why instructions work: It practiced following instructions. That's why the asking tips in Chapter 2 work.
  • The friendly tone and the way it says no: It was shaped toward answers people rated well.
  • Why "I don't know" is hard for it: People may rate a confident guess higher than "I don't know." Then it can lean toward guessing. (See hallucination in Chapter 1 and agreeing with you in Chapter 3.)

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Learning from people's ratings means learning people's tastes and blind spots too.

  • If people prefer answers that agree with them, the model agrees more (the study in Chapter 3).
  • If people prefer long, confident answers, you get more long, confident answers.
  • The culture and values of the raters soak into the model.

So a polite, confident tone doesn't mean an answer is right.

★ Going deeper

  • This idea was studied before InstructGPT. A 2019 paper by Daniel Ziegler and others, Fine-Tuning Language Models from Human Preferences, used people's comparisons to shape a language model. It also noticed a catch: on summaries, the model learned to copy whole sentences, and the raters liked it. The authors suspected it was taking advantage of the simple rules of thumb the raters used.
  • A common way to do step 3: first train a separate "scoring model" (a reward model) on people's rankings. Then use reinforcement learning to push the chatbot toward higher scores. Researchers are also studying ways to have AI help with the rating (Chapter 20).
  • For going deeper, Karpathy's "Deep Dive" lecture has chapters on "post-training data (conversations)" (01:01:06) and "reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)" (02:48:26).

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Ask the same thing in two ways.

1. How do I keep potatoes fresh for a long time?

2. Continue the text that comes after this sentence: "How do I keep potatoes
   fresh for a long time?" Don't answer the question. Write as if this
   sentence is part of a longer piece of writing.

Answer 1 will likely sound like a helper. Answer 2 may look more like text being continued. The difference is a trace of the "learned to follow instructions" stage. (Results can vary by service.)

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Give specific instructions. It was trained to follow instructions, so specific ones work well.
  2. Don't treat a polite tone as proof. The tone was polished; the facts are a separate matter.
  3. Instead of asking whether you're right, ask for reasons for and against. That helps with its habit of agreeing (Chapter 3).
  4. Find out what the thumbs-up and thumbs-down buttons do. Services differ on whether and how ratings are used. Check the settings and help pages.
  5. Keep saying "If you don't know, say so." That one line pushes back on the habit of guessing.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "People taught the AI every answer, one by one." It does pretraining on its own. People supply some good answers and some rankings.
  • "Bigger models follow instructions better." In the paper, a tuned model 100 times smaller was preferred.
  • "It was tuned with human feedback, so it's safe and accurate." Mistakes and bias went down, but they're still there.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Long Ouyang and others, Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback, arXiv, 2022-03-04. The three steps, 1.3B preferred over 175B, better truthfulness and less harmful output, and "still makes simple mistakes" come from the abstract.
  • Daniel M. Ziegler and others, Fine-Tuning Language Models from Human Preferences, arXiv, 2019-09-18. We summarized the abstract.
  • Mrinank Sharma and others, Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models, arXiv, 2023-10-20.
  • Andrej Karpathy, Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT, YouTube, 2025-02-05. Chapter titles checked through Rosetta's unofficial chapter list.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: We read only the abstracts. The "reward model, then reinforcement learning" description is a widely known summary, not a sentence from these abstracts. Public details on how today's models are tuned are limited, so we didn't go into specifics. Results of "Try it yourself" vary by service.

docs.title: Ch. 10 How Words Become Numbers
docs.text:
How tokens become lists of numbers, and how meaning becomes distance.

10.1.1Tokens become lists of numbers6 min read 10.1.2Similar meanings sit close together5 min read 10.1.3Meaning changes with context5 min read

docs.title: Similar meanings sit close together
docs.text:
Ch. 10 · 10.1About 5 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • If you think of the lists of numbers as locations, words with similar meanings tend to sit close together, and unlike words sit far apart.
  • There are famous examples where "direction" carries meaning too, but they don't always work exactly.
  • Close doesn't mean the same. And society's prejudices get built into the distances too.

docs.title: Seats in the lunchroom
docs.text:
In a lunchroom, close friends usually sit near each other, and kids who don't talk much sit farther apart. Just from the seating, you can tell who's close to whom.

Embeddings are easy to picture this way. On the last page, each token got a location. In that space, tokens with similar meanings gather close together. "Cat" and "dog" are close. "Cat" and "refrigerator" are far apart.

In 10-year-old words

Words with similar meanings sit at the same lunch table. That's how a computer can measure "similar" as a distance.

docs.title: Not just distance: direction carries meaning too
docs.text:
A 2013 study (the paper behind word2vec) reported that word vectors learned this way did well on tests of word similarity, catching both grammar patterns and meaning.

3Blue1Brown's lesson shows a more fun example. The difference between the vectors for "woman" and "man," which is a direction from one point to the other, looks a lot like the difference between "queen" and "king." So if you start at "king" and move in the "woman minus man" direction, you land near "queen." This is a classic example. But the lesson adds that it only works roughly. In the model used for the video, the real "queen" sat a bit farther away than the math predicted.

So remember it like this: differences in meaning can show up as directions, but the math isn't always exact.

docs.title: Where this gets used
docs.text:
(These are widely known uses. Each service builds them its own way.)

  • Searching by meaning. It finds text that means something close, even if the words don't match. For example, you search "food that helps with a cold" and get a post called "what to eat when you're feeling sick."
  • Recommending similar things. Distances help find similar articles or products.
  • Linking languages. Models can be trained so the same idea in different languages sits close together.

docs.title: The limits of "close"
docs.text:
• Similar isn't the same. "Cheap," "inexpensive," and "affordable" sit close, but they feel different. Opposites can sit close too, because they show up in the same kinds of sentences. ("Hot" and "cold" are both about temperature.)
  • The prejudices in text show up in the distances. The 2016 study from Chapter 3 found that, in word vectors learned from news, gender stereotypes lined up along a single direction. "Close" is shaped by what people have written.
  • It may not match the "close" you mean. Things that often appear together in the training text end up close. That may differ from what "similar" means in your work.

★ Going deeper

  • Closeness is usually measured by the angle between two vectors (cosine similarity) or by distance. The more two vectors point the same way, the closer their meanings.
  • 3Blue1Brown explains that a space with very many dimensions has a huge number of different directions. So many kinds of meaning, like gender, size, or feelings, can each get their own direction without crowding each other. This idea leads to the "features" in Chapter 19.
  • Today's meaning-based search tools turn a whole passage into one vector and compare those. Adding search to a chatbot (RAG) builds on this idea (Chapter 13).

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Make two groups. Split these 6 words into two groups of close words.

cat / dog / tiger / car / bus / train

Then ask a chatbot:

List these words in order of how close their meanings are, and explain why:
cat, dog, tiger, car, bus, train

Did it match your groups? Then ask about "how they're similar but different." You'll see that close and the same aren't the same thing.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Search with a description. In tools that search by meaning, a sentence describing your situation often works better than a few keywords.
  2. Ask for "3 similar examples." Finding close things is something AI does well.
  3. Also ask "how are they similar but different?" That keeps you from missing small differences in meaning.
  4. Try a similar word. If you don't like the answer, swap a key word for a close one. It can open a different path.
  5. Don't leave judgments about people to "closeness." It can carry prejudice (Chapter 3).

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "Similar words can be swapped with no change." They're close, but they feel and work differently.
  • "King minus man plus woman equals queen, every time." It's a classic example, and it only works roughly.
  • "Distance is neutral math." It's learned from human writing, so it carries society's prejudices too.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • 3Blue1Brown (Grant Sanderson), Transformers, the tech behind LLMs, 2024-04-01. The direction example (king, woman minus man, queen), the note that it's only rough, and the point about many directions in many dimensions. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Tomas Mikolov and others, Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space, arXiv, 2013-01-16. Word vectors catch both grammar and meaning similarity (abstract).
  • Tolga Bolukbasi and others, Man is to Computer Programmer as Woman is to Homemaker? Debiasing Word Embeddings, arXiv, 2016-07-21.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: The uses (meaning search, recommendations, linking languages) are a summary of widely known uses, not confirmed in these sources. The cosine similarity note is a general explanation. Results of "Try it yourself" vary by chatbot.

docs.title: Meaning changes with context
docs.text:
Ch. 10 · 10.1About 5 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • A "bat" can be an animal or something you swing in baseball. A chatbot figures out which one from the words around it.
  • Each word starts with one list of numbers, but it changes as it passes through the model's layers and takes in context.
  • That's why giving context in your question matters.

docs.title: One word, many meanings
docs.text:
In "A bat flew out of the cave," "He swung the bat," and "She went up to bat," the word "bat" means different things. You can tell right away from the words around it. Words like "bank," "light," and "bass" work the same way.

But the embedding from the last page gives each token one list of numbers. If "bat" has only one list, how can the model tell its meanings apart?

In 10-year-old words

"Bat" starts with one location, but it moves after looking at the words next to it. That's how the model knows whether it's the animal or the baseball bat.

docs.title: Two steps
docs.text:
Step 1: The starting location (the embedding). According to 3Blue1Brown's lesson, each token in the input first turns into one list of numbers from the lookup table. At this point, it hasn't looked at the words around it yet.

Step 2: Adjusting for context. Next, as the lists pass through the model's many layers, they change under the influence of the other tokens. In a chatbot, which reads from front to back, each token looks back at the tokens before it and gathers meaning from them. Here's a simple way to picture it. In "He swung the bat," "bat" looks back at "swung" and moves toward the baseball meaning. In "A bat flew out of the cave," the word "flew" comes right after "bat," so it picks up the animal meaning there. The key tool that does this is called attention, coming up in the next chapter.

So when the model picks the next word at the end, it uses locations adjusted for context, not the starting ones.

docs.title: A short history of context-aware meaning
docs.text:
A 2018 paper called ELMo, by Matthew Peters and others, showed this idea early on. It proposed word representations that change with context, to handle words with more than one meaning. It took the word vectors from the inner workings of a language model trained on lots of text in both directions. It reported big improvements on six hard language tasks, including answering questions and judging sentiment.

Today's chatbots push the same idea further, with a bigger, deeper design called the transformer.

docs.title: When chatbots misunderstand
docs.text:
• Too little context. With "How much is a bass?" and nothing else, it tends to go with the most common meaning. (It may also list the meanings, or ask you.)
  • Mixed-up context. If a sentence could fit several meanings, it may pick the wrong one.
  • Technical words. The same word can mean different things in different fields. "Consideration" in a contract is not the everyday "consideration." Tell it the field.

★ Going deeper

  • The model adjusts the lists a little at each layer. Some research suggests earlier layers handle things like grammar and word shape, and later layers handle more abstract meaning. But what each layer does differs from model to model, so it's hard to make general rules (interpretability, Chapter 19).
  • 3Blue1Brown explains that the vectors start as lookups of single words, then get updated as they pass through the network. Along the way, they soak in a richer meaning from the context around them. The next lesson in the series goes into this.
  • Chapter 11 on attention explains how these context-aware lists are made.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Ask a chatbot three times.

1. What does "bat" mean?
2. In "A bat flew out of the cave at sunset," what does "bat" mean?
3. In "He swung the bat and hit a home run," what does "bat" mean?

In question 1, did it list several meanings, or pick the most common one? In 2 and 3, did it use the context to pick the right meaning? Then try another word with several meanings, like "bank," "light," or "bass."

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Name the field and the situation first. For example: "In a legal contract, what does 'consideration' mean?"
  2. Spell out words that could be confusing. "Bass (the fish)" is clearer than "bass."
  3. Define technical terms. Saying "Here, X means this" cuts down on mix-ups.
  4. When translating, give the context too. Translate a single word alone, and you may get the wrong meaning.
  5. If an answer seems off, suspect a misunderstood word. Ask, "What did you take 'X' to mean?" That often shows the cause.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "AI gives each word one fixed meaning." Each word starts with one location, then context moves it.
  • "AI knows what I mean even without context." Without context, it goes with the most common meaning.
  • "Once it picks a meaning, it keeps it for the whole chat." It works out each new sentence again with its new context.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • 3Blue1Brown (Grant Sanderson), Transformers, the tech behind LLMs, 2024-04-01. The first embedding is a lookup for each token, and embeddings get updated and soak in context as they pass through the network. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Matthew E. Peters and others, Deep contextualized word representations, arXiv, 2018-02-15. Context-aware representations, modeling words with several meanings, a two-direction language model, and improvements on six tasks come from the abstract.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: The note about what different layers do sums up general observations. We didn't check a specific source for it. The "bat" examples are ours.

docs.title: Tokens become lists of numbers
docs.text:
Ch. 10 · 10.1About 6 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • A chatbot turns each token into an ID number, then turns each ID into its own long list of numbers (a vector) to do its math.
  • People don't choose these numbers. They get set during training.
  • Each list of numbers works like a "location for meaning."

docs.title: From an address to coordinates
docs.text:
An address like "1600 Pennsylvania Avenue, Washington, DC" means something to people. But a map app turns it into two numbers, latitude and longitude, to work out distances. It needs numbers to do math.

A chatbot is the same. In Chapter 1, text got split into tokens. A computer can't do math on letters directly (a neural network works with numbers). So each token gets an ID number, and each ID is turned into a list of many numbers (a vector). This step is called embedding.

In 10-year-old words

A token is like an address, and its embedding is like map coordinates. Once you have coordinates, you can measure distances.

docs.title: What a list of numbers looks like
docs.text:
For example, the token "potato" might become a list like this. (We made these numbers up and cut each list to 3 numbers to keep it simple.)

Token List of numbers (made-up example) potato 0.8, −0.2, 0.5 sweet potato 0.7, −0.1, 0.6 car −0.6, 0.9, 0.1

Real lists are much longer than 3. According to 3Blue1Brown's lesson, in GPT-3 each token becomes a list of 12,288 numbers. Its vocabulary has 50,257 tokens.

docs.title: The lookup table is the model's first part
docs.text:
The lookup table that turns token IDs into lists of numbers is the model's first part. 3Blue1Brown's lesson calls it the embedding matrix. Its values start out random and are learned during training. With 12,288 numbers for each of 50,257 tokens, this first step alone uses about 618 million numbers (617,558,016). These numbers are also part of the parameters from Chapter 9.

In other words, people don't decide which list each token gets. The model figures it out while practicing next-word guessing.

docs.title: Why lists of numbers?
docs.text:
• To do math. Everything inside the model is number crunching.
  • To show what's similar. A single ID can't show that "potato" and "sweet potato" are alike. With lists of numbers, nearby lists can stand for similar meanings (next page).
  • To handle new words. A word it has never seen can be split into known pieces, and each piece has its own list (tokens, Chapter 1).

★ Going deeper

  • Representing words as lists of numbers was common well before transformers. In 2013, Tomas Mikolov and others proposed two quick ways to learn word vectors from very large text collections. They reported learning good word vectors from 1.6 billion words in less than a day. This is the paper behind the well-known tool word2vec.
  • The list length (12,288) is a design choice made by the model's builders. 3Blue1Brown explains that very long lists give room for many different directions, which turns out to be useful.
  • Images and sound can also be turned into lists of numbers and handled in the same space as text (multimodal, Chapter 4).

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Do the math. See how big these numbers are.

  1. What is 50,257 × 12,288? Use a calculator. (It's 617,558,016.)
  2. About what percent is that of GPT-3's 175 billion parameters? (About 0.35%. This first step is huge, but it's a tiny slice of the whole.)

A quick puzzle. Which two of these tokens probably have the closest lists of numbers: "cat," "dog," "refrigerator"? (We can't be sure, but "cat" and "dog" are the likely pair. The next page explains why.)

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Spell key words exactly. A different spelling means a different token, which means a different list of numbers. This matters most for names.
  2. It's fine to try other words for the same idea. Similar meanings have similar lists, so you usually get similar answers.
  3. Spell out unusual abbreviations and slang. Rare words may split into many pieces or have fuzzy meanings.
  4. This is part of why the same idea works across languages. But the number of pieces can differ by language (Chapter 1).
  5. Don't try to read the numbers yourself. The meaning isn't in any single number. It's in where the whole list points.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "AI stores dictionary definitions of words." It stores lists of numbers learned in training, not a dictionary.
  • "Each number in the list means one thing." The meaning comes from the whole list's position, not from single numbers.
  • "Tokens with close ID numbers have close meanings." IDs are just labels given in order. It's the lists of numbers that need to be close.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • 3Blue1Brown (Grant Sanderson), Transformers, the tech behind LLMs, 2024-04-01. The embedding matrix, a vocabulary of 50,257, a dimension of 12,288, 617,558,016 weights, and values learned in training. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Tomas Mikolov and others, Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space, arXiv, 2013-01-16. We summarized the abstract.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: The numbers in the lesson are for GPT-3. Today's models differ. The 3-number lists in the table are made up. We worked out 0.35% ourselves (617,558,016 ÷ 175,000,000,000).

docs.title: Ch. 11 Attention
docs.text:
How a chatbot decides which parts of the text to look at.

11.1.1Attention: picking out what matters6 min read 11.1.2What one transformer layer looks like6 min read 11.1.3The context window: how much it sees at once5 min read

docs.title: Attention: picking out what matters
docs.text:
Ch. 11 · 11.1About 7 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Attention is a tool that lets each token in the text decide "Where should I look right now?" and pull in what it finds there.
  • Each token asks a question (a query). Other tokens answer with a key. The token takes in information (a value) from the best matches.
  • Many of these run at once (several "heads"), so the model sees many kinds of connections.

docs.title: Highlighting while you read
docs.text:
When you're reading a long passage and you hit the word "it," you look back and ask, "What was 'it' again?" You don't treat every word as equally important. You highlight what you need right now.

Attention is a tool built so the model does exactly this.

In 10-year-old words

Attention lets every word decide "Where should I look right now?" It highlights what it needs and pulls that in.

docs.title: Example: a fluffy blue creature
docs.text:
3Blue1Brown's lesson uses this sentence: "A fluffy blue creature roamed the verdant forest."

At the start, "creature" has the plain location for "creature," with no context (Chapter 10). But in front of it are "fluffy" and "blue." Attention adds what those describing words carry to the location of "creature." That moves it to a location that stands for "a fluffy, blue creature."

docs.title: Query, key, and value
docs.text:
The lesson breaks the process into three parts.

  1. Query. Imagine the noun "creature" asking, "Are there any describing words in front of me?" That question is also made into a list of numbers (a vector).
  2. Key. The other tokens offer an answer, like "I'm a describing word," as their key. The better a key matches the query, the higher the score.
  3. Value. The content (value) of high-scoring tokens is added to the asking token's location. The value from "fluffy" is added to "creature," and its location moves toward "fluffy creature."

The steps that make queries, keys, and values are also numbers set during training (Chapter 9). Nobody taught it "describing words change nouns." Rules like that grow because they help with next-word guessing.

docs.title: The score table: the attention pattern
docs.text:
When every token scores every other token, you get a grid. Each column is adjusted so it adds up to 1, with the same math (called softmax) that makes the score table from Chapter 1. The lesson calls this grid the attention pattern. Each column shows how much one token should pay attention to each of the others.

Masking. In models like GPT, later tokens are blocked from changing earlier ones. When it's practicing next-word guessing, it mustn't peek at the answer (what comes later).

docs.title: Many sets of eyes
docs.text:
Looking at only one kind of connection, like describing words and nouns, isn't enough. The model also needs to see who did what, when things happened, and what a word points to. So it runs many attention steps at once. Each one is called a head. According to the lesson, GPT-3 uses 96 attention heads in each block. Each head has its own query, key, and value steps, so each one can track a different kind of connection.

★ Going deeper

  • The transformer, a design built around attention, comes from a 2017 paper called Attention Is All You Need by Ashish Vaswani and others. Earlier translation models were built from more complicated parts. The transformer dropped them and used attention alone. It translated better, was easier to run in parallel, and trained much faster. On English to French translation, it set a new record after training for 3.5 days on eight graphics chips (GPUs).
  • The attention described above is self-attention. There is also cross-attention, where queries and keys come from two different sources, like two languages in translation.
  • The lesson works out that one head has about 6.3 million parameters. GPT-3 has 96 layers, with 96 heads in each. Altogether, attention uses just under 58 billion parameters, about a third of GPT-3's total.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Play the attention game. Read this and answer the question.

Maya lent Jordan a book. She was grateful.

Who is "she"? You probably said Jordan, even though "Jordan" could be anyone. Where did you put your highlighter? On "lent" and "grateful," probably. Now change one word:

Maya lent Jordan a book. She was proud.

Now who is "she"? One changed word moved where you put the highlighter. That's what attention does.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Use names instead of "it" or "this." When it's clear what a word points to, the chatbot is less likely to look in the wrong place.
  2. Keep key conditions close to your question. Conditions near the question are less likely to be missed.
  3. Cut stories that don't matter. The more there is to look at, the more its attention is split.
  4. Label things that could get mixed up. Names like "Document A" and "Document B" keep attention from getting confused (Chapter 6).
  5. If an answer is strange, ask "What does that refer to?" You can guess where the chatbot was looking.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "AI reads a sentence one word at a time, from the start." Attention connects all the tokens to each other at once. (Later words still can't change earlier ones.)
  • "Attention is the same as human attention." It's a comparison. In reality, it's a score table being computed.
  • "It looks at only one thing at a time." Many heads look at different connections at the same time.

docs.title: The context window: how much it sees at once
docs.text:
Ch. 11 · 11.1About 6 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • There's a limit to how much text a chatbot can see at once. That range is its context window.
  • Your whole chat and its new answer all have to fit inside, and the longer it gets, the more accuracy can drop.
  • Even as windows grow, choosing what goes in still matters.

docs.title: The size of a desk
docs.text:
How many books and notebooks you can spread out depends on the size of your desk. A small desk holds a few. A big desk holds many. But if the desk is a total mess, even a big one makes it hard to find what you need.

The context window is the chatbot's desk. Everything it can look at while writing an answer has to be on that desk.

In 10-year-old words

The context window is the chatbot's desk. It can only see what's on the desk, and if the desk is too messy, it gets confused.

docs.title: Why is there a limit?
docs.text:
3Blue1Brown's lesson explains that a transformer can only look at a fixed number of vectors at a time. That number is its context size. GPT-3 was trained with a context size of 2,048 tokens. The lesson says this limit is why, in long chats with early versions of ChatGPT, the bot seemed to lose the thread of the conversation.

There's a deeper reason too. The attention pattern from the earlier page is a grid where every token looks at every token. So its size is the context size squared. Double the tokens, and there are four times as many cells to work out. The lesson says this is why growing the context size isn't easy, and that researchers have come up with many changes to the design to make bigger contexts possible.

docs.title: How big is it now?
docs.text:
It's grown a lot since 2,048 tokens in 2020. Anthropic's docs (read on 2026-11-09) say many current Claude models have a context window of up to 1 million tokens, and some others have 200,000. The docs describe the context window as the whole conversation so far plus the new answer. Each turn, the full earlier conversation and your new message go in as input, and the answer piles up after them.

These numbers depend on the model, the service, and your plan. Check your own service's help pages for its limits.

docs.title: Bigger isn't automatically better
docs.text:
Anthropic's docs make this point clearly. A bigger window lets a model handle longer, more complicated input, but more context isn't automatically better. As the number of tokens grows, accuracy and recall drop. They call this context rot. So choosing what goes into the window matters as much as how much fits.

The study from Chapter 6, "Lost in the Middle," points the same way. Models did much worse when the key information sat in the middle of a long input (with the models of 2023).

★ Going deeper

  • When the window fills up, some services drop or summarize older parts to make room. Anthropic's docs present server-side compaction, where earlier parts get summarized automatically, as the main way to manage long conversations and agent tasks. Each service does this its own way.
  • Every token in the context also affects cost and speed (pricing by the token, Chapter 4). So cutting out what isn't needed helps with accuracy and with cost.
  • What a model saw during training (its knowledge) is different from what's in its context window (its working memory). It can refer to text in the context exactly, but it remembers training text only fuzzily. That's why pasting in your own material cuts down on made-up answers (Chapter 1).

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Play "the desk game." In a single chat, do this:

  1. At the very start, write: "My secret code is potato-1019. Remember it."
  2. Ask 10 to 20 unrelated questions. (Questions with long answers work best.)
  3. At the end, ask: "What was my secret code?"

Did it remember? Some services remember well even in very long chats, and some lose it. Either way, you get a feel for how the "stuff on the desk" is handled. (Results differ by service.)

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Put key conditions at the start and the end. The middle of a long input is easy to miss (Chapter 6).
  2. When a chat gets long, summarize it and move to a new chat. You learned this in Chapter 2.
  3. Paste in only the parts you need. Putting in more doesn't mean it understands more.
  4. Don't fill the window just because it's big. Organized input is more accurate and faster.
  5. Check your service's limits. Knowing them helps you understand "Why did it forget?"

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "A chatbot always remembers the whole chat perfectly." Even inside the window, it can miss things as the chat grows. And it can't see anything outside the window at all.
  • "With a 1-million-token window, ten books is no problem." Fitting in and being used well are not the same.
  • "It still knows everything when I open a new chat." A new chat starts with an empty desk (except for services with a separate memory feature).

docs.title: What one transformer layer looks like
docs.text:
Ch. 11 · 11.1About 6 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • A transformer is built from an attention block and another kind of block (an MLP), taking turns, repeated many times.
  • At the very end, the last vector becomes the score table for the next token.
  • Because there are so many layers, it's called "deep" learning.

docs.title: A factory conveyor belt
docs.text:
Picture a factory. A product rides a conveyor belt. The first machine shapes it, the second paints it, then it gets shaped and painted again and again. At the end, out comes the finished product.

A transformer is similar. Each token's list of numbers passes through the same kind of workstation many times, and it carries a richer meaning each time.

In 10-year-old words

It's a conveyor belt where the lists of numbers take turns "gathering info" (attention) and "thinking it over" (MLP), many times, getting smarter each time.

docs.title: The big picture
docs.text:
Here's the overall flow that 3Blue1Brown's lesson shows.

  1. Split into tokens (Chapter 1).
  2. Embedding: give each token a list of numbers (Chapter 10).
  3. Attention block: tokens share information with each other (the previous page).
  4. MLP block (multilayer perceptron): each list of numbers gets polished on its own. The lesson compares this to asking each vector a long list of questions, then updating it based on the answers.
  5. Repeat steps 3 and 4 many times. Attention, MLP, attention, MLP, and so on. Having this many layers is the "deep" in deep learning.
  6. Make the score table from the last vector: all the information ends up in the last vector. A final step turns it into chances for every possible next piece (the score table from Chapter 1).

docs.title: What the two blocks do
docs.text:
Block What it does Comparison Attention Shares information between tokens Group work: talking with others to gather information MLP Works on information inside one token Solo note-taking: thinking over what you gathered

Almost all of this math is matrix multiplication, which is big blocks of multiplying and adding numbers. The lesson calls a transformer a giant pile of matrix multiplications. It says understanding how to read those matrices is key to understanding the model.

docs.title: The last vector's job
docs.text:
After all the layers, the list of numbers for the last token must hold everything needed to predict the next word. The lesson gives an example. Say the text is about Harry Potter, and the last word is "Professor." To predict what comes next, the last vector needs to carry "this is a Harry Potter story, and the last word is Professor." That makes "Snape" a likely next word.

From that last vector, the model works out a score for every token. Turning those scores into chances gives you the score table from Chapter 1. Once it draws a token, it adds that token to the input and runs the whole thing again.

★ Going deeper

  • At each layer, the new information is added on to what was already there, instead of replacing it. This is called a residual connection, and it helps deep models train well. (We didn't confirm the lesson's exact explanation of this, so treat it as a general note.)
  • How MLP blocks might store facts is the topic of the next lesson in the series, How might LLMs store facts (Deep Learning Chapter 7).
  • The 2017 Attention Is All You Need design had two halves for translation, an encoder and a decoder. Models like GPT are generally described as closer to the decoder half. The exact names of the parts differ from model to model.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Draw the factory. On a sheet of paper, draw this:

[text] → [tokens] → [lists of numbers] → [attention] → [MLP] → [attention] → [MLP] → ... → [score table] → [next token]

Now label each step with the page you learned it on: 1.1.2 tokens, Chapter 10 embeddings, Chapter 11 attention, 1.1.1 the next word. Any gaps? Chapter 12 covers the last arrow: drawing from the score table.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Remember "one token at a time." The whole structure runs once to pick a single token. That's why long answers take time.
  2. Many layers doesn't mean it's always right. A complicated design is not proof of accuracy.
  3. Know where answers differ. The same question goes through the same math. The answers differ because of the draw at the end (Chapter 12).
  4. It's fine to skip the structure if it feels hard. To ask good questions, knowing about attention and context is enough.
  5. Want more? Watch the lessons. We recommend 3Blue1Brown's deep learning series.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "AI is built just like a human brain." That's a comparison, not a fact. They are not the same.
  • "More layers always means smarter." Size, data, and tuning all matter together (Chapter 9).
  • "Each layer does one clear human-like job." What each layer does is still being studied (Chapter 19).

docs.title: Ch. 12 Building Sentences with Probability
docs.text:
How the next word is drawn from a score sheet, and why answers change every time.

12.1.1Temperature: how adventurous to be5 min read 12.1.2Sampling: how it draws5 min read 12.1.3How a long answer keeps going5 min read

docs.title: How a long answer keeps going
docs.text:
Ch. 12 · 12.1About 5 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • A long answer is draw one token, add it to the input, and run the math again, over and over.
  • Once a word is drawn, it can't be taken back, and it affects every choice after it.
  • For long writing, get an outline first and write it in parts. The flow drifts less.

docs.title: A relay race
docs.text:
In a relay race, one runner runs and then hands the baton to the next. If the first runner stumbles, the next one has to start from wherever things stand. Nobody gets to run that leg over again.

That's how a long answer gets made. Each time a token is drawn, the baton (everything written so far) passes along, and what's already written can't change.

In 10-year-old words

A long answer is a relay race. A leg that's been run can't be redone, and the next leg starts from there.

docs.title: The life of one token
docs.text:
3Blue1Brown's lesson describes a simple way to make long text with a prediction model:

  1. Give it some starting text.
  2. Predict the next word. (Make the score table.)
  3. Draw one at random from the chances. (The last two pages.)
  4. Add it to the end of the text.
  5. Use the whole text, new word included, as input, and predict again.

This predict-and-draw loop is what happens when you chat with ChatGPT. That's why the words seem to come out one at a time, and why text appears bit by bit on the screen.

docs.title: What makes the relay tricky
docs.text:
Feature Result A drawn word can't be taken back A slip early on carries through to the end Earlier text becomes later input Phrases used early tend to repeat later The whole thing is recalculated every time Long answers take time and cost more On the surface, it adds one token at a time (inside, it may look ahead) The longer the piece, the more the flow can drift

That doesn't mean the model never plans. Research suggests some of its inner math looks ahead (see "Going deeper"). But on the surface, a token that's been drawn can't be undone.

★ Going deeper

  • Anthropic's interpretability research reported a surprise with poems. The researchers expected the model not to look ahead, but they found it planning in advance. Before writing a line, it picked a rhyme word for the end and then wrote toward it. So even a one-token-at-a-time design can do math that considers what comes later. Chapter 19 goes into this.
  • Having it write out its thinking in the middle before answering often makes answers more accurate, because that text gives later choices something to build on ("think step by step," Chapter 7). Today's reasoning models are trained to think at length before answering (Chapter 20).
  • In long writing, what's already written takes up room in the context window and affects later choices (Chapter 11). The longer the text so far, the longer the input, and the more math each new token needs.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Ask for a long piece in two ways.

1. Write a 300-word post introducing our town library.

2. I want to write a 300-word post introducing our town library.
   First, suggest an outline of 5 paragraphs (one line each). Don't write it yet.
   (I'll fix the outline, and then we'll write it paragraph by paragraph.)

Does the first one drift from its topic or repeat itself near the end? If you get an outline with the second one and write a paragraph at a time, how does the flow change?

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Get an outline first for long writing. If the direction is wrong, you can fix it early (Chapter 5).
  2. Have it write paragraph by paragraph. The shorter each stretch, the less it drifts.
  3. Check more closely toward the end. Contradictions with earlier parts and repetition show up there.
  4. Set length with a number, but treat it as rough. "Under 300 words" may not be exact (tokens, Chapter 1).
  5. If an answer stops in the middle, say "Keep going." It often hit a length limit (Chapter 11).

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "AI plans the whole piece and then writes it." On the surface, it draws one token at a time and keeps going. Inside, some math may look ahead.
  • "A long answer means it tried hard." Length and accuracy are separate.
  • "If I ask it to fix one part, the rest will adjust to match." Check that the whole thing still fits together.

docs.title: Sampling: how it draws
docs.text:
Ch. 12 · 12.1About 5 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • How the next word gets drawn from the score table (called decoding or sampling) can change the quality of writing a lot, even with the same model.
  • Always taking the top choice tends to make bland, repetitive writing.
  • Methods like "nucleus sampling" (top-p) cut out the weird long-shot choices first, then draw from the rest.

docs.title: The friend who always orders the same thing
docs.text:
Imagine a friend who always orders the most popular dish at every restaurant. It never goes wrong, but they eat the same thing every time, which gets boring. On the other hand, if you close your eyes and point at the menu, you'll sometimes end up with something really strange.

Drawing the next word from the score table swings between safe and varied in the same way.

In 10-year-old words

Always picking number one gets boring. Picking anything at all gets weird. So it picks evenly from just the good choices.

docs.title: Three ways to draw
docs.text: Method How it draws Result Always the top choice Always the most likely token Steady, but bland and easily repetitive Draw by the odds Roll dice weighted by the score table Varied, but odd long shots get picked now and then Trim, then draw First drop the weird long shots, then draw by the odds from what's left Varied, and less strange

docs.title: What research found
docs.text:
A 2019 paper by Ari Holtzman and others, The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration, found a puzzle.

  • Models are trained to make likely text more likely, and that makes them good at many language tasks. But when you make them write the single most likely text, it comes out bland and strangely repetitive.
  • Human writing and machine writing showed surprising differences in how their word choices are spread out.
  • With the exact same model, the drawing method alone can change the quality of writing a lot.

The paper proposed nucleus sampling as a fix. It draws only from the "core" of the chances and cuts off the unreliable tail, the choices with very low chances. The authors reported that this keeps variety while staying smooth and on track, so the writing looks more like human writing. A setting called "top-p" that you may see in some tools comes from this family of methods. (That's a general note.)

docs.title: How this connects to your questions
docs.text:
• When a chatbot keeps repeating the same phrases, this may be part of the reason.
  • The same question gets slightly different answers because of the draw (Chapter 1).
  • Services often set the drawing method and temperature themselves. You usually can't change them.

★ Going deeper

  • Common ways to trim choices include top-k, which keeps only the k most likely choices, and top-p (nucleus sampling), which keeps choices until their chances add up to p. The key idea in the paper is that the "nucleus" isn't a fixed number of choices. It grows or shrinks with the shape of the chances. (We didn't confirm the definition of top-k in this page's sources.)
  • The paper shows something interesting: "most likely" is not the same as "good." Writing we like is often not the single most likely text. That ties back to the last page: always taking the top choice is bland.
  • This is a 2019 study. Services differ in how much they share about the exact methods they use today.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Ask a chatbot:

Write one paragraph of a story that starts with "When I woke up this morning."

Get three of them. Do the sentence patterns or words repeat? Then ask:

Same opening, but this time go in a completely different direction
from the first three. Don't reuse any of the same phrases.

Compare what changed. You'll see the effect of asking for more varied choices in your question.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. If answers are bland or repetitive, ask for "something different from before." You can't change the drawing method, but you can change your question.
  2. Get several and pick. "Give me 5 very different versions" is the surest way.
  3. If a phrase keeps coming back, ban it. For example: "Don't use the word 'innovative.'"
  4. If an answer is odd, try again. A strange choice may have been drawn just once.
  5. Don't leave jobs that need exact answers to the draw. They need a checking step.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "AI always picks the single most likely word." Usually it draws by the odds. Always taking the top choice actually makes writing bland.
  • "Drawing more variety lowers quality." The paper found that trimming first gives you both variety and quality.
  • "I can't change the settings, so there's nothing I can do." You can change your question to steer variety and repetition.

docs.text:

  • 3Blue1Brown (Grant Sanderson), Transformers, the tech behind LLMs, 2024-04-01. Sampling from the distribution and adding to the text.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09

docs.title: Temperature: how adventurous to be
docs.text:
Ch. 12 · 12.1About 5 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Temperature is a setting that decides how much to favor the most popular choices when drawing the next word from the score table.
  • At high temperature, choices get drawn more evenly. At low temperature, the top choice wins almost every time.
  • Setting the temperature to 0 doesn't get rid of wrong answers.

docs.title: How many of each ball in the box
docs.text:
Picture a box of balls: 30 red, 20 blue, and 15 yellow. Red comes up most often, but the others come up too. (That's the score table from Chapter 1.)

Temperature is a dial that changes the box. Turn it down, and there are even more red balls and fewer of the others, so you get red almost every time. Turn it up, and the counts even out, so blue and yellow come up more often.

In 10-year-old words

Temperature is an adventure dial. Turn it down and it always takes the safe path. Turn it up and it sometimes takes a strange path.

docs.title: How the lesson explains temperature
docs.text:
3Blue1Brown's lesson explains it like this. In the last step, a bit of math called softmax turns scores into chances. If you add a number T to that math, you can change how spread out the chances are. It's called "temperature" because it looks like temperature in physics.

  • When T is large: lower scores get more weight, so the chances are spread more evenly. Draws become more varied.
  • When T is small: the biggest scores take over. The top choice gets picked almost every time.
  • When T is 0: all the weight goes to the biggest score. In theory, the same top choice gets picked every time. (In real services, "temperature 0" doesn't promise exactly the same answer every time.)

docs.title: Low and high temperature
docs.text:
Low temperature High temperature What answers look like Safe and similar Varied, sometimes strange Asking the same thing again Nearly the same answer Different answers each time Good for Jobs with one right answer, like sorting facts, summaries, labeling Jobs that need variety, like ideas, names, creative writing

(The "Good for" row sums up common practice. Every job is different, so test it yourself.)

docs.title: What temperature can't do
docs.text:
• Lowering the temperature doesn't remove hallucinations. If the top choice on the score table is wrong, a low temperature makes it pick that wrong choice more consistently. Low temperature means "steady," not "correct."
  • High temperature doesn't promise creativity. It just lets less common words come up, which can be merely odd.
  • Many apps hide the temperature. In most everyday chatbot apps, you won't see a dial. Developer settings (an API) sometimes have one, but whether you can change it, and how far, depends on the model and the service.

★ Going deeper

  • The raw scores before they become chances are called logits. Temperature works by dividing the logits by T before softmax. (The lesson describes this as putting T in the exponent.)
  • Temperature 0 is the same as always taking the top choice, which is called greedy decoding. Research shows that this doesn't always make good writing (next page).
  • Some services may give slightly different results even at temperature 0, for example because of tiny differences in how the math runs. We didn't confirm a source for this, so treat it as a note to check.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Make the same request three times, then try changing the "temperature" with your wording.

1. Give me 5 names for a cafe that's perfect on rainy days. (Ask this three times.)
2. Give me 5 of the most common, safe names.
3. Give me 5 really unusual, quirky names.

How different were the three tries of question 1? How did 2 and 3 differ? You'll see that wording can have a similar effect. (Wording doesn't change the temperature itself. It changes the score table.)

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. For jobs that must be right, rely on checking, not on "steady." Wrong answers can stay even at low temperature.
  2. For ideas, ask for several. "Give me 10" has an effect a bit like a higher temperature.
  3. If the answers feel bland, say "more unusual." Wording can add variety.
  4. Different answers to the same question are normal. For answers that matter, get a few and compare (Chapter 3).
  5. If your tool shows a temperature setting, experiment. The best value differs by job.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "Temperature 0 makes it accurate." It makes it consistent, not accurate.
  • "Higher temperature makes it more cleverly creative." It just lets less common words through.
  • "Every chatbot lets you set the temperature." Many hide it and don't let you change it.

docs.title: Ch. 13 AI That Uses Tools
docs.text:
What changes when you connect a chatbot to search, files, and tools.

13.1.1What changes when you add search6 min read 13.1.2AI that reads files and runs code5 min read 13.1.3The standard for connecting tools: MCP5 min read

docs.title: The standard for connecting tools: MCP
docs.text:
Ch. 13 · 13.1About 5 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a shared standard for connecting AI apps to outside systems, like files, databases, and tools.
  • It's like a USB-C port: one kind of plug for many devices.
  • Connecting something means giving permission, so deciding how much to allow matters.

docs.title: A USB-C port
docs.text:
Not long ago, every phone had a different charger, so you'd pack several for a trip. A shared standard called USB-C fixed that with one plug.

AI had a similar problem. To connect a chatbot to a calendar, a notes app, or a database, someone had to build a separate connection for each service. MCP is an attempt to give these connections a shared standard.

In 10-year-old words

MCP is AI's USB-C port. With one kind of plug, you can connect lots of tools.

docs.title: What the official MCP docs say
docs.text:
The official MCP docs describe it this way. MCP is an open-source standard for connecting AI apps to outside systems. With it, AI apps like Claude or ChatGPT can connect to:

  • data sources (files on your computer, databases),
  • tools (search engines, calculators),
  • workflows (special prompts),

so they can reach important information and get things done. The docs compare MCP to "a USB-C port for AI applications."

The docs give examples of what it makes possible. An agent can use your Google Calendar and Notion to act as a more personal assistant. Claude Code can build a whole web app from a Figma design. A company chatbot can connect to many databases so people can analyze data by chatting. And an AI can make a 3D design in Blender and print it on a 3D printer.

docs.title: Who benefits?
docs.text:
Who Benefit (from the docs) Developers Less time and complexity when building or connecting AI apps and agents AI apps and agents Access to a wide set of data, tools, and apps, which makes them more capable Everyday users More capable AI that can reach your data and act for you when needed

The docs say MCP is supported by many apps, including Claude, ChatGPT, Visual Studio Code, and Cursor.

docs.title: Connecting means giving permission
docs.text:
Once you connect a tool, the chatbot can read your data or act on your behalf. That's handy, and it raises the risk too.

  • Tell reading apart from writing. Should it only view your calendar, or also create and delete events?
  • Allow only what's needed. "This one folder," not "all my files."
  • Use connections only from sources you trust. If you don't know who made it, don't use it.
  • Read approval requests. When the chatbot asks "May I do this?", read what it wants before you approve.
  • Do things that can't be undone yourself. Deleting, paying, and sending things outside should be done by a person.

★ Going deeper

  • The MCP docs have a separate security section. Outside connections can open a path for prompt injection (Chapter 2): text a connected tool pulls in might hide instructions. We didn't read the security section in detail for this page.
  • MCP servers can run on your own computer (local) or somewhere else (remote). A local server can more easily reach your files. A remote one can more easily reach outside services. (What it can actually reach depends on its setup and permissions.) The risks are different.
  • A standard also makes tools easier to swap. Apps that support MCP can reuse the same connections.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Look in your AI app for a menu called something like "Connections," "Connectors," "Apps," or "Extensions."

  1. What can it connect to? (Calendar, file storage, notes, and so on.)
  2. What permissions does each connection ask for? (Read only? Write too?)
  3. Where do you go to disconnect?

You don't have to connect anything. Just reading the permission screens is good practice.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Read the permission list before you connect. Ask yourself whether read-only would be enough.
  2. Start small. Try it with one folder or one calendar.
  3. Disconnect what you don't use. Permissions stay open even when you're not using them.
  4. Be careful with important accounts. Think hard before connecting work accounts or anything that handles payments.
  5. Don't click "approve" out of habit. Check that the action is what you actually wanted.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "MCP is the name of an AI model." It's not a model. It's a standard for connections.
  • "It's a standard, so it's safe." Having a standard doesn't make every connected server or its content safe.
  • "Once it's connected, the chatbot will handle everything." What it can do depends on the connected tool and on what you approve.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Model Context Protocol, What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?, official docs (version 2026-07-28). The definition, the USB-C comparison, the examples, the benefits, and the list of supporting apps. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: The five permission tips and the read/write distinction are our own practical tips. We didn't read MCP's security section in detail. The link to prompt injection is a general explanation. The MCP docs are updated often.

docs.title: AI that reads files and runs code
docs.text:
Ch. 13 · 13.1About 6 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Chatbots can read files, and some can write code, run it, and bring back the results.
  • For things that must be exact, like math, tables, and charts, code is more reliable than the chatbot just talking.
  • But watch for personal details in files, hidden instructions, and wrong code.

docs.title: A student with a calculator and pencil
docs.text:
Try big multiplication on a test with no calculator or pencil, and mistakes come easily. With a calculator and pencil, you get it right. The student didn't suddenly get smarter. They got to use tools.

As Chapter 7 showed, chatbots can slip on long math. But if they write code and have a computer run it, the math comes out exact. That's what a code execution tool does.

In 10-year-old words

When a chatbot gets a calculator and pencil (running code), its math and tables get much more accurate. But you still need to check what it calculated.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
It's the same kind of tool use as on the last page. According to Anthropic's tool use docs, when the chatbot wants a tool, it sends back a structured request to call it, and either your app or Anthropic runs it. Anthropic's code execution tool runs Python and Bash code in a sandboxed container to analyze data and make files. Roughly, it goes like this:

  1. You ask: "Add up the monthly sales in this file and make a chart."
  2. The chatbot writes code that does the job.
  3. The code runs, and results come out (numbers, a chart).
  4. The chatbot reads the results and explains them to you.

So the math is done by the computer, not by the chatbot "talking." Anthropic's docs also list a web fetch tool that pulls in the full content of web pages and PDFs.

docs.title: What happens when you upload a file
docs.text:
• The file gets turned into text the chatbot can read (a PDF may also be handled as page images), and goes into the context (Chapter 6). Tables and charts can get scrambled along the way.
  • If the file is long, it may only be able to read part of it, because of the context limit (Chapter 11).
  • Allowed file types and sizes differ by service.

docs.title: Jobs where running code helps
docs.text: Job Why Totals, averages, percentages Code does math exactly Cleaning tables, removing duplicates, changing formats These follow clear rules Making charts Code can draw pictures Handling lots of files at once Code is good at repeating things

docs.title: What to watch for
docs.text:
• See which code ran. If the formula is wrong, an exact value is still a wrong answer (Chapter 7). Ask "Show me the code you ran."
  • Check files for personal details. Uploaded files are sent to the service (Chapter 3).
  • Files can hide instructions. A document someone sent you might hide a line like "Ignore your earlier instructions," and the chatbot might follow it (prompt injection, Chapter 2).
  • Keep the original separately. Don't let a converted file replace your original.
  • Check a few lines of the result yourself. For a table, work out a few rows by hand.

★ Going deeper

  • A sandbox is a walled-off space, set up so the code can't touch your own computer. But some tools run code directly on your computer, like a terminal tool. Those have much more power, and much more risk. Chapter 14 on agents comes back to this.
  • A tool call may not happen just once. It's common to look at the result, fix the code, and run it again (Chapter 14).
  • The step-by-step flow above is a general description. Each service builds it differently.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
If your service lets you upload files and run code:

  1. Make a small table (5 to 10 rows). Columns for name, date, and amount work well. Use fake names.
  2. Upload it and say:
Add up the amounts by month and show me a table.
Also show me the code you used, so I can see what you calculated.
  1. Compare the result with your own math. Read which columns the code used, and how.

If your service can't run code, you can do the same thing by asking for a spreadsheet formula (Chapter 7).

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. For exact math, ask it to run code. Some services understand "Use code to calculate this."
  2. Ask to see the code it ran. Even if you can't read code, you can usually spot the column names and conditions.
  3. Remove personal details before uploading. Once you upload a file, it's been sent.
  4. Upload a copy, not your original. That protects it from accidental changes.
  5. Check part of the result by hand. About three rows is enough.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "If code did the math, it must be right." The math is exact, but if the formula is wrong, so is the answer.
  • "It read my file, so it understands all of it." With long or complicated files, it can miss parts.
  • "Running code is dangerous, so I shouldn't use it." Tools that run code in a sandbox are fairly safe. Tools with lots of power over your computer are the risky ones.

docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Anthropic, Tool use with Claude, Claude Platform Docs. Structured tool calls run by your app or by Anthropic, the code execution tool (Python and Bash in a sandboxed container), and the web fetch tool. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: How file conversion works differs by service, so that part is general. We didn't read the code execution tool's own page in full. The calculator-and-pencil comparison is ours.

docs.title: What changes when you add search
docs.text:
Ch. 13 · 13.1About 6 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Adding search to a chatbot turns a closed-book test into an open-book test.
  • Finding text close to the question, adding it in, and then answering is called RAG (retrieval-augmented generation).
  • It gets better at recent facts and sources, but what it finds can be wrong or summed up badly.

docs.title: An open-book test
docs.text:
On a closed-book test, you answer only from what's in your head. When your memory is fuzzy, you might make something up that sounds right (hallucination, Chapter 1). On an open-book test, you can open the textbook and look things up as you answer.

A chatbot with search is taking an open-book test. When a question comes in, it first finds related text, puts it on its desk (the context window, Chapter 11), and answers while looking at it.

In 10-year-old words

Adding search turns a closed-book test into an open-book test. Looking things up can make answers more accurate, but not if it opens the wrong book.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A question comes in. "What's our company's vacation policy?"
  2. It finds related text. It searches policy documents or web pages for the parts closest in meaning to the question. This uses "similar meanings sit close together" from Chapter 10 (meaning-based search).
  3. It puts what it found into the context, along with the question.
  4. The chatbot answers by reading that text. Often it shows the sources too.

docs.title: What the original paper said
docs.text: A 2020 paper by Patrick Lewis and others, Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks, gave this approach its name. Here's the problem they saw. Big language models store facts inside their parameters. But they're limited at reaching that knowledge and using it precisely. And two problems were still unsolved: showing where an answer came from, and keeping the knowledge up to date. So the researchers connected the model's own memory (its parameters) to an outside memory, in this case Wikipedia turned into searchable vectors. A search part pulled in what was needed. They reported top results at the time on three open question-answering tasks.

docs.title: How it calls tools
docs.text: Search is one kind of tool. Anthropic's tool use docs explain how tools work in general. Based on your request and each tool's description, Claude decides on its own when to call a tool. It sends back a structured request to call it. Then either your application runs it (client tools) or Anthropic runs it (server tools, like web search). With the web search tool, the search runs and the answer comes back with cited sources.

docs.title: What changes, and what doesn't
docs.text:
What changes What stays the same It can see recent information If what it found is wrong, the answer likely will be too It can show sources It can still sum up a source the wrong way It answers based on your own documents If it finds the wrong text, it gives a wrong answer It can know things after its training date The order of search results isn't the order of truth

★ Going deeper

  • In RAG, documents are usually cut into small chunks, and each chunk is turned into a vector and stored (Chapter 10). Then it fetches the chunks closest to the question's vector. How you cut the chunks and how many you fetch make a big difference.
  • A web page or document it finds may hide a line like "Ignore your earlier instructions and do this" (prompt injection, Chapter 2). With search turned on, the chatbot reads text you didn't write, so the risk goes up.
  • The paper used 2020 models and Wikipedia. Today's services work differently, and they share different amounts about how their search works.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
If you have a chatbot with search and one without (or a service where you can turn search on and off), compare them.

Tell me about one big AI-related news story from this week,
with the source and the date.
  1. How did the answer differ with search off and with search on?
  2. Open the source link from the search answer, and use the checks from Chapter 3. Does the source really say what the chatbot claims?

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Turn on search for recent information. Things that happened after training aren't in a plain answer.
  2. Ask for "the source and the date." That gives you a way to check.
  3. Open the sources and check them. See whether the chatbot's summary matches the original (Chapter 3).
  4. Don't put personal details in search questions. Your question may be passed on to a search service (Chapter 3).
  5. Ask for two different sources. For example: "Give me reasons for and against, each with its own source."

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "Adding search gets rid of hallucinations." It reduces them, but doesn't remove them. It can also misread what it found.
  • "If there's a source, it's true." The source itself may be wrong, or it may be summed up wrong.
  • "RAG means the model learns again every time." It doesn't retrain. It finds text and adds it in at answer time. (The paper's model combined parameter memory with outside memory.)

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Patrick Lewis and others, Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks, arXiv, 2020-05-22. Combining parameter memory with non-parametric memory, a vector index of Wikipedia, and top results on three open question-answering tasks come from the abstract.
  • Anthropic, Tool use with Claude, Claude Platform Docs. How Claude decides to call tools, client tools and server tools, and the web search tool's cited results. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Our earlier page: Similar meanings sit close together.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: The notes on chunking and prompt injection are general explanations, not confirmed in these sources. Most services don't publish how their search works, so we didn't describe it. The open-book comparison is ours.

docs.title: Ch. 14 Agents
docs.text:
What AI that plans and acts on its own is, and how it fails.

14.1.1What is an agent?6 min read 14.1.2Plan, act, check6 min read 14.1.3How agents fail6 min read

docs.title: How agents fail, and the guardrails
docs.text:
Ch. 14 · 14.1About 7 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Agents can fail by being easy to talk into things, repeating mistakes, and letting errors pile up.
  • Anthropic's office shop experiment, Project Vend, shows real examples.
  • The heart of a guardrail is giving an agent freedom while people stay in control.

docs.title: Put it in charge of a shop
docs.text:
In 2025, Anthropic tried a fun experiment. It let Claude run a small office shop (a mini fridge and a checkout tablet) for about a month. The project was called Project Vend. The agent got the nickname "Claudius," and it ran on the Claude Sonnet 3.7 model. Its tools were:

  • web search to find products and suppliers,
  • an email tool to contact wholesalers and ask for help (for the experiment, it couldn't send real emails),
  • a notes tool to keep key facts like its cash balance, because the full history would overflow its context window,
  • Slack to chat with customers (Anthropic employees),
  • the power to change prices at checkout.

Claudius decided what to sell, what to charge, and when to restock.

In 10-year-old words

They let an AI run a little shop. It was so nice and so eager to please that it lost money.

docs.title: The verdict: "We would not hire Claudius"
docs.text:
Anthropic was honest about the results. If it were deciding today to go into the office vending business, it wrote, "we would not hire Claudius." It made too many mistakes. Still, Anthropic added that most of the failures looked fixable, with better setup and better models.

What went well

  • Finding suppliers. When asked to stock a Dutch chocolate milk brand, it used web search to quickly find suppliers.
  • Adapting to customers. An employee jokingly asked for a tungsten cube, which kicked off a trend of "specialty metal items." It also started a pre-order service an employee suggested, called "Custom Concierge."
  • Resisting tricks. Employees tried to get it to misbehave, but it refused to order sensitive items or give harmful instructions.

What went poorly

  • Pricing. It raised a price only once (Sumo Citrus, from $2.50 to $2.95). It kept selling Coke Zero for $3.00, even after someone pointed out it was free in the employee fridge.
  • Talked into discounts. When people coaxed it on Slack, it handed out discount codes, and even gave things away for free, from a bag of chips to a tungsten cube.
  • Not learning from mistakes. An employee pointed out that 99% of its customers were Anthropic employees, so an employee discount made no sense. Claudius agreed and said it would end the discount codes. Within days, it was offering them again.
  • Missing a deal. Someone offered $100 for a six-pack of a soda that costs about $15 online. It only said it would keep the request in mind.

In the end, the shop didn't make money.

docs.title: Four ways agents fail
docs.text: Failure In this case Related idea Easy to talk into things Gave discounts and freebies when coaxed The habit of agreeing with people (Chapter 3) Repeats mistakes Agreed it was wrong, then went back to it Context piles up in long jobs, and things get missed (Chapter 11) Errors pile up One bad price stayed in place Anthropic's warning that errors can compound More power, more damage It could change prices and sell directly Connecting means giving permission (Chapter 13)

docs.title: Guardrails: people stay in control
docs.text:
In August 2025, Anthropic published a framework for safe and trustworthy agents. Its first principle is "keeping humans in control while enabling agent autonomy."

  • Agents are useful because they can work on their own. But people should keep control over how their goals are reached, especially before big decisions.
  • Example: a cost-tracking agent finds the company is overspending on software. It should get a person's approval before canceling any subscriptions.
  • Example: in Claude Code, people can stop it or change direction at any time. By default it's read-only. It asks for approval before changing code or systems. For routine jobs you trust it with, you can give it lasting permission.

The second principle is transparency. People should be able to see how the agent is solving the problem. Claude Code, for example, shows its planned steps as a live to-do list.

And the earlier post, Building effective agents, recommends testing agents a lot in a sandbox, with the right guardrails.

★ Going deeper

  • If text an agent reads (a web page, a document, an email) hides instructions, the agent may follow them. This is called prompt injection. OWASP's list of top risks for language model apps ranks it first, as LLM01. (We checked only that page's title and ranking.)
  • In Project Vend, the agent used a notes tool so its context window wouldn't overflow during the long job (Chapter 11). How an agent manages memory is a key problem for agents that work a long time.
  • The framework lists five principles in all. The other three cover lining agents up with human values, protecting privacy, and keeping agents' connections secure. We read only the first two in detail. The experiment used a 2025 model, and later models and setups may behave differently.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Imagine a job you'd give an agent, and fill in this safety checklist.

Item Your answer The job The tools and permissions it gets Read only? Or can it change things? Where a person must approve When it stops (number of tries, money, time) How to undo it if something goes wrong

If you can't fill in the boxes, it may be too early to hand off that job.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Start with the fewest permissions. Begin read-only, and add more only when needed.
  2. Leave big decisions to a person. Money, deleting, sending things outside, and contracts all need approval.
  3. Set limits. Caps on time, number of tries, and money.
  4. Know that coaxing works on agents. If outside people can talk to your agent, lock in its rules first.
  5. Test with practice material first. Not with important accounts or real money.
  6. Make sure you can undo things before you start. Backups, records, and a way to cancel.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "AI is smart, so it'll follow the rules on its own." Its eagerness to please can be a weakness.
  • "The experiment failed, so agents are useless." Anthropic said it sees ways to improve, and the agent did some things well.
  • "Guardrails slow agents down." If you only add approval steps for big decisions, most work still runs freely.
