docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Anthropic, Project Vend: Can Claude run a small shop?, 2025-06-27. The tools, the verdict, what went well and poorly, and the pricing and discount examples. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Anthropic, Our framework for developing safe and trustworthy agents, 2025-08-04. The five principles, with details from the first two. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Anthropic, Building effective agents, 2024-12-19. Testing in a sandbox, with guardrails.
  • OWASP, LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection. We checked only the title and ranking.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: Project Vend used Claude Sonnet 3.7 in 2025. There may be later reports that we didn't read. The "four ways agents fail" table and the safety checklist are ours.

docs.title: Plan, act, check
docs.text:
Ch. 14 · 14.1About 6 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • An agent's basic shape is a loop: plan → act (use a tool) → check the result → decide what's next.
  • There are a few common ways to build that loop: chains, routing, parallel work, a conductor with workers, and a writer with a reviewer.
  • Good loops include checkpoints where a person looks, and conditions for stopping.

docs.title: A scavenger hunt
docs.text:
Picture a scavenger hunt. You read a clue (plan), go to the spot (act), see whether you found the next clue (check), and head to wherever it points (decide what's next). The loop keeps going until you find the treasure.

That's how an agent works. As on the last page, it repeats while watching the feedback from its surroundings.

In 10-year-old words

An agent runs a scavenger hunt loop: read the clue, go look, check, and move on to the next clue.

docs.title: One trip around the loop
docs.text:
1. Get the goal. A person tells it the job.
  2. Plan. Decide what to do.
  3. Act. Use a tool, like search, reading a file, or running code (Chapter 13).
  4. Look at the result. Read what the tool returned and judge the progress.
  5. Decide whether to keep going. If there's more to do, go back to step 2. If it's done, stop.

Anthropic's post on agents names two common ways to stay in control. One is pausing to ask a person, at checkpoints or when it's stuck. The other is stopping conditions, like a maximum number of steps.

docs.title: Five ways to build the loop
docs.text:
The same post describes five workflow patterns that agents build on.

Pattern What it does Everyday comparison Prompt chaining Splits a job into set steps in order, where each step takes the last one's result. Checks ("gates") can go in between A relay race Routing Sorts the input and sends it to the right specialist A hospital front desk Parallelization Runs parts at the same time (splitting the work), or runs the same job several times and gathers different results (voting) Splitting a group project; solving a problem several ways and comparing Orchestrator-workers A central model breaks the job down as it goes, hands pieces to worker models, and combines the results A director assigning crew on the spot Evaluator-optimizer One model writes, another grades it and gives feedback, and it improves round by round Writing and then revising

The post explains that orchestrator-workers looks like parallelization, but the difference is that the smaller jobs aren't set ahead of time. They depend on the input. In coding, for example, which files need changing, and how, differs every time. Evaluator-optimizer fits when there are clear standards for grading, and when another round of fixing really makes things better.

docs.title: What matters in a loop
docs.text:
• Stopping conditions. Decide when it's done, and set a maximum number of rounds. Without them, it may keep going.
  • Real feedback. It has to actually read what happened. It must not carry on as if a failure were a success.
  • A person's checks. At important points, it pauses for a person's approval.
  • A record. Keep track of what it did, so you can look back later.

★ Going deeper

  • "Voting" in parallelization is the same idea as asking the same question several times and comparing from Chapter 3. You run the same job several times and pick the more trustworthy result.
  • In a separate post, Effective context engineering for AI agents (2025-09-29), Anthropic looks at how agents should manage their context during long jobs. (We checked only its title and date for this page.) The longer an agent works, the more its context window fills up (Chapter 11), so this problem grows.
  • The post on agents says again and again: add complexity only when it clearly improves results. Measuring and improving is the heart of it (Chapter 15).

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Break an everyday job into a loop. For example, "plan a family day out this weekend."

Goal: Plan a family day out this weekend that works even if it rains.
Go in this order, and show me each step when it's done.
1) Suggest 3 places.
2) When I pick one, look up travel time and cost.
3) When I say it's OK, make a schedule.
  • At which points do you stop and check?
  • If the agent had a search tool, which step would use it?

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Make "Show me the plan first" a habit. You can check the direction before the loop starts.
  2. Set a pause after each step. For example: "After each step, check with me before going on."
  3. Give a stopping condition. "If it doesn't work after 5 tries, stop and tell me."
  4. Check the results yourself. Even if the agent says "Done," look at what actually happened.
  5. Give it a standard to grade against. "Check your work against these standards and fix it" is a tiny version of evaluator-optimizer.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "An agent makes the whole plan at once, then carries it out." It's a loop that changes the plan as results come in.
  • "The more rounds, the better the result." More rounds cost more, and mistakes can pile up.
  • "Several models working together is always better." The post suggests adding complexity only when simple methods fall short.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Anthropic, Building effective agents, 2024-12-19. Checkpoints, stopping conditions, prompt chaining, routing, parallelization (splitting and voting), orchestrator-workers, and evaluator-optimizer. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents, 2025-09-29. We checked only the title and date.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: The everyday comparisons (relay race, front desk, and so on) and the four "what matters" points are ours. The post notes that its tools have changed since December 2024.

docs.title: What is an agent?
docs.text:
Ch. 14 · 14.1About 6 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • An agent is an AI that decides how to do a job, uses tools, looks at the results, and keeps working.
  • It differs from a workflow, which follows set steps, in who decides the steps.
  • Agents cost more and can pile up mistakes, so experts suggest using them only when you really need them.

docs.title: A recipe card and a chef
docs.text:
A recipe card lists the steps: "1. Chop the onion. 2. Fry it. 3. Add salt." If you follow the card, you don't have to think about the order. But picture a chef who's only told, "Make our guests a great dinner." The chef opens the fridge, sees what's there, and decides on their own what to make.

The first is a workflow. The second is an agent.

In 10-year-old words

A workflow is a robot following a recipe card. An agent is a chef who opens the fridge and decides what to cook.

docs.title: How Anthropic draws the line
docs.text:
In December 2024, Anthropic published a post called Building effective agents. It separates the two like this:

  • Workflows: systems where language models and tools follow paths set in code ahead of time.
  • Agents: systems where the language model directs its own process and tool use. The model is in charge of how the job gets done.

The post describes how an agent works. It starts from a person's request or a conversation. Once the job is clear, it plans and acts on its own. At each step, it checks real feedback from its surroundings, like the result of a tool call or of running code, to judge its progress. It can pause at checkpoints, or when it's stuck, to ask a person. It stops when the job is done, but it's also common to set stopping conditions, like a maximum number of steps. And the post adds: agents can handle complicated jobs, but how they're built is often simple. Usually it's just a language model using tools in a loop, based on feedback from its surroundings.

docs.title: When to use one, and when not to
docs.text:
The post's advice is surprisingly careful.

  • Find the simplest solution that works, and add complexity only when it helps. Sometimes the answer is not to build an agent at all.
  • Agent systems usually trade speed and cost for better results. Check whether that trade is worth it.
  • Often, a single request improved with search and examples is enough.
  • Agents fit open-ended problems where you can't predict the number of steps or set a fixed path. But they cost more and can pile up mistakes, so the post suggests testing them a lot in a sandbox, with guardrails.

Please note

The post carries a note saying the tools it describes have changed a lot since December 2024. Remember the distinctions and principles, more than specific tool names.

docs.title: Agents around us
docs.text:
The post's examples include customer support agents, which can look up orders and issue refunds, and coding agents, whose work can be checked with automatic tests. Tools like these read files, change code, run it, look at the results, and decide what to do next.

★ Going deeper

  • The post names three principles: keep the agent's design simple, put transparency first by showing the agent's planning steps, and carefully build the connection between the agent and its tools (the agent-computer interface) with good tool docs and testing.
  • You can think of an agent as the "one token at a time" loop from Chapter 12, wrapped in one more loop on the outside. Inside the writing loop, there's another loop of calling tools.
  • The post we read is from December 2024, and this field moves fast. For newer approaches, see Anthropic's later posts and docs.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Think of three jobs you recently gave an AI, and sort them.

Job Were the steps set? Did it use tools? Did it have to make its own decisions?
  • If the steps were set and no decisions were needed, a plain question or a workflow is enough.
  • If you couldn't know the steps ahead of time and it needed tools several times, that's a job for an agent.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Try the simplest way first. An agent is too much for a job one question can handle.
  2. Hand off fixed-order jobs step by step. That's "one thing at a time" from Chapter 2.
  3. Set a stopping point when you hand a job to an agent. For example: "within 10 steps," or "do this much, then report back."
  4. Build in checkpoints. The classic one: "Show me your plan first, and start once I approve."
  5. Test in a setting you're watching. Use practice files, not important accounts or files.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "Agents are always better than plain chatbots." They cost more and risk more mistakes, so they're too much for simple jobs.
  • "An agent is a totally new kind of AI." According to the post, it's a language model using tools in a loop.
  • "An agent handles it, so I don't need to watch." Mistakes can pile up, so it needs checking.

docs.title: Ch. 15 Try Building an Agent
docs.text:
A taste of agent design, focused on instructions, tools, and evaluation.

15.1.1Write good instructions6 min read 15.1.2Design good tools6 min read 15.1.3Test it and fix it6 min read

docs.title: Test it and fix it
docs.text:
Ch. 15 · 15.1About 6 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Instead of "it seems to work," set success criteria, make test questions, and measure a score, then improve.
  • Include tricky cases in your tests, and when you fix things, change one thing at a time and measure again.
  • Add complexity only when the score clearly gets better.

docs.title: Practice tests
docs.text:
Athletes don't enter a race because they "feel fast." They time themselves, find weak spots, fix them, and time themselves again. Agents and prompt templates are the same. If you don't measure, you can't tell whether it got better.

In 10-year-old words

Take a practice test, fix the questions you got wrong, and take the test again. Check with numbers whether your score went up.

docs.title: The cycle Anthropic describes
docs.text:
Anthropic's guide to testing describes a cycle for improving a prompt (a template or set of instructions):

  1. Set success criteria.
  2. Write test cases. Don't forget the unusual ones.
  3. Write a first prompt.
  4. Run it on the test cases.
  5. Improve it. Then go back to step 4.
  6. Do a final check before you ship it.

Good success criteria are specific and measurable. Not "good performance," but something like "sorts customer feedback by feeling correctly." Numbers work best. When numbers are hard, use a rating scale that's applied the same way every time. The guide says even fuzzy-sounding goals like safety can become numbers, for example: "fewer than 0.1% of 10,000 outputs get flagged as harmful."

docs.title: A light version for you
docs.text:
For one person or a small team, try a lighter version.

1. One line of success criteria. "In 9 out of 10 customer questions, it quotes the right policy."

2. Ten test questions. Six easy, three hard, and one strange on purpose (a question the policy doesn't cover, or a vague one). That follows the guide's advice to cover unusual cases.

3. A scorecard. Mark each answer right or wrong (or use a 3-point scale). Write one line about what went wrong.

4. Gather the misses and find the cause. Were the instructions vague? Was material missing? Did a tool find the wrong thing?

5. Fix one thing, then measure again. If you change several things at once, you won't know which one helped.

6. Hide a few test questions. Keep two or three that you don't look at while fixing, and use them only at the end. That stops you from fixing it to fit just your test questions. Anthropic's post on tool design recommends this kind of held-out test set too.

docs.title: Who does the grading?
docs.text:
• Jobs with a clear right answer: a person or a simple rule can grade them (Are the numbers right? Are the needed words there?).
  • Jobs without one clear answer (like writing quality): grade with a rubric a person wrote ahead of time. Anthropic's guide covers many ways to grade, from checking for an exact match to having an AI do the grading.
  • Even when AI grades, have a person check some of them to make sure the grading can be trusted.

★ Going deeper

  • The post on building agents says again and again that measuring performance and improving is the heart of it, and to add complexity only when results clearly improve (Chapter 14). Evaluation is how you decide what "clearly" means.
  • The tool design post (previous page) measures tools with evaluations and then works with an agent like Claude Code to improve them. Anthropic's post Demystifying evals for AI agents (2026-01-09) looks at evaluating agents in more depth. We checked only its title and date for this page.
  • A test score is not the same as real-world performance. If the test questions don't look like the real job, the score can rise without the work getting better (the traps in benchmarks, Chapter 21).

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Make a practice test for one template from Chapter 8 (or the guide you wrote earlier in this chapter).

# Test input Expected result Right / Wrong Notes 1 (easy) 2 (easy) ... 10 (strange on purpose)
  1. Run all 10 with the template as it is, and write down the score.
  2. Find the most common cause of the misses, and fix just that one thing.
  3. Run all 10 again. Did the score go up?

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Write your success criteria in one line. Without them, you can't say "it got better."
  2. Start with 10 test questions. (Add more later.) Always include at least one tricky one.
  3. Fix one thing at a time. That's how you find what worked.
  4. Hide a few test questions. Use questions you didn't look at while fixing for the final check.
  5. When the model or service changes, measure again. Compare with the same test (Chapter 8).

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "I tried it a few times and it worked." A few tries can be luck. Measure with the same test.
  • "The more test questions, the better." Ten is enough to start. What matters is including tricky cases.
  • "AI does the grading, so no person needs to look." Check some yourself, so you can trust the grading.

docs.title: Write good instructions
docs.text:
Ch. 15 · 15.1About 6 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Write an agent's instructions like a first-day guide for a smart new employee.
  • Include its role, its goal, its limits, rules for using tools, when to stop, and what to do when it doesn't know.
  • Have a coworker read your instructions, then improve them.

docs.title: A first-day guide
docs.text:
When someone new joins, you tell them: "Here's what this place does. Here's your job. Don't do these things. If you're unsure, ask this person." Without a guide like that, even a smart person can end up doing the wrong thing.

Agents are the same. The asking tips from Chapter 2 matter even more in instructions for an agent that works for a long time. It works through many steps on its own, so if the first direction is off, it can stay off to the very end.

In 10-year-old words

Give your agent a first-day guide. The clearer the guide, the better it works on its own.

docs.title: What goes in the guide
docs.text:
Anthropic's docs compare Claude to a brilliant new employee who doesn't know how your team works. The more clearly you explain what you want, the better the result. Add the principles from the post on building agents (keep it simple, make the plan visible, set stopping conditions), and you get a guide like this.

Section What to write Example Role Who it's acting as An events helper for the town library Goal What it's for, and why it matters Help visitors find events that suit them Tools Which tools, and when to use them Search the events file to find answers Limits What it must not do Don't make bookings, take payments, or ask for personal details Steps In order, if needed 1) Check the question 2) Search 3) Answer with evidence When unsure What to do Say it doesn't know, and give the help desk contact When to stop When to finish or hand off to a person If two searches find nothing, stop and point to a person Report format How to show results A list of date, place, and who it's for, plus the supporting lines

docs.title: Sample instructions
docs.text:
You are an events helper for our town library.
Goal: Help visitors find events that suit them. Accuracy matters most,
because wrong information sends people on a wasted trip.
Tools: Search the events file. Don't mention anything that isn't in it.
Don't: Make bookings or take payments. Don't ask for personal details.
Steps: 1) Check what kind of event the person wants. If it's unclear,
ask one question. 2) Search the events file. 3) List the date, place,
and who it's for, and show the rows you used.
If you don't know: Say "I couldn't find that in the events list," and
give the library help desk's contact details.
When to stop: If two searches find nothing, stop searching and give
the message above.

docs.title: Writing tips
docs.text:
• Give reasons. "Accuracy matters, because people could make a wasted trip." A reason helps it stay on course in similar situations (Chapter 2).
  • Number the steps when order matters.
  • Don't just list "don'ts." Say "do this instead." Next to each closed road, point out an open one.
  • Make its plan and reasoning visible. Anthropic's post on agents recommends showing the agent's planning steps to make it more transparent.
  • Start simple. The same post says to find the simplest solution first. Add rules one at a time, when you need them.

★ Going deeper

  • Instructions take up room in the agent's context window and go in as input at every step (Chapter 11). If they're too long, key rules can get buried. A common tip is to put the most important rules at the start and the end (Chapter 6; that research used 2023 models).
  • Rules in the instructions can bend when users push. In Project Vend (Chapter 14), the agent gave discounts when people coaxed it. For rules that truly must hold, it's safer to also enforce them a second way, through tool permissions or approval steps.
  • In developer tools, instructions usually go in the system prompt, with information that changes each conversation added separately. Everyday users often put them in an app's "custom instructions" or "projects" feature (it differs by service).

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Write a guide for a job you give AI over and over (or one you'd like to hand off).

  1. Fill in the eight sections from the table above.
  2. The coworker test: have a friend read only your guide. Is anything confusing? If they're confused, the chatbot will be too (Chapter 2).
  3. Give the guide to a chatbot, then ask one easy question and one tricky one. Does it follow the guide?

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Put the role, the goal, and the reason in the first three lines. That sets the direction.
  2. Always include "when you don't know." It's a key section for cutting down on made-up answers and wild guesses.
  3. Include when to stop. So it doesn't loop forever.
  4. Pair each limit with an alternative. Next to "don't," write "instead, do this."
  5. Keep improving the guide. Each time you see odd behavior, add a line, and save it in your prompt collection from Chapter 8.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "The longer the instructions, the better the agent follows them." Long instructions bury what matters. Write only what's needed.
  • "Write it well once, and it works everywhere." It goes off course in situations you didn't expect. Test and fix it.
  • "Once the rules are written, it's safe." Written rules can bend. Back them up with permissions and approvals.

docs.text:

  • Anthropic, Prompting best practices, Claude Platform Docs. The new-employee comparison, specific instructions, giving reasons, and numbered steps. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Anthropic, Building effective agents, 2024-12-19. Simplicity, transparent planning steps, and stopping conditions.
  • Anthropic, Project Vend: Can Claude run a small shop?, 2025-06-27.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: The eight sections and the library example are ours. "Enforce it a second way through permissions" is our own takeaway from the Chapter 14 case, not a direct recommendation from these sources. Custom instruction features differ by service.

docs.title: Design good tools
docs.text:
Ch. 15 · 15.1About 6 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • An agent's work depends a lot on its tools. And tools for agents should be built for an AI to read and use, not just for people.
  • Anthropic names five principles: choose the right tools, name them clearly, return useful information, save tokens, and write careful descriptions.
  • Even if you're not a developer, you can use the same ideas when you organize the files and material you give an AI.

docs.title: A toolbox for a new hire
docs.text:
Imagine giving a new hire a toolbox with hundreds of tools and no labels on the drawers. They'd wander around, unsure what to use. Now imagine each drawer says "Use this when...", with only the tools they need. They'd get to work fast.

Tools for agents are the same. Anthropic's post on tool design, Writing effective tools for agents — with agents (2025-09-11), starts with a question. With MCP (Chapter 13), an agent might have hundreds of tools. How do you make those tools work well?

In 10-year-old words

A good toolbox has labels and instructions on every drawer, and only the tools you really need.

docs.title: A tool is a deal between two kinds of systems
docs.text: The post explains it this way. Ordinary computer programs are deterministic: the same input always gives the same output. An agent is non-deterministic: it can respond differently even in the same situation. Ordinary software is a deal between deterministic systems. A tool is a deal between a deterministic system and a non-deterministic agent. So you have to design it with the agent in mind, thinking about how it might read the tool and how it might misunderstand it.

docs.title: Five principles
docs.text:
The post names five key principles for making tools.

Principle What it means Everyday comparison Choose the right tools Build fewer tools, made for the jobs that matter most. Too many, or overlapping ones, can distract an agent Only the tools you need in the box Name them clearly Group tools by service and resource so their limits are clear, like asana_search and asana_users_search A label on every drawer Return useful information Give back what the agent can use for its next decision, like readable names instead of long ID codes A clue that says "next, go here" Save tokens Keep responses short, with page-by-page results, filters, and trimming (the context window is limited, Chapter 11). Claude Code limits tool responses to 25,000 tokens by default Keep reports short and to the point Write careful descriptions Treat tool descriptions as prompts, and write them carefully An instruction manual

docs.title: How to write the manual
docs.text:
The post explains that a tool's description goes into the agent's context and guides how it calls the tool. Describe the tool as you would to a new teammate. Write down the context you take for granted: special ways of asking for things, what technical terms mean, how pieces of information relate. Avoid anything vague. Use clear names for inputs, like user_id instead of user. The post says that even small fixes to descriptions can make a big difference.

It also says error messages should explain how to fix the problem, instead of giving a code nobody understands.

docs.title: Using this as an everyday user
docs.text:
(This section is our own take on how to apply a developer post to everyday use. The post doesn't say this directly.)

Even if you never write code, you can use the same ideas when you give an AI files and material.

  • Fewer, clearer files. If a folder has hundreds of files, the AI gets lost too. Give it only what this job needs.
  • Label file names and column names. "2026_sales_by_month.xlsx" beats "final_FINAL_v2.xlsx." Give columns clear names too.
  • A one-page guide. Add a note: "This folder holds these files, and this column means this."
  • Short results. Asking the AI to "summarize the results" keeps the context from filling up for the next step.

★ Going deeper

  • The post says to measure tools with evaluations. Build a quick version, test it on many realistic, multi-step tasks with checkable outcomes, then work with an agent like Claude Code to improve the tools. It tracks accuracy, time, number of tool calls, token use, and errors. The next page covers evaluation.
  • The post gives one example of saving tokens: a "concise" response option used about a third of the tokens of the "detailed" one. Giving the agent that choice lets it trade detail for cost.
  • The earlier post, Building effective agents, calls the point where an agent meets its tools the agent-computer interface (ACI). It says to put as much care into it as people put into interfaces for humans.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Give a "toolbox check" to some material you often share with AI (files or a folder).

Check Yes / No Are only the files this job needs included? Can you tell what's in each file from its name? Do the table's columns have clear names? Is there a one-page guide? Are personal details included? (Chapter 3)

Fix the rows where you answered "No," then ask the same question again. Does the answer change?

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Give the AI less material. Only what's needed is the best kind of organizing.
  2. Name things so both future-you and the AI can understand them.
  3. Add a line like "this column means this." Without it, the AI guesses.
  4. Ask for short results. Long tool results fill up the context.
  5. Write as if explaining to a new hire. The key is getting what's in your head down in writing.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "More tools make an agent smarter." Too many make it hard to choose. Keep only what's needed.
  • "AI figures out what my files mean." Without names and notes, it guesses.
  • "Only developers need to think about tools." The files and settings you give an AI are tools to it too.

docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Anthropic, Building effective agents, 2024-12-19. The agent-computer interface (ACI).
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: "Using this as an everyday user" and the toolbox checklist are our own adaptation of a developer post. The toolbox and drawer-label comparisons are ours.

docs.title: Experiment freely with rewind
docs.text:
Ch. 16 · 16.3About 6 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Each time you send a message, Claude Code automatically saves the state of your files just before it (a checkpoint).
  • With /rewind (or pressing Esc twice in an empty prompt), you can take the conversation and the files back, separately or together.
  • Some things can't be undone. The next page covers those.

docs.title: Like a save point in a game
docs.text: In a game, if you save before a boss fight, you can try again when you lose. Claude Code saves "the state of the files right now" every time you send a message. So when you think "That's not the direction I wanted," you can go back to that point. That means you can say "What if we tried this?" without worry.

docs.title: How to rewind
docs.text:
Press Esc twice when the prompt is empty, or type /rewind. A list of the messages you sent appears. Pick the point you want, then pick what to do.

Option What it means Restore code and conversation Both files and conversation go back to that point Restore conversation Files stay as they are now; only the conversation goes back Restore code Only the files go back; the conversation stays Summarize from here Squeeze everything after that point into a summary, to free up memory space Summarize up to here Squeeze everything before that point into a summary Never mind Leave without changing anything

If there's text in the prompt, pressing Esc twice clears the text instead. In that case, /rewind is the surer way.

The summarize options are like running /compact from a point you choose. Summarizing doesn't change any files, and the original messages stay in the session record, so Claude can still look back at the details.

In 10-year-old words

Every message you send is an automatic save. If things go the wrong way, go back to a save point.

★ Going deeper

Claude Code keeps file snapshots for the 100 most recent checkpoints in a session. They're saved with the conversation, so /rewind still works after you resume a session. By default, a session's snapshots are cleaned up about 30 days after it last saved one, so rewinding in a very old session can fail. If you want to branch off and try a different approach while keeping the original session untouched, use /branch instead of rewinding.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
In a practice folder, try this:

  1. Ask it to make a file called notes.txt with a short shopping list.
  2. Then ask: "Rewrite everything in notes.txt in Spanish."
  3. Open /rewind and pick the point just before step 2. Choose Restore code.
  4. Open notes.txt. Is it back in English? The conversation should still be there.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
• Before asking for a big change, think "my last message is a save point," and go ahead.
  • If you can't decide between two approaches, try one. If you don't like it, restore just the code and try the other.
  • In a long chat where memory space is full, summarize from the middle so your first instructions stay intact.
/rewind

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "Rewinding always erases the conversation." No. You can choose files only, conversation only, or both.
  • "Once I rewind, that's it." After rewinding, sending a new message starts a new path. So look carefully at which point you pick.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
• Version checked: Claude Code 2.1.319, checked on 2026-11-09.
  • Source of facts: Official docs: Checkpointing and Commands. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Learning order: claude-howto 08-checkpoints (MIT; rewritten in our own words).

docs.title: How are checkpoints different from git?
docs.text:
Ch. 16 · 16.3About 6 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Checkpoints are a quick undo inside the current session. Long-lasting history is git's job.
  • Learn the four kinds of things checkpoints can't undo.
  • The safe habit is two layers: save points plus commits.

docs.title: A pencil eraser and a photo album
docs.text: Checkpoints are like an eraser for pencil writing. You can quickly erase what you just wrote, but if the notebook sits for a long time, things fade. Git is a photo album. You take pictures of important moments, look them up months later, and share them with others. The official docs say the same: checkpoints are for quick recovery within a session, and long-lasting history and teamwork belong to version control like git.

docs.title: What checkpoints can't do
docs.text:
Can't undo Why, and what to do Files changed only by terminal (Bash) commands If Claude never edited the file with its file-editing tools, it isn't tracked. Use git to undo it Files changed by subagents These usually aren't restored. Use git Files you changed yourself, or work in another window Changes outside this Claude Code session usually aren't tracked Shortcut files (symlinks) and hard-linked files They're skipped, with a warning

One more: a message you send while Claude is still working has no save point of its own, so it may show "No code restore." In that case, pick the message that started that turn and rewind from there.

docs.title: The two-layer habit
docs.text:
1. Before starting new work, commit the current state. A commit is putting it in the photo album.
  2. While working, try things freely. If something goes wrong, /rewind takes you back fast.
  3. When you get a result you like, commit again.

This book's repository gets a commit after every page. For jobs with lots of files, like making videos, relying only on checkpoints may not protect video files made by terminal commands.

In 10-year-old words

Checkpoints are an eraser. Git is a photo album. Put the important stuff in the photo album.

★ Going deeper

There's also /branch, which forks the same conversation so you can try another approach, and "worktrees," which give you separate working folders so jobs don't get in each other's way. You'll see both again in Chapter 18.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text: In a practice folder, run git init. Have Claude make a file, and commit it. Then ask, "Rename all the files." This time, undo it with git restore or git checkout instead of /rewind. How do the two ways feel different?

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
• Before big jobs, ask for this first:
Check which files have changed so far, and draft a one-line commit message. Don't commit until I've checked it.
  • Always commit before using subagents (17.4).

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "I have checkpoints, so I don't need git." Not true. Old snapshots get cleaned up, and some changes aren't tracked at all.
  • "If I don't know git, I can't use Claude Code." You can. But as your work gets more important, learning git is worth more and more.

docs.text:

  • Source of facts: Official docs: Checkpointing (Limitations). Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Learning order: claude-howto 08-checkpoints (MIT; rewritten in our own words).

docs.title: The note Claude reads every time: CLAUDE.md
docs.text:
Ch. 16 · 16.2About 6 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Each new Claude Code session starts with no memory of past conversations (though it does reread CLAUDE.md and its own auto memory).
  • CLAUDE.md is a note it reads first, every time. Write something there once, and you don't have to explain it again.
  • The note is read as background, not as a command. So there are ways to write it that make it more likely to be followed.

docs.title: A smart friend who forgets every morning
docs.text:
Picture a movie character who loses their memory every morning. They keep a note by the bed and read it first thing when they wake up: "You're a chef. The kitchen is on the left." With that note, they can start the day right, even without their memory.

Claude Code is just like that. Start a new session, and it knows nothing about yesterday's conversation (its context window, from Chapter 11, starts empty). So if you put a note file called CLAUDE.md in your folder, Claude reads it when it starts.

docs.title: Where it goes
docs.text:
Where you put the note decides who it's for.

Where File Who is it for? Your whole computer ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md Just you, in all your projects The project ./CLAUDE.md Everyone working in this folder (you can share it with your team) Your private project note ./CLAUDE.local.md Just you, in this project only (add it to .gitignore so others don't see it)

Claude Code reads the notes in the folder you're working in and in every folder above it, and joins them together. Notes in folders below are read when Claude works with files in those folders.

docs.title: The easiest way to make one
docs.text:
Open Claude Code in your folder and type /init. Claude looks around the folder and writes a first note for you. If a note already exists, it suggests improvements instead of overwriting it. To check that the note loaded, run /context all and look under Memory files.

To add something yourself, /memory lists your note files so you can open them.

In 10-year-old words

CLAUDE.md is the note by the bed of a friend who forgets every morning. They read it first, every time they wake up.

★ Going deeper

There are two kinds of notes. CLAUDE.md is the one you write. Auto memory is notes Claude writes for itself, based on your corrections and preferences. Both are read at the start of every session. But the official docs say both are background, not enforced settings. For anything that must be blocked no matter what, don't rely on a note. Use a hook instead (17.2).

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Make an empty practice folder and run claude inside it.
  2. Ask it to add one line to the note:
Create a CLAUDE.md and write this one line: "Always answer politely, in words a 10-year-old can follow."
  1. Run /clear to wipe the conversation, then ask any question. You didn't repeat the note, so is the tone still followed?

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
• The moment you're about to explain something a second time, make a note of it.
  • When it gets something wrong once, add a line that same day.
  • After writing the note, check with /context all that it loaded.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "If it's in the note, it's followed 100% of the time." No. It's read as background, so it's sometimes ignored. The more specific and short it is, the better it's followed (next page).
  • "Changes to the note take effect in the middle of a chat." The note is read when a session starts. After you edit it, the change is surest in a new session.

docs.title: How to write a good CLAUDE.md
docs.text:
Ch. 16 · 16.2About 7 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Notes get followed best when they're short, specific, and don't contradict each other.
  • The official docs suggest keeping each file under about 200 lines.
  • We look at this book project's real CLAUDE.md to see what works and what could be better.

docs.title: Vague words don't get followed
docs.text:
"Keep it tidy" is hard even for a person to act on. The official docs give examples like these:

Vague Checkable Format code properly Use 2-space indentation Test your changes Run npm test before committing Keep files organized API handlers live in src/api/handlers/

The trick is to write things you can check were done or not done.

docs.title: Short, grouped, and consistent
docs.text:
• Short. Aim for under about 200 lines per file. Longer files use more memory space and get followed less.
  • Grouped. Use headings and bullet points. They're easier to follow than dense paragraphs.
  • Consistent. If two instructions contradict each other, Claude may pick either one. Clear out old instructions now and then. Running /doctor prompt-audit has Claude look for outdated or conflicting instructions and suggest fixes. It doesn't change your files until you ask it to.

Also sort what belongs in the note and what doesn't. Facts it always needs (commands, rules, decisions you can't see from the code) go in the note. Multi-step procedures go in a skill (17.1).

docs.title: A real example: this book's CLAUDE.md
docs.text:
This book's repository has a CLAUDE.md. Here are the kinds of things in it:

  • The book's name and subtitle, and a rule not to put a personal name in the site address
  • The book's structure (part > chapter > section > topic page) and its readers
  • Writing rules: high-level content, explained so a 10-year-old can follow
  • The work order: check source links → write → build → design check → commit
  • The development branch name and the build command

What works: it writes down decisions that are easy to forget, like naming rules. You can't figure those out from the code or the files. The official docs agree: don't write what Claude can learn by reading the repository, like the folder layout. Write only what isn't there. What could be better: some long procedures, like how to check video content, are mixed in. Moving those into skills would make the note lighter.

In 10-year-old words

Keep the note short, and write it in words you can check: did it do it or not?

★ Going deeper

When the note grows, you can split it into topic files in a .claude/rules/ folder, and scope a rule so it applies only to certain kinds of files. You can also pull in another file with @path, but imported content still uses memory space, so it doesn't make things shorter. After /compact, Claude rereads the project's root CLAUDE.md from disk. So unlike something you only said in the chat, a rule in the note survives the summary.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text: Open the CLAUDE.md of your project (or this book's folder) and pick three instructions. Is each one something you could check? Rewrite the vague ones.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
Read CLAUDE.md and find any instructions that contradict each other or look outdated. Don't change anything. Just give me a list.
  • Put the most important rules at the top, with one line explaining why.
  • Write each new rule as one line: what, where, and how.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "The longer I write, the better it understands." It's the opposite. Longer notes use more memory space and get followed less.
  • "Write the note once and you're done." When the project changes, the note goes stale. Check it now and then.

docs.title: Chat mode and one-line mode
docs.text:
Ch. 16 · 16.4About 6 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • claude opens a back-and-forth chat mode. claude -p "question" is a one-line mode that gives you an answer and ends.
  • One-line mode runs without a person, so it's the door to automation.
  • With continue (-c) and resume (-r), you can pick up yesterday's conversation.

docs.title: A restaurant vs a vending machine
docs.text:
Chat mode is a restaurant. You order, change your mind, and talk with the chef. One-line mode is a vending machine. Press one button, a drink comes out, and that's it. Nobody has to stand there watching.

What you want Command Start a chat claude Start a chat with a first question claude "explain this project" Get just an answer, then end claude -p "explain this function" Continue the most recent chat (in this folder) claude -c Reopen a chat by name or ID claude -r "name" "finish this" Check the version claude -v

In chat mode, typing /resume also lets you pick a past conversation.

docs.title: Choosing the model and folders
docs.text:
You can set a few things when you start.

claude --model sonnet                 # the model to use in this session
claude --add-dir ../another-folder    # one more folder it can read and edit
claude --permission-mode plan         # start in a mode that only makes a plan first

Adding a folder with --add-dir gives it permission to read and edit files there. Only add folders you trust. Chapter 18 covers permission modes.

In 10-year-old words

claude is a restaurant. claude -p is a vending machine, and a vending machine runs on its own.

★ Going deeper

When you use one-line mode for automation, adding --bare makes it start faster. It skips loading hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md. The official docs recommend --bare for scripts, and say it will become the default for -p in a future release. But --bare doesn't use your subscription login. To use the Anthropic API, set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in your environment. (Other providers like Amazon Bedrock use their own credentials.) On the other hand, -p without --bare runs the project's hooks and connects its MCP servers, even in a folder you've never trusted, with no warning dialog. So be careful in folders you don't know (17.2, 17.3).

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Run claude -p "What is 1 plus 2 plus 3 plus 4 plus 5? Answer with just the number." One line comes back, and the program ends.
  2. Open claude, ask anything, then leave with /exit.
  3. Run claude -c to reopen the chat you just had.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
• For one-off questions, use claude -p. No need to open and close a window.
  • Pick up yesterday's work with claude -c. You don't have to explain everything again.
  • Open a named conversation with claude -r "name".

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "One-line mode is a weaker AI." No. It's the same AI, working without a back-and-forth.
  • "-c remembers everything from yesterday." The reopened chat keeps its history. In a brand-new chat, though, it's still the CLAUDE.md note (16.2) that gets read.

docs.title: Hand it a file and give it a job in one line
docs.text:
Ch. 16 · 16.4About 6 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • In the terminal, | (a pipe) is a tube that passes one command's output to the next command.
  • With one line, cat file | claude -p "...", you can have it read a file and do a job.
  • This one line is the first piece of the automation pipeline in 18.2.

docs.title: A conveyor belt
docs.text:
Picture a factory conveyor belt. The first machine makes something, and the belt carries it to the second machine. The | symbol in the terminal is that belt. cat is a machine that pulls out a file's contents, and claude -p is a machine that reads and works on them.

cat error.log | claude -p "Explain in three lines why this error happened"

To save the result to a file, add >.

cat script.md | claude -p "Mark any words that are hard to read" > review.md

The official docs show the same shape: pipe in a build error file, ask for a short explanation of the cause, and save it to a file.

docs.title: Using it for our channel's videos
docs.text:
After writing a script, we want to run a check on it. That check can be one line.

cat docs-en/part1/ch01/next-word.md | claude -p "Find words that would be hard for a 10-year-old. Just give me a list."

You can also check only what changed. The official docs show git diff main | claude -p "...", which passes just the changes to look for typos.

docs.title: Setting the shape of the result
docs.text:
Plain text is fine for a person to read. But if another program will read it, the shape needs to be fixed.

claude -p "List the part titles of this book" --output-format json

--output-format can be text (the default), json, or stream-json. If the result must follow an exact shape, you can give it one with --json-schema. We'll try that in 18.2.

In 10-year-old words

| is a conveyor belt. Send a file down it to the AI, and the job's done in one line.

★ Going deeper

In one-line mode, there's nobody to answer a permission question. So jobs like editing files or running commands need permission ahead of time. An option like --allowedTools "Read,Edit" lets those tools run without asking. Give only the permission you need, as narrowly as you can. The wider the permission, the bigger the damage if something goes wrong. (Since v2.1.302, a -p run with no permission mode set denies any call that needs approval.)

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Pick any text file (a Markdown file from this book's docs-en folder works well).
  2. Run cat file | claude -p "Summarize this in three lines".
  3. Add > summary.txt at the end and check that the result is saved to a file.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
• Don't copy and paste long error messages. Pipe them in.
  • If you run the same check twice, save the one-line command in a note. It'll soon become a skill (17.1) or a script (18.2).
  • Before you pipe in a file, make sure it has no passwords or personal details. Whatever you pipe in is sent to the AI service.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "Only developers use pipes." No. It just passes a file's contents along. You only need to learn it once.
  • "One-line mode can edit any file." --allowedTools sets which tools can run without asking. To limit which tools exist at all, use --tools. In one-line mode there's no one to ask, so tool calls without permission can be denied. Don't give wide permission.

docs.title: Slash commands you'll use often
docs.text:
Ch. 16 · 16.1About 6 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • In Claude Code, anything that starts with / is a shortcut button, not a chat message.
  • Seven are enough to start: /help /clear /compact /context /model /init /rewind
  • The list changes often, so don't memorize it. Get in the habit of looking things up with /help.

docs.title: Slash commands are remote control buttons
docs.text:
Think of a TV remote. Instead of saying "Please turn up the volume," you press one button. In Claude Code, messages that start with / are those buttons. Type just / and a list pops up. Type more letters and the list narrows down.

There are two kinds of buttons.

  • Built-in commands: buttons Claude Code comes with, like /help and /clear.
  • Commands you make: things you ask for often, turned into buttons. You'll make one on the next page.

docs.title: The first seven
docs.text:
Command What it does When to use it /help Shows help and the list of commands When you're not sure what to press /clear Starts a new, empty conversation When you're switching to a totally different job /compact Summarizes the conversation so far to free up room When the chat is long but you want to keep going /context Shows how much of its memory space is used, as a colored grid When answers start going off track /model Switches the AI model When you want a faster or a smarter one /init Makes a CLAUDE.md note for this folder When you open a new project for the first time /rewind Takes the conversation or files back to an earlier point When something went wrong (more in 16.3)

/clear and /compact look alike, but they're different. /clear is wiping the whiteboard and starting over. /compact is summing up the whiteboard on one page of notes and continuing from there. As Chapter 11 showed, an AI's memory space (the context window) has limits, so you need both.

In 10-year-old words

Slash commands are remote control buttons. You press one instead of explaining in a long message.

★ Going deeper

Some commands are really "bundled skills." For example, /doctor (checks your setup) and /batch (splits a big change into pieces and works on them in parallel) look like commands but are skills. They run on a prompt and a set of steps, not on built-in code. Section 17.1 covers skills. Some commands also exist only from a certain version on. If you type a name and see "Unknown command," check your version first (claude --version).

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
It takes two minutes.

  1. In your terminal, run claude.
  2. Type /help and skim the list.
  3. Type /context to see how much memory space is used. Even in a brand-new chat, some is already used, because the default instructions and tool descriptions go in first.
  4. Type /model, check which model you're using, and close it.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
• When a long chat makes answers fuzzy, check /context first. If you're continuing the same job, use /compact. If it's a new job, use /clear.
  • You can tell /compact what to focus on in its summary.
/compact Keep only the decisions and the remaining to-dos for the skill we're building
  • If you can't remember a name, type / and add letters one at a time to find it.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "Does /clear delete the files I made?" No. It clears the conversation. Files that are already saved stay as they are.
  • "Does the AI handle every command?" No. Many, like /help and /context, are shown right away by the program without asking the AI.

docs.title: Make your own shortcut commands
docs.text:
Ch. 16 · 16.1About 7 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Things you ask for often can be saved in a file and called with /name.
  • "Commands" have now merged with skills. There's one way to make them, and the folder name becomes the command name.
  • If you've typed the same request three times, it's time to make a button.

docs.title: If you keep typing the same request
docs.text: Say that every time you finish a video script, you ask the same thing: "Rewrite this so a grade schooler gets it. Explain hard words with one comparison. Keep sentences short." Typing it every time is a chore, and some days you forget part of it. Write that request in a file, name it /easy, and you can call it up in one go.

docs.title: The old way and the new way
docs.text: It used to be that putting a file in .claude/commands/ made it a command. The official docs now say custom commands have merged into skills. A file at .claude/commands/deploy.md and a skill at .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md both make the same /deploy command, and old command files keep working. For new ones, skills are the better choice. A skill folder can hold extra reference files, and there are settings for who can call it.

docs.title: Make one: /easy
docs.text:
Let's make it a "personal skill" you can use anywhere on your computer. Create the folder under ~/.claude/skills/.

mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills/easy

Inside that folder, write a SKILL.md file like this:

---
description: Use when rewriting hard text so a 10-year-old can follow it.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

Rewrite the text below so a 10-year-old can follow it. $ARGUMENTS

- The first time a hard word appears, explain it with one comparison
- Keep sentences short and friendly
- Don't change any facts. If you don't know something, say so

The part between the --- lines describes what the skill is. Below that are the instructions Claude follows.

  • $ARGUMENTS gets replaced with whatever you type after the command. Call /easy the paragraph about tokens, and those words go in.
  • disable-model-invocation: true means "run only when I call it." Without it, Claude may read the description and decide to use it on its own. For jobs where you want to control the timing, it's safer to turn this on.

Save it, open Claude Code, and type /easy. It shows up in the list. If you edit the file, Claude Code picks up the change in the same session, with no restart. (Content that was already loaded stays in the conversation.)

In 10-year-old words

Write down a request you make often in one folder, and you can call it up with one name.

★ Going deeper

Where you put a skill decides where it works. A personal folder (~/.claude/skills/) works in all your projects. A project folder (.claude/skills/) works in that repository, and if you commit it, your team can use it too. If the same name exists in both, the personal one wins (and company-managed skills beat both). You can also take several values by position, with $0, $1, and so on. Section 17.1 covers how skills are built.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text: Make the /easy skill above and give it one hard paragraph. If you don't like the result, change one line in SKILL.md and call it again. Does it change? Learning to change results by editing instructions is the real lesson of this page.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
• If you've typed the same request three or more times, make it a file.
  • Keep names short (lowercase letters and hyphens are safest): /easy, /summary, /check.
  • In the instructions, write one line each for what to do, what shape it should take, and what not to do.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "You have to program to make a command." No. Plain-language instructions are all it takes.
  • "Once I make it, it'll always be followed." A skill is just instructions, so it sometimes drifts. For things that must always happen, use hooks (17.2).

docs.title: Run something automatically at the right moment: hooks
docs.text:
Ch. 17 · 17.2About 7 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • A hook is a promise: "When Claude does X, run the program I set up, without leaving it to the AI's judgment."
  • With skills and notes, the AI chooses whether to follow them. Hooks run without the AI deciding, whenever the moment comes (as long as they're set up right and not turned off).
  • You'll learn four common moments (events) and where the settings file goes.

docs.title: A motion-sensor porch light
docs.text: A motion-sensor light on your porch turns on for anyone who walks up. That's different from asking someone, "Don't forget to turn on the light." A hook is the motion-sensor light. The official docs say hooks give you deterministic control: certain actions always happen, rather than relying on the model to choose to run them. CLAUDE.md rules are read as background and can be ignored. A hook can't be.

docs.title: Four common moments
docs.text:
Moment (event) When Use PreToolUse Just before a tool runs Blocking risky actions PostToolUse Just after a tool runs Checks, automatic cleanup Notification When Claude is waiting for your input Sending you an alert SessionStart When a session starts or is resumed Loading needed information ahead of time

There are many more, like Stop (when Claude finishes answering) and PreCompact (just before a summary). The full list is in the official hooks reference.

docs.title: Where the settings go
docs.text:
Hooks go in the hooks section of a settings file. Where the file lives decides its reach.

Location Reach ~/.claude/settings.json All your projects .claude/settings.json This project (commit it to share) .claude/settings.local.json This project, just you

Here's a hook that alerts you when Claude is waiting for input (for macOS), from the official docs:

{
  "hooks": {
    "Notification": [
      {
        "matcher": "",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "osascript -e 'display notification \"Claude Code needs your attention\" with title \"Claude Code\"'"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

The matcher is a filter that picks "only in these cases." What it filters depends on the event. For PreToolUse and PostToolUse, it's the tool name (like Edit|Write). For Notification, it's the kind of notification. For SessionStart, it's how the session started (fresh, resumed, cleared, and so on). Leave it empty to run in every case. After setting it up, type /hooks to see the list of registered hooks. If yours isn't there, check the brackets and commas in the settings file first.

In 10-year-old words

A hook is a motion-sensor light. It turns on at the promised moment, even if nobody asks.

★ Going deeper

Shell commands aren't the only kind of hook. There are also prompt-based and agent-based hooks, where a Claude model makes a judgment, and HTTP hooks that send a signal to a web address. Use the AI kinds for checks that need judgment, and command hooks for checks with clear rules. In this book, we'll try just a command hook.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text: Put the Notification hook above in ~/.claude/settings.json. (Not on a Mac? The docs give commands for Linux, like notify-send, and for Windows.) Check with /hooks that it's listed. Then ask Claude to do something that needs permission, switch to another window, and wait for the alert. If no alert comes, check the brackets and commas, and make sure the command matches your operating system.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
• Turn "must always happen" into a hook, not a note.
  • Start with harmless hooks, like alerts.
  • After adding a hook, always check it with /hooks.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "A hook is something the AI does." No. It's a program your computer runs. That's why the last page of this section is all about safety.
  • "Adding hooks makes Claude smarter." It doesn't get smarter. Your promises just get kept.

docs.title: Hands-on: add an automatic checker
docs.text:
Ch. 17 · 17.2About 7 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • You'll build a hook that automatically checks for a "Sources and date checked" section every time a book page is edited.
  • A hook script reads its input, then answers with a number when it ends (an exit code). 2 means "there's a problem."
  • The trick is to run the script on its own first.

docs.title: A checker that keeps our book's promise
docs.text: One of this book's promises is "every page lists its sources and the date checked." People (and AI) sometimes forget. So let's have a checker look right after each file edit.

docs.title: Write the check script
docs.text:
Save this as .claude/hooks/check-page-en.sh:

#!/bin/bash
# English edition: after a page is edited, check that it has a "Sources and date checked" section.
INPUT=$(cat)
FILE=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_input.file_path // empty')

case "$FILE" in
  */docs-en/*.md) ;;
  *) exit 0 ;;
esac

if ! grep -q "^## Sources and date checked" "$FILE"; then
  echo "This page has no '## Sources and date checked' section. Please add sources and the date checked: $FILE" >&2
  exit 2
fi
exit 0

Here's how to read it, line by line.

  • INPUT=$(cat): a hook receives what happened as JSON text. This puts it in a variable.
  • jq -r '.tool_input.file_path': pulls just "the path of the edited file" out of the JSON. (You need jq installed.)
  • case … */docs-en/*.md: if it isn't a Markdown file in the docs-en folder, it does nothing and ends.
  • exit 2 with >&2: the problem message goes to the error output (>&2), and the script ends with 2. That message is passed to Claude.

Make it runnable:

chmod +x .claude/hooks/check-page-en.sh

docs.title: Run it on its own first (important!)
docs.text:
Before Claude ever calls the hook, run it yourself with fake input:

echo '{"tool_input":{"file_path":"/path/docs-en/test.md"}}' | .claude/hooks/check-page-en.sh; echo "exit code: $?"

For a file without the section, you should see the message and exit code 2. For a file with it, you should see 0. We ran this exact script on both cases, plus a file outside docs-en, before writing this page.

docs.title: Register it
docs.text:
Add this to .claude/settings.json:

{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "\"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/.claude/hooks/check-page-en.sh"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

Edit|Write means "when a file is edited or newly written." PostToolUse runs right after the tool finishes, so the file has already changed. Ending with 2 here passes your message to Claude, which helps it fix the page on its own. (It's not a guarantee that it will.)

In 10-year-old words

A checker hook is a short program that only ever answers "there's a problem (2)" or "all good (0)."

★ Going deeper

The hook that "stops it before it happens" is PreToolUse. For example, a script can block edits to a secrets file like .env. PostToolUse tells Claude after the fact; PreToolUse stops the action before it happens. What exit code 2 means differs by event (some events block, some only pass on a message), so check the table in the hooks reference.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Make the script above, and run it on its own first to see 0 and 2.
  2. Register it, and check with /hooks that it appears under PostToolUse.
  3. Ask Claude: "Create test.md in the docs-en folder with just a title." Does Claude get the checker's message and add a "Sources and date checked" section?

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
• If there's a check you always ask for in the same words, move it into a hook.
  • Always run a new hook on its own before registering it.
  • Don't run heavy checks (like a full build) on every file edit. Save them for when Claude finishes answering (Stop).

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "If a hook errors out, the job stops." Exit codes other than 0 and 2 mostly just let things continue. Checks that must block need their own setup.
  • "With a checker, I don't need to look." The checker only sees whether the section exists. Whether the sources are right still needs a person to open them.
  • "An Edit|Write hook sees every file change." No. Claude can also create or change files by running shell commands, and this hook may not see those. If you need to catch every change, the official docs suggest adding a Stop hook that scans the working folder once when Claude finishes.

docs.text:

docs.title: Hooks run with your permissions
docs.text:
Ch. 17 · 17.2About 6 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Command hooks run with all of your account's permissions. They can delete files, and they can read them.
  • Hooks that come with someone else's repository can run on your computer, under your name.
  • You'll learn five safety rules for before and after adding a hook.

docs.title: Handing over your keys
docs.text: A motion-sensor light is handy, but installing one means working with electrical wiring. Wire it wrong, and you could start a fire. Hooks are like that. The official docs carry a warning: command hooks run shell commands with your full user permissions, and they can change, delete, or read any file your account can reach. So the docs say to read and test every hook command before you add it.

docs.title: Hooks from someone else's repository
docs.text:
A repository's .claude/settings.json can contain hooks. Here are the rules the official docs describe:

  • In chat mode, Claude Code holds back hooks from every settings file, even your own ~/.claude/settings.json, until you accept the trust prompt for the folder (or for a parent folder whose trust covers it).
  • But one-line mode (claude -p) and the SDK never show the prompt and treat the folder as trusted. So hooks committed in a repository you've never trusted run anyway.

If you must run -p on someone else's repository, the official docs suggest three things: read its .claude/ settings first, start with --bare, or turn hooks off for that run with --settings '{"disableAllHooks": true}'. Putting disableAllHooks in your own settings isn't enough, because the project's settings take priority and can switch it back.

docs.title: Five safety rules
docs.text:
1. Read before you add. Don't add commands you don't understand. Read someone else's hook line by line, and add it only when you can explain what it does.
  2. Run it on its own first. Test with fake input, as in the hands-on page.
  3. Start small. Begin with hooks that don't delete or send anything, like alerts and checks.
  4. Be careful with paths. File paths and names a hook receives can be untrustworthy input. Always put variables in quotes ("$VAR", not $VAR) so spaces and odd characters are handled safely. The official docs also say to check paths for .. and to stay away from sensitive files like .env, .git/, and keys.
  5. Know how to turn them off. If something seems wrong, check the list with /hooks. You can turn all hooks off at once with "disableAllHooks": true in your settings. But hooks set by your organization's managed policy can't be turned off from your own settings.

In 10-year-old words

A hook opens doors with your keys. Read it, test it small, and know how to turn it off.

★ Going deeper

Hook settings are combined from many places: your settings, the project, local settings, your organization's policy, plugins, and the top of skill and subagent files. They add up instead of replacing each other. So a hook you never added yourself can run. When you install a plugin (18.2), check whether it contains hooks too.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Count how many hooks are on your computer.

  1. In Claude Code, type /hooks.
  2. Read which commands are attached to each event.
  3. If there's a hook you don't remember adding, or can't explain, find where it came from (your settings, the project, or a plugin).

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
• When you get a new repository, look for hooks in .claude/settings.json first and read it.
  • When you use claude -p for automation, make --bare a habit.
  • Don't use delete commands (rm) in hook scripts. If you need to, first make a test version that only prints what it would delete.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "Hooks made by AI are safe." No. Commands AI writes still run with your permissions. You still need to read and test them.
  • "I can rely on the trust prompt." The prompt helps in chat mode, but -p has no prompt.

docs.title: Hands-on: connect an outside service
docs.text:
Ch. 17 · 17.3About 7 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Connect a remote server with one command, then give permission by signing in (OAuth) from /mcp.
  • Learn the order: connect, then test by asking Claude to only read.
  • The example is Notion. Other services follow the same pattern.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Claude Code (we checked against version 2.1.319)
  • An account on the service you want to connect. We use Notion as the example. It's safest to use a practice page or workspace, not an account full of important documents.

docs.title: Connect it
docs.text:
Here's the pattern for a remote HTTP server, with the Notion example from the official docs:

claude mcp add --transport http notion https://mcp.notion.com/mcp
  • --transport http: connect to a remote server.
  • notion: a name you choose.
  • The last part is the server's address.

When you see a line like Added …, the setting is saved. At this point, you haven't signed in yet.

docs.title: Sign in (give permission)
docs.text:
Open Claude Code and type /mcp. Pick notion from the list. It shows that sign-in is needed, and your browser opens a sign-in and permission screen. Read the access the service lists carefully, and where you get a choice, choose the least. Note, though, that a connection like this may not be limited to "just one page." It may reach whatever your account can see. (This differs by service, and we didn't confirm Notion's scope ourselves.) That's why a separate practice account or workspace with nothing important in it is the safest choice.

When it's connected, /mcp shows it as connected. claude mcp list also shows a status next to each server, like ✔ Connected or ! Needs authentication. If you remove the server (claude mcp remove notion), Claude Code deletes the sign-in tokens it stored. But it doesn't cancel those tokens at the service that issued them. The next page covers that.

docs.title: Test it by asking it only to read
docs.text:
In Notion, read just the title and first paragraph of the "Practice" page and tell me. Don't change anything.

If you get an answer, it worked. But asking it to "only read" doesn't actually block writing. To block writes, connect with read-only permission on the service's side, or block write tools with Claude Code's permission rules (18.1). When a permission prompt appears, read it, and say no to writes you didn't want. Depending on your mode or earlier approvals, a prompt may not appear at all.

In 10-year-old words

One line to connect, one sign-in, one reading test. Do it in that order, and it's safe.

★ Going deeper

To share a server with your team, save it at project scope (--scope project) in .mcp.json. When someone else gets the repository, Claude Code asks them for permission before connecting a .mcp.json server the first time. But with claude -p, it connects without asking (see the safety page in 17.1). So read and trust .mcp.json too.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Get a practice account or workspace ready.
  2. Run the connect command above, and sign in from /mcp.
  3. Try the "read only" test. If it works, check the connection status in /mcp.
  4. When you're done, disconnect with claude mcp remove notion, and also remove the app's access in the service's own settings. Cleaning up like this is the topic of the next page.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
• Before connecting, decide "read only" or "read and write." If you can, allow reading only.
  • Practice with a practice account or page.
  • Name servers after their service (notion, github). It's easier to tell them apart as the list grows.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "Connecting means the AI learns from all my documents." A connection is a path Claude uses to read things when needed. How your documents are handled depends on the service's and the AI company's policies, which you should check separately. We don't claim either way.
  • "Once /mcp says connected, I'm done." Not quite. You also need to know how to disconnect.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
• Version checked: Claude Code 2.1.319, checked on 2026-11-09. The Notion server address is the example from the official docs. An actual connection and sign-in can only be tested with a real account, so we didn't run them ourselves for this book.
  • Source of facts: Official docs: Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Learning order: claude-howto 05-mcp (MIT; rewritten in our own words).

docs.title: MCP is Claude's plug socket
docs.text:
Ch. 17 · 17.3About 6 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • MCP is a standard plug for connecting Claude Code to outside services like Notion, GitHub, or databases.
  • It takes "AI that uses tools" from Chapter 13 and stretches it to your own services.
  • The more you connect, the handier it gets, and the more risk you take on.

docs.title: Holes in a power strip
docs.text:
If every device had a different plug, life would be a pain. That's why wall sockets follow a standard. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the "socket standard" for AI tools. A service can run a server that follows the standard. Then Claude Code can plug into it. The official docs call MCP an open standard for linking AI and tools.

When do you need it? The docs give a simple test: if you keep copying things from another tool into the chat, it's time to connect. Then Claude can read those things itself. No more pasting issue lists or Notion pages by hand.

docs.title: Skills, hooks, and MCP side by side
docs.text: What it does Comparison Skills (17.1) Teach Claude how to do a job A recipe card Hooks (17.2) Run automatically at set moments A motion-sensor light MCP (17.3) Connect to outside services A wall socket Subagents (17.4) Share out the work An assistant

docs.title: What kinds are there?
docs.text:
There are a few ways to connect (called transports). To start, you only need one: remote HTTP servers. The official docs suggest HTTP for online services. Some servers run right on your computer instead (stdio). Those run programs with your permissions, so the safety page covers them.

Where the connection info is saved (its scope) also differs.

Scope Where it works Shared with team Local This project only No Project This project only Yes (the repository's .mcp.json) User All your projects No

In 10-year-old words

MCP is AI's socket standard. Because the shape is the same, you can plug in any service.

★ Going deeper

MCP servers can offer more than tools. They can also share data ("resources") and prompts. With lots of tools connected, their descriptions take up memory space. Claude Code has a tool search feature, on by default. It looks up only the tools it needs, which cuts that cost. Claude Code can also act as an MCP server itself, so other apps can call it.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
In Claude Code, type /mcp. You'll see the list of connected servers and their status. If you haven't connected anything yet, it'll be empty. You can also check from the terminal:

claude mcp list

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
• Copied the same outside content more than three times? Note it as something to connect.
  • Before connecting, decide: does Claude only need to read from this service, or also write to it?
  • Check your connections with /mcp now and then, and disconnect what you don't use.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "Once I connect MCP, Claude knows the service perfectly." Connecting just opens the door. You still have to tell it what to do.
  • "If it's in an official directory, it's safe." The official docs say to check that you trust a server before you connect it. Anthropic checks connectors against its rules before listing them. But it does not security-audit or manage any MCP server.

docs.text:
