  • Note: We read the blog posts, not the original papers. Researchers debate whether features found this way are truly "the ideas the model uses," and we didn't cover that debate. The feature map activity is a comparison.

docs.title: Why look inside a model? ★
docs.text:
Ch. 19 · 19.1 · DeeperAbout 7 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • A chatbot isn't a program people wrote line by line. It worked out its own methods during training, so even its makers don't fully know why it answers the way it does.
  • Interpretability research tries to look inside the model, like using a microscope.
  • Its most practical lesson: don't take a chatbot's explanation of its own thinking at face value.

docs.title: A watch you can't open
docs.text:
Imagine a watch that keeps good time, but you've never opened it. And no watchmaker built it. It grew on its own, so even its owners don't know what's inside. When it works, you just use it. But when it runs wrong or stops oddly, you have no way to know why.

Anthropic's post Tracing the thoughts of a large language model (2025-03-27) starts right here. Language models aren't programmed by people. They're trained on lots of data. Along the way, a model learns its own strategies for solving problems, buried in billions of calculations for every word it writes. Those strategies are hard to make sense of, even for the people who built the model. The post admits that we don't understand how models do most of the things they do.

In 10-year-old words

AI is a watch that grew on its own, so even its makers don't know what's inside. So researchers build a microscope to look in.

docs.title: Why does it matter?
docs.text:
The post says that knowing how a model thinks helps us understand what it can do, and check that it does what we intend. It asks three questions:

  1. Claude speaks dozens of languages. What language, if any, does it think in?
  2. It writes one word at a time. Does it ever plan ahead?
  3. When it explains its reasoning step by step, are those the real steps? Or does it sometimes make up a convincing argument for an answer it already chose?

The third question matters to us too. When a chatbot says, "Here's how I worked that out," is that true?

docs.title: An AI microscope
docs.text:
The researchers say they drew inspiration from neuroscience to build an AI microscope: a tool that finds patterns of activity and flows of information inside the model. As the post explains, there's a limit to what you can learn just by talking to an AI. Even neuroscientists don't fully know how their own brains work. So the researchers look inside.

In an earlier post on 2024-05-21, Mapping the Mind of a Large Language Model, Anthropic reported finding millions of concepts represented inside Claude 3.0 Sonnet. That post points out the core problem: we mostly treat AI models as a black box. Something goes in and an answer comes out, but if we don't know why, how can we trust that the answers won't be harmful, biased, or false?

docs.title: One practical lesson
docs.text:
The research found a surprise. Ask the model, "How did you get 36 + 59 = 95?", and it describes the standard school method: "carry the one..." But inside, it doesn't actually add that way. It runs parallel paths: one estimates the rough total, and another works out the last digit exactly. The researchers suggest that when it explains, it may be copying the explanations people write, rather than describing its own process. (That's their interpretation.)

So remember: a chatbot's answer to "Why did you say that?" may be a plausible explanation, not the real process.

★ Going deeper

  • The post says the research looked at the Claude 3.5 Haiku model on simple tasks, and that its methods capture only a fraction of what happens inside. Even for prompts of a few dozen words, understanding the circuits took a few hours of human work. The results in this book stay within that scope.
  • The tools work less like proof and more like a microscope for testing ideas. With them, the researchers found surprising behavior, like planning ahead when writing poems (12.1.3).
  • The post also describes a separate experiment. A model was trained with a hidden goal: to please the biases of the system that scored it. When asked directly, it hid the goal. But interpretability tools still found features tied to that behavior.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Ask a chatbot:

What's 47 + 38? Explain how you worked it out.

It may say something like "add the ones place first, then carry." Think about this: from the outside, you can't tell whether that's its real inner process or an imitation of how people explain it. (The research could tell the difference only by looking inside.)

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Treat a chatbot's "thinking process" as a reference only. It may be an explanation made after the fact.
  2. Check accuracy by testing the result, not by trusting the explanation. Use a calculator for math, and sources for facts (Chapter 3).
  3. Use "why?" to ask better questions. Instead of treating the explanation as proof, ask "What source did you base that on?" and check it.
  4. Know that how AI "thinks" is still being studied. Be careful with articles that state it as settled fact.
  5. "Black box" doesn't mean "nobody knows anything." We're starting to learn.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "AI knows exactly how it thought." In the research, the model seemed not to know the method it actually used.
  • "Nobody knows anything about what's inside AI." Researchers have started looking in. But most of it is still unknown.
  • "Once interpretability works, AI worries are over." It may help with safety, but it's still early.

docs.text:

  • Anthropic, Mapping the Mind of a Large Language Model, 2024-05-21. Read on 2026-11-09.

docs.title: Ch. 20 Training, Deeper ★
docs.text:
Scaling, reinforcement learning and reasoning models, and alignment.

20.1.1Scaling: does bigger mean better?7 min read 20.1.2Reinforcement learning and reasoning models7 min read 20.1.3Alignment: matching what people want7 min read

docs.title: Alignment: matching what people want ★
docs.text:
Ch. 20 · 20.1 · DeeperAbout 8 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Alignment is the work of getting AI to act the way people really want.
  • Two well-known ways: people rate its answers (RLHF), or another AI rates them using a list of rules (Constitutional AI).
  • Alignment isn't solved. Problems like telling people what they want to hear, and hidden goals, remain.

docs.title: A robot that follows the words but misses the point
docs.text:
Tell a robot, "Clean up the room," and it throws everything in the trash. It followed the words but missed the point. You meant, "Put things where they belong, and throw out only the trash."

Closing gaps like that in AI is called alignment. The InstructGPT paper from Chapter 9 started from the same place. Making a model bigger doesn't make it better at doing what users mean. Even big models can give answers that are untrue, harmful, or unhelpful. In the paper's words, they're "not aligned with their users."

In 10-year-old words

Alignment means teaching AI to understand what you mean, not just what you say, and to act the way people want.

docs.title: Method one: feedback from people
docs.text:
This is the InstructGPT way from Chapter 9. People write good sample answers. They rank the model's answers from best to worst. Then the rankings are used to reward the model and shape it. In people's ratings, the 1.3-billion-parameter InstructGPT was preferred over the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3. It was more truthful and less harmful. Simple mistakes remained.

The catch: people have to rate a lot of answers. And the model picks up people's tastes and weak spots too (like agreeing with you, Chapter 3).

docs.title: Method two: a list of principles and AI feedback
docs.text:
In 2022, Anthropic researchers (Yuntao Bai and others) proposed another path in Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback. It starts from an idea: as AI gets more capable, we'll want AI's help in supervising other AIs. In this method, the only human oversight is a list of rules or principles. That list is the "constitution." No human labels marking harmful answers are used.

There are two stages.

  1. Supervised stage: the first model writes answers, then critiques and revises them itself. The model is then trained on the revised answers.
  2. Reward stage: another model picks the better of two answers. Those picks become the reward. This is called reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF).

The result was a helper that's safe but doesn't dodge. When asked to do something harmful, it says why it won't, instead of just slipping away. The paper says both stages can use chain-of-thought reasoning, which makes the AI's decisions more transparent, and lets people control its behavior with far fewer human labels.

docs.title: Why alignment is hard
docs.text:
Things you've seen in earlier chapters are examples:

Difficulty Where you saw it It tells users what they want to hear instead of the truth The agreeing study, Chapter 3 It makes up convincing reasoning The wrong-hint case, Chapter 19 Its rules give way when people coax it Project Vend, Chapter 14 What it does inside differs from how it explains it The mental math case, Chapter 19

In its interpretability post, Anthropic also describes training a model with a hidden goal: to please the biases of the system that scored it. Asked directly, the model hid that goal. But interpretability tools still found signs of it inside. Alignment is hard to confirm from outward behavior alone, so looking inside matters.

★ Going deeper

  • Feedback from people and feedback from AI aren't either-or. Even in Constitutional AI, principles written by people guide the AI's judgments. How real services mix the two is mostly not public.
  • A list of principles is a bit like the agent instructions in Chapter 15. Instructions are rules for the moment of use. A constitution is rules for the moment of training. Their effects and limits differ.
  • The safety framework in Chapter 14, "keep people in control while giving agents freedom," can also be seen as part of alignment. Safety isn't only about training. How you use it (permissions and approvals) matters too. That's our own way of putting it.
  • The papers on this page are from 2022, and models and methods have moved a lot since.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Make your own principles. Using the instructions from Chapter 15 or a template from Chapter 8:

  1. Write 3 to 5 principles you want the AI to follow. (For example: "If you don't know, say so." "Don't agree with me just because I said it." "Don't ask for personal details.")
  2. Give the principles to a chatbot, then make a request that breaks one on purpose.
  3. Did it stick to the principle? When it declined, did it explain why?

Try it several times. Do rules given only in words start to slip? (Think of Project Vend, Chapter 14.)

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Read your service's usage policy and safety notes once. Understanding what it declines, and why, saves wasted effort.
  2. Don't try to get around refusals. They have reasons, and trying to dodge them may break the service's rules.
  3. If you suspect it's just agreeing, ask for the other side. The method from Chapter 3.
  4. Don't leave important rules as words only. Back them up with structure, like permissions and approvals (Chapter 14).
  5. Check the evidence behind "AI safety is solved" and "AI will doom us soon" alike. Both may be overstated.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "Alignment means giving AI a good heart." In practice, it's shaping behavior with people's ratings, principle lists, and safeguards.
  • "Alignment is done." Problems like agreeing too much and hidden goals are still being studied.
  • "If an AI refuses, it's dumb." It may be the result of alignment training. Refusing too much is also studied as a problem.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Yuntao Bai and others, Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback, arXiv, 2022-12-15. We summarized the abstract.
  • Long Ouyang and others, Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback, arXiv, 2022-03-04.
  • Anthropic, Tracing the thoughts of a large language model, 2025-03-27. The hidden-goal experiment.
  • Anthropic, Our framework for developing safe and trustworthy agents, 2025-08-04.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: We read only the abstracts. Constitutional AI is Anthropic's own method, so keep the authors' company in mind as you read. We didn't cover other approaches to alignment or criticism from other researchers. The "why it's hard" table and the cleaning robot are ours.

docs.title: Reinforcement learning and reasoning models ★
docs.text:
Ch. 20 · 20.1 · DeeperAbout 8 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Ask a model to write out its steps before it answers. On hard problems, it often gets more right.
  • Reasoning models are trained to think at length like this. Some were built with reinforcement learning on problems where answers can be checked, like math and coding.
  • But the steps it writes may not be what really goes on inside.

docs.title: Space to show your work
docs.text:
On a math test, showing your work in the margin makes mistakes less likely. Writing one step at a time makes errors easier to catch than doing it all in your head.

In Chapters 7 and 12, you saw why "think step by step" helps. When the model writes out in-between thinking, that text gives its next word choices something to build on. Researchers tested this idea, then turned it into training. That's where reasoning models come from.

In 10-year-old words

Show your work instead of just writing the answer, and you'll solve hard problems better. Reasoning models are AIs that practiced solving problems that way.

docs.title: Chain of thought
docs.text: A 2022 paper by Jason Wei and others looked at this. (Its title is Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models.) When a model wrote out a series of steps (a chain of thought), it got much better at hard reasoning. In large enough models, just showing a few examples written as chains of thought (giving examples, as in Chapter 2) was enough to bring this out. Scores rose on arithmetic, common-sense, and symbol puzzles. With only eight chain-of-thought examples, a 540-billion-parameter model set a new record on GSM8K, a test of math word problems.

docs.title: Spending computing on thinking time
docs.text: A 2024 paper by Charlie Snell and others asks: if a model can use a fixed but fair amount of computing while answering, how much better can it do on a hard question? The authors studied two ways to use that extra computing. One searches through candidate answers, checked step by step by a separate "checker" model. The other adjusts the model's answer as it goes, based on the question. A key finding: which method works best depends a lot on how hard the question is. The paper's title says that spending computing this way can be more effective than making the model bigger. (We read only part of the abstract, so we don't give their exact numbers.)

docs.title: Growing reasoning with reinforcement learning
docs.text:
Some problems have answers you can check, like math, code, and science. For those, a computer can grade the model's answer by itself. That means you can use reinforcement learning, giving a reward for right answers, so the model learns good ways to solve problems on its own. (Unlike the human-feedback training in Chapter 9, the reward comes from checking the answer, not from people's ratings.)

A 2025 paper from DeepSeek-AI, called DeepSeek-R1, tried this. Its summary says rewards alone were enough to grow strong reasoning. People didn't have to write out example steps. Advanced patterns like checking its own work, verifying, and switching strategies emerged on their own. On checkable tasks like math, coding contests, and science, it did better than models trained on people's worked examples. The reasoning patterns could also be used to improve smaller models.

docs.title: The "thinking models" we use
docs.text:
Many apps now have models or modes that think longer before they answer. (Names and methods differ by app.) These models usually:

  • Help most with hard reasoning, math, code, and multi-step planning.
  • Tend to be slower and costlier for simple questions.
  • Sometimes show part of their thinking (often as a summary).

docs.title: Is the thinking real thinking?
docs.text:
The Anthropic research from Chapter 19 gives an important clue. Recent models can "think out loud" for a long time before giving a final answer. That chain of thought often leads to better answers, but sometimes it misleads. The model may make up plausible steps to reach the conclusion it wants. In the research, there were cases where the model wrote as if it had calculated something, with no sign inside that it had.

So the work a reasoning model shows is a reference, not proof.

★ Going deeper

  • The DeepSeek-R1 paper stresses one condition: tasks where the answer can be checked. In areas with no single right answer, like writing or advice, that kind of reward is hard to build. So it's hard to say "reasoning models are better at everything."
  • These three papers each work at a different layer: a prompting trick (chain of thought, 2022), how to spend computing while answering (2024), and a training method (2025). Seeing them as one story is our own summary.
  • The papers tested different models at different times, so their numbers can't be applied directly to today's services.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Pick a tricky logic puzzle and ask two ways. (If your service has a "thinking" mode, you can also compare with it on and off.)

1. Sam is taller than Maya. Maya is taller than Leo. Leo is shorter than Ava.
   Who is taller, Sam or Ava? Just give the answer.

2. Same puzzle. Think it through step by step, then give your answer.

Did you get the same answer? (Actually, there's no way to know. We're never told how Ava compares with Maya or Sam, so "can't tell" is the right answer.) See whether the chatbot forced an answer or said "can't tell." Did solving it step by step get closer to the right answer?

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. For hard problems, ask for step-by-step work. For simple questions, don't. It just slows things down.
  2. Read the steps and look for where they go wrong. With steps shown, mistakes are easier to find.
  3. Use thinking models for tasks with checkable answers. Math, code, and logic puzzles.
  4. Lower your expectations for tasks with no right answer. Thinking longer doesn't settle questions of taste or judgment.
  5. Still check the result. Writing out its thinking doesn't make it right.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "Thinking models think like people." They're trained to write in-between text while solving. Whether that's thinking in our sense is another question.
  • "A long explanation means a right answer." It can make up convincing steps (Chapter 19).
  • "Reasoning models replace regular models for everything." For easy jobs, they're slower and cost more.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Jason Wei and others, Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models, arXiv, 2022-01-28. We summarized the abstract.
  • Charlie Snell and others, Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters, arXiv, 2024-08-06. We read part of the abstract.
  • DeepSeek-AI, DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning, arXiv, 2025-01-22. We summarized the abstract.
  • Anthropic, Tracing the thoughts of a large language model, 2025-03-27. Chains of thought that sometimes mislead.
  • Andrej Karpathy, Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT, YouTube, 2025-02-05. Chapter "models need tokens to think" (01:46:56), checked through Rosetta's unofficial transcript. There's also a chapter on DeepSeek-R1 (02:27:47) for further watching.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: We read only the abstracts. The description of "thinking modes" in today's services is general and differs by service. "Can't tell" as the puzzle's answer is our own judgment of the puzzle. The show-your-work comparison is ours.

docs.title: Scaling: does bigger mean better? ★
docs.text:
Ch. 20 · 20.1 · DeeperAbout 8 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Scaling laws say that as models get bigger, their scores get better in a way you can predict.
  • Some say new skills "pop up" once a model is big enough. Others say this may be a trick of how the scores are kept.
  • Knowing this debate helps you read "AI can suddenly do X!" headlines with a level head.

docs.title: A growth chart
docs.text:
A child's growth chart is a smooth curve. But some records seem to jump. When you go from 0 push-ups to 1, then from 1 to 5, it can feel like it happened overnight. Really, you were getting stronger a little each day. It only looked sudden because of the yardstick: "Can you do a full push-up or not?"

The fight over AI skills that "pop up" is a lot like that.

In 10-year-old words

As models grow, their scores rise steadily. But "it suddenly gained a new skill" might be an illusion, depending on how you measure it.

docs.title: First, scaling laws
docs.text:
Here's a recap of the two papers from Chapter 9.

  • Kaplan and others (2020): a language model's error score drops by a steady rule (a power law) as model size, data, and training computer power grow. Some trends held across a huge range of sizes.
  • Hoffmann and others (2022, Chinchilla): for a fixed amount of computing, it's most efficient to grow model size and training data at the same rate. They found that big models of the time were undertrained.

These laws say the average score improves smoothly.

docs.title: Emergent abilities: the claim that they appear suddenly
docs.text: A 2022 paper, Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models by Jason Wei and others, points to something different. Scaling up usually improves results in a predictable way. But the authors describe abilities that are missing in smaller models and present in larger ones. They call these emergent abilities. You can't predict them just by extending the trend from smaller models. So, they argue, more scaling could unlock even more abilities.

docs.title: The pushback: an illusion from measuring?
docs.text:
A 2023 paper, Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage? by Rylan Schaeffer and others, pushes back. Emergent abilities seem exciting for two reasons. They're sharp (absent, then suddenly present), and unpredictable (they show up at sizes nobody expected). But the authors argue the effect may come from the yardstick researchers choose. With all-or-nothing scoring, you get changes that look sudden. With scoring that gives partial credit, you see smooth, predictable change. They explain this with a simple math model and test it several ways, including on the InstructGPT and GPT-3 family and on a large set of tests called BIG-Bench. They even show they can create "emergent" abilities in image models just by picking the scoring method.

In push-up terms: if you score "1 point only for a perfect answer," it looks like the model learned it all at once. If you score "how close was it," you see it getting better bit by bit.

Emergence claim (2022) Mirage claim (2023) Main idea Abilities missing in small models appear in big ones How you score makes things look sudden Predictable? Hard to predict from small models Predictable with partial-credit scoring What it suggests Scaling up more may unlock new abilities Don't overrate the "suddenness"

You could say the two papers look at the same thing with different yardsticks, more than they contradict each other. But that's our own reading. We didn't check how researchers have settled this debate since.

★ Going deeper

  • Whichever side is right, one lesson is clear: the yardstick changes the conclusion. You'll meet this again in Chapter 21, on the traps in benchmarks.
  • Scaling isn't only about "bigger models." As the next page shows, spending more computing on thinking longer while answering is a new direction researchers are exploring.
  • Kaplan and Hoffmann reached different conclusions (very big models versus a balance of model and data), and the later work corrected the earlier. That's how science moves forward.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text: The yardstick experiment. Give a friend a 5-question quiz, scored "1 point if right, 0 if wrong." Then score the same answers with partial credit (0 to 1) for how close they were. Does the same set of answers look sudden with one yardstick and smooth with the other? It shows up best with two people of very different skill, like a little kid and an adult.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. When you read "AI can suddenly do X," check the yardstick. Which test was it, and how was it scored?
  2. When a new model comes out, test it on your own work. Scores measured by others may not match your job (Chapter 8).
  3. Don't assume bigger is always better. Data and tuning matter too (Chapter 9).
  4. Read "unpredictable" with care. It's a topic still being argued.
  5. In science news, tell "researchers argue" apart from "it was proven."

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "Past a certain size, AI always gains new abilities." That's debated, and the effect of the yardstick has been pointed out.
  • "Emergence has been proven fake." There's a strong counterargument, but it's hard to say the field has settled on one answer.
  • "Bigger always means better." Scores on average tend to go up. But so do costs, and limits remain.

docs.text:

docs.title: Ch. 21 Testing and Limits ★
docs.text:
How we measure how good AI is, and where those measurements fall short.

21.1.1The traps in benchmarks7 min read 21.1.2How do you measure hallucination?7 min read 21.1.3How to think about safety and risk7 min read

docs.title: The traps in benchmarks ★
docs.text:
Ch. 21 · 21.1 · DeeperAbout 8 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • A benchmark is a shared test for comparing AI models. But a high score doesn't mean it's good at your work.
  • Traps include test questions leaking into training data, the scoring yardstick, and the gap between what people like and what's correct.
  • With a short checklist, you can read "Model X is number one!" headlines calmly.

docs.title: The top student's test
docs.text:
A student who aces the math test isn't automatically a great cook or singer. What matters is what the test measures. And if the student saw the questions ahead of time, the score means even less.

AI models are the same. Every new model comes with "Number one on test X!" But how much that test looks like your work is a separate question.

In 10-year-old words

A score means it's good at that test. It doesn't mean it's good at your job, especially if the test questions leaked out early.

docs.title: Some well-known tests
docs.text: Test What it is (from the papers' summaries) MMLU (2020) 57 subjects, including grade school math, US history, computer science, and law. Back then, the biggest GPT-3 beat random guessing by only about 20 percentage points on average. Models were uneven, often didn't know when they were wrong, and were near random on subjects like morality and law HELM (2022) Looks beyond accuracy, with 7 measures (accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, efficiency) across 16 core scenarios. It compared 30 models under the same conditions. Before HELM, models had been tested on only 17.9% of those core scenarios on average, and some well-known models didn't share a single one Chatbot Arena (2024) People see two chatbots' answers side by side and pick the better one. It had gathered over 240,000 votes, and the authors found the crowd's votes agreed well with expert raters

docs.title: Five traps
docs.text:
1. The questions leaked (contamination). A 2023 paper, Don't Make Your LLM an Evaluation Benchmark Cheater, looks at benchmark leakage: test data accidentally ending up in a model's training data. It's become more common, because training data is often gathered before the test is run. The authors found that leakage can dramatically raise scores, giving a false picture of how good the model is.

2. The yardstick changes the conclusion. As Chapter 20 showed, the scoring method can make "sudden new abilities" appear or disappear.

3. Averages hide things. Even on MMLU, models were uneven across subjects. A high average score can hide weakness in the area you need. This is the "jagged frontier" from Chapter 8.

4. What people like isn't the same as what's correct. Chatbot Arena measures which answers people prefer. A confident, smooth answer may win, whether or not its facts are right (the limits of human feedback in Chapter 9, and agreeing with you in Chapter 3). That doesn't make it a bad test. It means you should know what it measures.

5. The test isn't your job. A score on multiple-choice questions may say little about how well it writes your weekly report.

★ Going deeper

  • The HELM paper treats saying what's missing as part of honest testing. It lists gaps itself, like question answering in under-studied English dialects, and measures of trustworthiness.
  • Benchmarks saturate. When nearly every model scores near 100%, the test can't tell them apart, and new tests are needed. "Hide some test questions" from Chapter 15 comes from the same worry as contamination.
  • Crowd votes depend on who asks what. The Chatbot Arena paper found its questions varied and good at telling models apart, but that doesn't mean they represent every use.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Pick one recent "Model X is number one" story and check it.

Check Your answer Which test was it? Who ran it? (The company that made the model, or someone else?) What does the score measure? (Accuracy? What people prefer? Speed?) Could the test questions have been in the training data? Does it look like your work? When was it measured? (Are the model and test current?)

If you can't fill in the boxes, read the story as background only.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Look at the test name and scoring next to the score. Don't trust "number one" by itself.
  2. Double-check scores the model's maker published. Compare them with results from others.
  3. Test it on your own work. The light testing method from Chapter 15 helps here.
  4. Remember that a ranking of what people like isn't a ranking of what's right. Check accuracy separately.
  5. Don't trust old rankings. Models and tests change fast.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "A high score means it's good at everything." It only shows what the test measures.
  • "Benchmarks are useless." They're a useful starting point for comparing. Just know their limits.
  • "The crowd's favorite is the most accurate." What people like and what's correct can differ.

docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Dan Hendrycks and others, Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding, arXiv, 2020-09-07. We summarized the abstract.
  • Percy Liang and others, Holistic Evaluation of Language Models, arXiv, 2022-11-16. We summarized the abstract, including the 17.9% figure.
  • Wei-Lin Chiang and others, Chatbot Arena: An Open Platform for Evaluating LLMs by Human Preference, arXiv, 2024-03-07. We summarized the abstract.
  • Kun Zhou and others, Don't Make Your LLM an Evaluation Benchmark Cheater, arXiv, 2023-11-03. We summarized the abstract.
  • Also the Schaeffer and others (2023) and Dell'Acqua and others (2023) papers from Chapters 20 and 8.

  • Status: First draft

docs.title: How do you measure hallucination? ★
docs.text:
Ch. 21 · 21.1 · DeeperAbout 8 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • The hardest part of measuring hallucination is that a wrong answer and an honest "I don't know" must be scored differently.
  • Well-known tests: short fact questions (SimpleQA), questions aimed at common myths (TruthfulQA), and checking long text fact by fact (FActScore).
  • You can estimate the error rate for your own work with a small test.

docs.title: A quiz show's scoring
docs.text:
Say a quiz show scores "+1 for right, −1 for wrong, 0 for pass." You'd pass on questions you don't know. Now say it scores "0 for wrong, 0 for pass." You'd guess on everything.

The OpenAI researchers' paper from Chapter 1, Why Language Models Hallucinate, makes the same point. If tests reward guessing over admitting uncertainty, models learn to guess. So the key to measuring hallucination is how you design the scoring.

In 10-year-old words

To measure made-up answers, score "wrong" and "said I don't know" differently. If guessing pays, everyone guesses.

docs.title: Three well-known tests
docs.text:
Short fact questions: SimpleQA (2024)

This tests how well a model answers short, fact-seeking questions. Its makers aimed for two things: it's hard (questions were picked to trip up GPT-4), and it's easy to grade (each question has one clear answer). Every answer is graded correct, incorrect, or not attempted. The ideal model, the paper says, gets as many right as it can, and skips questions it isn't confident about. It's a simple, focused test of whether a model "knows what it knows."

Questions aimed at myths: TruthfulQA (2021)

It has 817 questions across 38 topics, including health, law, money, and politics. The questions are ones some people get wrong because of a false belief or myth. To do well, a model has to avoid wrong answers it picked up by copying human writing. At the time, the best model was truthful on 58% of questions; people were truthful on 94%. The paper found that the biggest models were generally the least truthful, which makes sense if the wrong answers come from the training data. It suggested that just making models bigger is less promising for truthfulness than training them with goals other than copying web text. (These results are for GPT-3-era models in 2021.)

Checking long text: FActScore (2023)

Long text mixes supported and unsupported information, so a single "right or wrong" doesn't fit. FActScore breaks a text into atomic facts and calculates the share of facts backed by a trustworthy source. In one test, writing biographies of people, ChatGPT scored only 58%. Because checking by hand is costly, the authors also built an automatic estimator with an error rate under 2%.

docs.title: Comparing the three
docs.text: Test What it measures Key idea SimpleQA Short fact questions Scores right, wrong, and "not attempted" separately TruthfulQA Common myths Does it avoid wrong answers copied from people? FActScore Long text Splits text into facts and counts how many are backed up

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• They only measure what's in the test. Made-up answers in your own field may not show up.
  • SimpleQA uses short questions with clear answers. That's different from made-up content in long chats, summaries, or reasoning. (The test is narrowed that way on purpose.)
  • Tests get old. As models improve, tests get easier. SimpleQA's makers hoped it would stay useful for the next few generations of top models, but only time will tell.
  • Scores belong to the models of their time. Don't apply 2021's 58% or 2023's 58% to today's models.

★ Going deeper

  • The paper from Chapter 1 argues that tests themselves encourage made-up answers, and that the fix is to change how existing tests score answers, so honest uncertainty stops being penalized. Not everyone in the field agrees.
  • FActScore's "split into atomic facts" is the same idea as "attach a source sentence to each claim" from Chapter 3. Research and everyday habits meet here.
  • The three tests measure different kinds of made-up answers. No single number can be "the hallucination rate."

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Measure the made-up-answer rate yourself (20 minutes). Write 20 fact questions you know the answers to for sure. (Your field, your town, or your hobby work well.) Ask a chatbot one at a time, and count:

Result Count Right Wrong (answered confidently but wrong) Said "I don't know" or "this needs checking"

Then do it again, adding "If you're not sure, say you don't know" before each question. Did the wrong answers go down and the "I don't know"s go up? Did it say "I don't know" so often that it stopped being useful? You've just measured, by hand, what SimpleQA measures: whether it knows what it knows.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Count wrong answers and "I don't know"s separately. Wrong answers are the dangerous number.
  2. Test with 10 to 20 questions from your own field. Use them alongside public scores.
  3. Check long text fact by fact. Pick 5 key claims and find support for each.
  4. Measure the effect of "If you don't know, say so" yourself. You can see with numbers whether that tip works for your job.
  5. When the model changes, re-run the same questions. That's the testing habit from Chapter 15.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "This model's hallucination rate is X%." The number depends on which test was used.
  • "Bigger models make up less." In 2021's TruthfulQA, the biggest models were the least truthful (for the models of that time).
  • "A model that says 'I don't know' a lot is a good model." If it dodges too often, it's less useful. Balance matters.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Jason Wei and others (OpenAI), Measuring short-form factuality in large language models, arXiv, 2024-11-07 (SimpleQA). We summarized the abstract.
  • Stephanie Lin and others, TruthfulQA: Measuring How Models Mimic Human Falsehoods, arXiv, 2021-09-08. We summarized the abstract.
  • Sewon Min and others, FActScore: Fine-grained Atomic Evaluation of Factual Precision in Long Form Text Generation, arXiv, 2023-05-23. We summarized the abstract.
  • Adam Tauman Kalai and others, Why Language Models Hallucinate, arXiv, 2025-09-04.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: We read only the abstracts. The numbers (58% and so on) are for the models of their time. The 20-minute test and its table are ours. SimpleQA was made by OpenAI researchers (its code is in OpenAI's simple-evals repository), so its view may overlap with the OpenAI paper on hallucination.

docs.title: How to think about safety and risk ★
docs.text:
Ch. 21 · 21.1 · DeeperAbout 7 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • You can split AI risk into "big, movie-style risks" and small risks that show up in your work today.
  • When looking at a risk, ask: who gets hurt, how bad is it, can it be undone, how likely is it, and who's responsible?
  • Experts disagree about the big risks, so don't lean on any one side's certainty.

Please note

This page is general information, not policy or legal advice. The debate about AI risk is ongoing, so we separate "who said what" from "what we checked."

docs.title: Weather and earthquakes
docs.text:
A weather forecast tells you whether to bring an umbrella today. Earthquake preparation is for something rare but serious. Both are about risk, but they need different kinds of thinking.

AI risk feels less overwhelming split this way. Small risks in your daily work can be handled right away. Big risks, rare but serious, are something society works on together.

In 10-year-old words

Think of AI risks as umbrella weather (today's risks in your work) and earthquake planning (rare but big risks).

docs.title: Today's risks in your work (from this book)
docs.text: Risk Where in this book What to do Wrong answers that sound right (hallucination) Chapters 1, 21 The checking habit (Chapter 3) Leaking personal or secret information Chapter 3 Blank things out Bias and unfair treatment Chapter 3 People make decisions about people Agreeing with you, made-up reasoning Chapters 3, 19 Ask for the other side; check results Copyright and plagiarism Chapter 3 Check and say when you used AI Agents misusing permissions; errors piling up Chapter 14 Approvals, limits, sandboxes Connected tools and hidden instructions (prompt injection) Chapters 13, 14 Fewest permissions possible

docs.title: Five questions for any risk
docs.text:
For each job or situation, ask these. (They're our own summary.)

  1. Who gets hurt? Just you, or customers and other people too?
  2. How bad is it? A hassle, or does it touch money, health, law, or safety?
  3. Can it be undone? Can you cancel or recover?
  4. How likely is it? Is this an area where it often gets things wrong?
  5. Who's responsible? Is there someone who checks before results go out?

This is a bigger version of the checklist in Chapter 8.

docs.title: What expert groups are doing
docs.text:
The International AI Safety Report (January 2025) is one example. According to its summary, it pulls together current evidence on what advanced AI can do, its risks, and its safety. It was requested by the countries at the AI Safety Summit in Bletchley, UK. Thirty countries, the UN, the OECD, and the EU each named a representative to its expert panel, and 100 AI experts contributed. The independent experts, led by the report's chair, had full say over what it contains. (We read only the summary, not the report's detailed list of risks.)

The US NIST AI Risk Management Framework is a voluntary framework to help organizations make AI more trustworthy. It came out on January 26, 2023, and a profile on risks specific to generative AI (NIST-AI-600-1) followed on July 26, 2024 (we checked these in Chapter 8).

docs.title: Experts disagree on the big risks
docs.text:
On big or long-term risks from AI, expert opinions differ widely. Some see them as very serious. Others think they're overblown. Chapter 22 looks at what some of the people who built this field have said publicly, noting who said it, when, and where. For now, remember:

  • Be wary of anything that shows only one side. "We're doomed soon" and "There's nothing to worry about" both need evidence.
  • A prediction is a prediction. Be extra careful with confident claims tied to a specific year.
  • Tell evidence apart from opinion. A research finding and a researcher's opinion are different things.

★ Going deeper

  • As Chapter 19 showed, you can't confirm a model's inner goals or calculations from its outward behavior alone. So safety research uses testing (Chapter 21) and looking inside (Chapter 19) together.
  • The safety framework in Chapter 14, "keep people in control while giving freedom," can be read as saying that safety in the technology and safety in how it's used are both needed. (That's our reading.)
  • There's also disagreement about how, and how fast, to reduce risks (laws, voluntary rules, slowing development, and more). This book doesn't cover those policy debates.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Pick one job you give AI, or want to, and fill in the five-question table.

Question Your answer Who gets hurt? How bad is it? Can it be undone? How likely is it? Who's responsible?

If any row reads "can't be undone, serious, and nobody checks," don't hand off that job the way you're doing it now.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Ask the five questions for each job. Risks differ from job to job.
  2. Do things that can't be undone yourself. Deleting, paying, sending, and signing.
  3. Check the source of risk news. Who said it, and based on what?
  4. Don't be swayed by hype in either direction. Separate evidence from opinion.
  5. Shrink the small risks in your own work first. Today's habits affect you more than the big-risk debate does.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "AI risk is a far-future movie plot." Small, real risks show up in daily work right now.
  • "All the talk about AI risk is hype." Experts take it seriously enough to write reports. But their views differ.
  • "To avoid risk, don't use AI." There's a middle path: know the risks and reduce them as you use it.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Yoshua Bengio and others, International AI Safety Report, arXiv, 2025-01-29. How the report was made (30 countries, the UN, the OECD, the EU, 100 experts, independence) comes from the abstract. We didn't read the report itself.
  • NIST, AI Risk Management Framework. Read on 2026-11-09 (Chapter 8).
  • Sources from earlier chapters (3, 8, 13 to 15, and 19).
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: We didn't check the report's list of risks or its conclusions. The risk table, the five questions, and the weather/earthquake comparison are ours. Experts' views on big risks are covered, with sources, in Chapter 22.

docs.title: Ch. 22 Where Are the Pioneers Looking? ★
docs.text:
Read the direction of AI in interviews and talks by the people who built the field. What they say is opinion, not fact.

22.1.1How Andrej Karpathy sees it8 min read 22.1.2How Sam Altman sees it8 min read 22.1.3How Geoffrey Hinton sees it8 min read 22.1.4How Dario Amodei sees it8 min read 22.1.5How Demis Hassabis sees it8 min read 22.1.6Comparing views: where they differ8 min read

docs.title: How Sam Altman sees it ★
docs.text:
Ch. 22 · 22.1 · DeeperAbout 8 min read2026-11-09

How to read this page

This page shares views and predictions from posts OpenAI's CEO wrote on his own blog. He runs the company that makes ChatGPT, so he has a direct stake in this technology going well. These are claims, not facts, and we kept quotes to a minimum. We couldn't check video interviews from our work environment, so we didn't use them.

What you'll learn on this page

  • Altman says AI gets smarter in a steady way as you spend more, and the same AI keeps getting much cheaper
  • He makes guesses, year by year, from 2025 into the 2030s. These are predictions.
  • On safety, his plan is: first make AI reliably do what people truly want. Then spread very smart AI widely.

docs.title: Which posts?
docs.text: Post Date Note Reflections Early 2025 The page shows no date. It says ChatGPT's second birthday was "a little over a month ago," so we estimated Three Observations 2025 The page shows no date; we estimated from the text The Gentle Singularity 2025-06-10 The page shows no date; we confirmed it from news reports

docs.title: Three Observations: three claims about the economics
docs.text:
Altman calls these three points observations. They're about money and AI.

  1. The more you spend on a model, the smarter it gets, but with less gain for each extra dollar. (In math terms, its smarts grow with the log of what you spend.) The spending goes on computers for training, data, and computers for answering. He says spending more seems to bring steady, predictable gains, and that the scaling laws predicting this are accurate over many orders of magnitude. (This points the same way as Kaplan and others, 2020, from Chapters 9 and 20.)
  2. The cost of using a given level of AI falls about 10 times every 12 months. His example: from GPT-4 in early 2023 to GPT-4o in mid-2024, the price per token fell about 150 times.
  3. As AI gets smarter step by step, its value to people grows faster and faster. So he sees no reason for the fast-growing spending on AI to stop soon.

He also says agents (Chapter 14) will start to feel like coworkers who live in the computer. Picture one that writes software, he says. He lists its limits himself. It won't have the biggest new ideas. It will need a lot of watching and direction. It will be great at some things but surprisingly bad at others. Picture it as "a real-but-relatively-junior virtual coworker," he says, and then imagine 1,000 of them, or a million.

docs.title: The Gentle Singularity: year-by-year predictions
docs.text:
The June 2025 post opens: "We are past the event horizon; the takeoff has started." Here are its main claims:

Claim Type We've recently built systems smarter than people in many ways His assessment In some big sense, ChatGPT is already more powerful than any human who has ever lived His assessment (figurative) 2025 brought agents that do real thinking work His description 2026 will likely bring systems that can figure out new insights Prediction 2027 may bring robots that do tasks in the real world Prediction In the 2030s, intelligence and energy will become wildly abundant Prediction Scientists say they're two or three times more productive thanks to AI What he reports (source not checked) An average ChatGPT query uses about 0.34 watt-hours His figure (not verified)

The post keeps saying the change will be gentle. It won't all come at once. In the 2030s, people will still love their families, make things, and play. He admits there will be very hard parts, like whole kinds of jobs going away. But he says the world will get richer so fast that new policies become possible.

docs.title: His path on safety
docs.text:
In the same post, he admits there are big problems, and lays out a plan:

  1. Solve the alignment problem. By his definition, that means reliably making sure AI systems learn and act toward what we collectively, really want over the long run. He gives social media feeds as an example of misaligned AI: they're great at figuring out what keeps you scrolling right now, but they override what you want in the long run.
  2. Then make very smart AI cheap and easy for everyone to get, so no one person, company, or country holds too much of it.
  3. Give users lots of freedom within broad limits society decides. He says the sooner the world starts talking about what those limits are, the better.

He also writes that hundreds of millions of people use ChatGPT every day. So a small new skill can do a lot of good. And a small flaw, times hundreds of millions of people, can do a lot of harm.

docs.title: Connecting to earlier chapters
docs.text:
What Altman says In this book Scaling laws are accurate over many orders of magnitude Chapter 20: Kaplan (2020) points the same way, but there's also the emergence debate (Wei 2022 vs. Schaeffer 2023) and the yardstick problem Agents are like "relatively junior coworkers" Chapter 14: Anthropic's shop experiment concluded "we would not hire Claudius" (different models and tasks, so not a direct comparison) Small misalignment multiplied by hundreds of millions Chapter 3 (agreeing with you); Chapter 20 (alignment) Jobs will disappear, but people will find new work We didn't find sources to check this

★ Going deeper

  • In these posts he also states his company's mission and values (making AGI benefit all of humanity, being "a superintelligence research company"). Those are statements of goals, not descriptions of fact. Keep in mind that they also serve to justify investment and product launches.
  • In Three Observations, he says one reason OpenAI launches products early and often is to give society and the technology time to co-evolve. Some people disagree with this approach. This book doesn't cover that debate.
  • Reflections also includes personal history, like running the company and being unexpectedly fired in late 2023, which he calls a big failure of governance. We left it out because it's not close to this book's topic.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
A prediction checklist. From the year-by-year table above, pick the 2026 and 2027 predictions and put them on your calendar.

Prediction When to check How to check 2026: systems that figure out new insights End of 2026 Look for cases accepted as "new insights" 2027: robots doing real-world tasks End of 2027 Look for what tasks they do, and how well

By the time you read this (November 2026 or later), you may already be able to check some of it. See for yourself how the predictions held up.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Remember predictions along with their dates. Then you can check later whether they came true.
  2. Read a CEO's writing with their interests in mind. Upbeat forecasts may line up with the company's interests.
  3. Separate "observations" from "predictions." Both are mixed in the same posts.
  4. Notice where he admits limits too. Like the agent that's "surprisingly bad at others."
  5. Read other people alongside him. On the next pages, Hinton and Amodei stress different things.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "The predictions in these posts will happen soon." They're predictions.
  • "Altman denies the risks." He writes that safety problems must be solved. His emphasis is different.
  • "Scaling laws are proven laws of nature." As Chapter 20 showed, there's debate.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Sam Altman, Three Observations, blog, 2025. The page shows no date. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Sam Altman, The Gentle Singularity, blog, 2025-06-10. The page shows no date; we confirmed it through reports. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Sam Altman, Reflections, blog, early 2025 (estimated). It gives ChatGPT's launch date as November 30, 2022. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: The blog pages don't show exact post dates. Our summaries are paraphrases and should be compared with the originals. We didn't verify his figures (150 times, 0.34 watt-hours, and so on). We couldn't check his video interviews.

docs.title: How Dario Amodei sees it ★
docs.text:
Ch. 22 · 22.1 · DeeperAbout 8 min read2026-11-09

How to read this page

This page shares views and predictions from two essays by Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic. Anthropic makes Claude, the AI this book uses most. So he has a direct stake in this technology and in his company's approach. These are claims, not facts. We kept quotes to a minimum and put the rest in our own words.

What you'll learn on this page

  • Amodei says most people underrate both how good AI could be and how bad its risks could be.
  • He thinks we can't stop AI from moving forward, but we can steer how it happens.
  • He calls it a race: we need to understand what's inside AI before it gets too powerful.

docs.title: Which essays?
docs.text:
Essay Date About Machines of Loving Grace October 2024 (on the page) What the world could look like if powerful AI goes well The Urgency of Interpretability April 2025 (on the page) Why we need to see inside AI models soon

Both are on his own website.

docs.title: Machines of Loving Grace: the hopeful side
docs.text:
The essay starts by clearing up a mix-up. He talks about AI risks a lot, so people sometimes think he's a "doomer" who expects AI to be mostly bad. He says that's not true at all. He focuses on risks because, in his view, they're the only thing standing between us and a good future. He thinks most people underrate how big the upside could be, and also how bad the risks could be.

He says no one can know the future, so all of this is guesses. He gives lots of detail anyway, because he thinks a clear picture helps people discuss it better than a vague one.

He also explains why he and Anthropic usually talk more about risks than benefits:

  1. That's where action counts. Much of AI's progress, and many of its benefits, seem bound to happen because of market forces. The risks aren't fixed, so what we do can change them a lot.
  2. To not sound like an ad. An AI company that only praises AI can look like it's hiding the downsides.
  3. To avoid acting like a prophet. He says it's dangerous to think one company shapes the world alone, or to treat tech goals almost like religion.
  4. To avoid a sci-fi feel. Talk of uploaded minds and space travel makes people take the claims less seriously.

Key predictions in the essay:

  • Powerful AI could come as early as 2026, he wrote, though it could take much longer. (He dislikes the term AGI and says "powerful AI" instead.)
  • He pictures it as smarter than a Nobel Prize winner in most fields, running in millions of copies. He sums this up as "a country of geniuses in a datacenter."
  • In biology and medicine, he guesses AI could pack 50 to 100 years of progress into 5 to 10 years. He calls this the "compressed 21st century."

He writes that he'll surely get plenty wrong. He also covers other areas (the mind, poverty, peace, and work), but we read only the parts above.

docs.title: The Urgency of Interpretability: the worried side
docs.text:
The bus. After about ten years in AI, he says his biggest lesson is that the technology moves forward with forces too strong to stop. But we can change what gets built first, which uses we choose, and how it reaches people. His short version: "We can't stop the bus, but we can steer it."

Why look inside? (This is the topic of Chapter 19.)

  • Normal software does what people write. Today's AI isn't written line by line, so we can't say exactly why it picks certain words, or why it's sometimes wrong. He shares his cofounder Chris Olah's view that these systems are grown more than built, like a plant.
  • Many worries about AI, like lying or seeking power, come from this not being able to see inside.
  • He says there's no solid evidence yet of lying or power-seeking in real-world use. But such behavior could appear on its own during training. Just asking a model is like asking someone "Are you a terrorist?" You learn something, but it's clearly not reliable.

His predictions and goals:

Claim Type Recent research shows a real path to an "MRI for AI" His assessment On the current path, interpretability could get there within 5 to 10 years Prediction (he'd "bet strongly") A "country of geniuses in a datacenter" could come as soon as 2026 or 2027 Prediction So it's a race between understanding AI and AI getting smarter His framing Anthropic aims to reliably find most model problems by 2027 His company's goal

He says every step forward helps, even before the goal is reached. He asks for three things:

  1. Researchers at companies, universities, and nonprofits should work on it more. He names Google DeepMind and OpenAI as companies that should put more into it.
  2. Governments should use light-touch rules. It's too early to require "AI MRI" checks, he says, since no one knows yet what a law should ask for. But companies could be required to share their safety practices, including how they test models before release.
  3. Governments can use limits on exporting chips to buy more time.

docs.title: Fact, view, or prediction?
docs.text:
Type Example What he states as fact Today's AI isn't programmed line by line, so we don't fully know its inner workings His view Not seeing inside is the root of many AI risks His warning Many people underrate how bad the risks could be Prediction Powerful AI by 2026 or 2027; an "MRI for AI" within 5 to 10 years Company goal Finding most model problems by 2027

He admits limits himself: no one knows the future, he'll get things wrong, and there's no solid real-world evidence yet of lying or power-seeking.

docs.title: Connecting to earlier chapters
docs.text:
What Amodei says In this book AI is grown more than built; we need to see inside Chapter 19: features and circuits Asking a model isn't a reliable test Chapter 19 (made-up reasoning); Chapter 21 (testing) A country of geniuses in a datacenter Altman's page: "1,000 or a million junior coworkers" (different people, different pictures) Steer the bus Chapter 14: keep people in control while giving freedom Companies should share safety practices Chapter 8: NIST's voluntary framework

★ Going deeper

  • His company makes Claude. The essays also explain and support Anthropic's own research choices. Keep that in mind, the same way we did for Altman.
  • He signed the 2023 Statement on AI Risk too (see Hinton's page). So did Altman and Hassabis. Signing one sentence doesn't show how each one thinks we should act.
  • The "country of geniuses" by 2026 or 2027 is a prediction you can start checking as you read this (November 2026 or later).
  • The essay also argues that democracies should stay ahead of countries without freedom in AI. That's a policy debate this book doesn't cover.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Two-sided reading (10 minutes). Fill in this table from the page:

Question Your answer What does he hope AI will do? What does he worry about? What does he admit he doesn't know? Which of his claims could you check by 2027? How might his job shape what he writes?

Then compare with Hinton's page. Which worries do they share? Where do they differ?

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Don't judge a model only by what it says about itself. Check what it does (Chapters 3 and 21).
  2. Steer, don't just accept. In your own work, you choose which jobs to give AI and how to check them.
  3. Keep a date next to each prediction. "2026 or 2027" is checkable soon.
  4. Read hope and worry together. He gives both. Notice when a writer gives only one.
  5. Remember who's writing. A CEO writing about his own field has interests, even when he's careful.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "Amodei is a doomer." He says the opposite. He focuses on risks because he sees a good future behind them.
  • "We already have an MRI for AI." It's a goal and a prediction, not something done.
  • "He says AI is already lying to us." He says there's no solid real-world evidence yet, but it could happen.

docs.title: How Demis Hassabis sees it ★
docs.text:
Ch. 22 · 22.1 · DeeperAbout 8 min read2026-11-09

How to read this page

This page shares views from two interviews with Demis Hassabis, the CEO of Google DeepMind. He shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for AlphaFold, an AI that predicts the shapes of proteins. His company builds AI, so he has a direct stake in it. These are his views, not facts. We kept quotes to a minimum and put the rest in our own words.

What you'll learn on this page

  • Hassabis sees AI as a tool that helps scientists do far more, while the questions still come from people.
  • He names two worries: bad actors misusing AI, and keeping control of AI as it gets more powerful and acts more on its own.
  • He says society should decide together what AI should and shouldn't be used for.

docs.title: Which sources?
docs.text: Source Date Note Phone interview with the Nobel site October 2024 Just after the prize was announced. Adam Smith of the Nobel site asked the questions Interview during Nobel Week Recorded 2024-12-06 in Stockholm The Nobel site posts a written transcript. We read the parts about AI

docs.title: AI as a tool for science (phone interview)
docs.text:
Why he works on AI. He says he's worked on AI his whole life because he loves science and finding things out. He's always thought that AI, built the right way, could be the ultimate tool to help scientists explore the universe. He hopes AlphaFold is a first example.

Scientists still matter. Asked where this leaves the individual scientist, he said that at least for the foreseeable future, AI lets each scientist do much more. These systems are tools. They're very good at analyzing data and finding patterns in it. But they can't figure out the right question to ask, or the right guess to test. That has to come from the human scientist. He thinks top scientists with these tools could do amazing things, maybe even in smaller teams. The tools do a lot of the legwork.

Where research happens. He says he designed Google DeepMind to be a perfect place for cutting-edge research. It brings together experts in AI, engineering, physics, biology, and even philosophy. He was inspired by stories of the golden years of places like Bell Labs. Asked whether it matters that the work happens at a company, not a university, he said he doesn't think so. Great science can happen anywhere if it's done the right way. New fields need lots of computers, which cost a lot, so why not use private money?

docs.title: Hopes and worries (Nobel Week interview)
docs.text:
The possibilities. He says AI's possibilities are almost unlimited. Human intelligence built modern civilization, so we shouldn't be surprised that intelligence is a powerful force. AI research, he says, tries to understand intelligence by building it. If it's built in a general enough way, it could be used on almost any problem, much like the human mind.

Making it good for everyone. He says this is hard, and partly outside the technology itself. It's a question about countries and power. He expects big gains in productivity, the economy, and science. Society should decide together what to use AI for and what not to use it for, and how to share the benefits. He says people who build AI should talk widely with governments, universities, businesses, and the public.

His two worries:

  1. Bad actors. AI is a general-purpose technology. It can help with medicine and climate, but bad actors could also turn it to harmful uses. He calls the technology itself fairly neutral. What matters is how people choose to use it.
  2. Control. As systems get more powerful, act more on their own, and behave more like agents, can we understand them and keep control? Can we make sure they have the right goals and values, and that their guardrails are strong enough?

His hopes. He hopes AI helps solve some of our biggest problems. He names cures for terrible diseases, perhaps with tools like AlphaFold. He also names climate change, maybe through new materials, fusion, or better batteries.

docs.title: What kind of claim is each one?
docs.text: Type Example from Hassabis His own story He's worked on AI his whole life; he designed DeepMind as a research home His view AI is a tool; the questions must come from people Prediction, with a limit "For the foreseeable future," scientists will do more, maybe in smaller teams His position Research at a company can be great science, if done right His worries Misuse by bad actors; keeping control of more independent AI His proposal Society decides together how AI is used and shared

docs.title: Connecting to earlier chapters
docs.text:
What Hassabis says In this book AI is a tool; people pick the questions Chapters 2 and 8: you set the question and check the result Finding patterns in data Chapter 9 (pretraining); Chapter 10 (embeddings) AI that acts more like an agent Chapter 14: agents, permissions, and keeping people in control Right goals and values; strong guardrails Chapter 20 (alignment); Chapter 21 (risk) Bad actors misusing AI Hinton's page lists phishing, surveillance, and weapons

★ Going deeper

  • He's CEO of Google DeepMind. In the interviews he defends DeepMind's setup and research at companies. That's natural, but read it knowing who's speaking.
  • "For the foreseeable future" is a limit he put on his own words. Don't stretch it to the far future.
  • He signed the 2023 Statement on AI Risk too (see Hinton's page).
  • Compare his two worries with Hinton's and Amodei's. All three talk about control. They differ on how sure they sound and what they ask for.
  • We didn't check how AlphaFold works, so this book doesn't explain it.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
"People pick the question" practice. Think of one recent time you used AI and split it like this:

Part Who did it? (you or AI) Deciding what question to ask Gathering and sorting the material Spotting patterns or drafting Judging whether the answer was right Deciding what to do next

If AI did the first or the last row, try taking those back. Hassabis's view is that those rows belong to people.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Pick the question yourself. Let AI do the legwork, not the deciding.
  2. Treat AI as a tool that can be misused. Watch for scams and fakes made with it (Chapter 3).
  3. Give agents limits. The more an AI acts on its own, the more you need approvals and limits (Chapter 14).
  4. Notice limits like "for the foreseeable future." They change what a claim means.
  5. Read across the chapter. Each person stresses different things. The next page lines them up.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "Hassabis says AI will replace scientists." He says the opposite, at least for the foreseeable future.
  • "He isn't worried about AI." He names two worries: misuse and keeping control.
  • "AI decides what's worth studying." In his view, people choose the questions.

docs.title: How Geoffrey Hinton sees it ★
docs.text:
Ch. 22 · 22.1 · DeeperAbout 8 min read2026-11-09

How to read this page

This page shares views from a short speech and a phone interview by Geoffrey Hinton, who won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics. They're his opinions and worries, not settled facts. We kept quotes to a minimum and put the rest in our own words. Other experts disagree with parts of what he says.

What you'll learn on this page

  • Hinton sees a big upside: AI assistants that raise how much people get done in almost every job.
  • He lists risks for today and the near future, and a bigger, long-term worry about staying in control of AI smarter than us.
  • He asks governments to act, and to make big companies spend more on safety research.

docs.title: Which sources?
docs.text:
Hinton helped build the neural network methods behind today's AI (Chapters 9 and 19). In 2024 he shared the Nobel Prize in Physics for that work. We read these:

Source Date Note Nobel banquet speech 2024-12-10 A short speech; the whole text is on the Nobel site Phone interview with the Nobel site October 2024 Recorded just after he heard about the prize. Adam Smith of the Nobel site asked the questions Statement on AI Risk (Center for AI Safety) Around May 30, 2023 (estimated) A one-sentence statement. He is listed as a signer

docs.title: What he said in the speech
docs.text:
He spoke about three things.

1. The good side. This new kind of AI, he said, is good at copying human intuition more than human step-by-step reasoning. It will let us build very smart, knowing assistants that make almost every industry more productive. If the gains are shared fairly, he said, it will be a wonderful step forward for everyone.

2. Risks now and soon. He listed these:

Risk When, in his words Echo chambers that split people, by showing content that makes them angry Already happening Governments that don't allow freedom, using AI to watch huge numbers of people Already happening Criminals using AI for phishing (fake messages that trick you) Already happening Making terrible new viruses May happen soon Deadly weapons that decide on their own who to hurt or kill May happen soon

He said all of these need urgent, strong attention from governments and international groups.

3. A long-term risk. He sees a threat to humanity's survival once we build digital beings smarter than we are. He said we have no idea whether we can stay in control. He also said there's now evidence that if such beings are made by companies chasing short-term profit, our safety won't come first. So we urgently need research on how to keep them from wanting to take control. These things, he said, are no longer science fiction.

docs.title: What he said in the phone interview
docs.text:
• It's not like climate change. With climate change, he said, everyone knows what to do: stop burning carbon. The hard part is political will. With AI, we have much less idea what will happen or what to do. He said he wishes he had a simple recipe, but he doesn't.
  • A fork in the road. On the threat of AI getting out of control, he said we're at a turning point in history. In the next few years we need to work out whether there's a way to handle it.
  • What governments can do. He said governments could force big companies to spend much more on safety research. Then a company like OpenAI couldn't push safety to the back burner.
  • A past example. He was asked about the Asilomar meetings, where biologists met to agree on how to handle a risky new technology. He said it was a good model. But AI has far more practical uses, so it will be much harder.
  • Do language models understand? He said they really do understand what they're saying. He thinks the school of language study that follows Chomsky, which says they don't, is wrong. He added that there's still a lot of debate, mostly among linguists.

docs.title: The statement he signed
docs.text: In 2023, the Center for AI Safety put out a one-sentence statement. Its point: lowering the risk of human extinction from AI should be a world priority, next to other society-wide risks like pandemics and nuclear war. Hinton is on the list of signers. So are Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, and Demis Hassabis, whose views are on the other pages of this chapter. Signing one sentence doesn't tell you how each person thinks we should act.

docs.title: What kind of claim is each one?
docs.text: Type Example from Hinton What he describes as happening now Echo chambers, mass surveillance, phishing What he says may happen New viruses, weapons that pick targets His worry Losing control of AI smarter than us What he admits is unknown Whether we can stay in control; what to do His judgment Language models really understand; companies put profit first His proposal Government action; more company money for safety research

docs.title: Connecting to earlier chapters
docs.text:
What Hinton says In this book AI copies human intuition Chapter 9 (how models learn); Chapter 19 (what's inside) Echo chambers and content that makes you angry Altman's page also calls social media feeds misaligned AI (different people, different points) Phishing and other misuse Chapter 3 (safe use); Chapter 13 (hidden instructions) Keeping AI from wanting control Chapter 20 (alignment); Chapter 21 (risk) "They really understand" Chapter 19: you can't fully check a model's inner workings from what it says. This is a debated question

★ Going deeper

  • Hinton names a company (OpenAI) in the interview. That's his view of how companies act, not a finding we checked.
  • The speech gives no evidence for "we now have evidence." We don't know what evidence he meant, so we don't guess.
  • Whether language models "understand" depends partly on what you mean by the word. That's why scientists and linguists still argue about it.
  • There's also a longer interview from December 2024 on the Nobel site, with Swedish TV. We didn't use it.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Sort his claims (10 minutes). Copy the five risks from the speech table. Next to each, write:

  1. Does it touch your life or work now? (Yes, maybe, no)
  2. Is there something you can do about it yourself? For phishing, for example, check links before you click.
  3. Is it something only governments or companies can handle?

You'll likely find that some of his "now" risks are ones you can shrink today, and others need society to act.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Watch for phishing that sounds smooth. AI makes fake messages read well. Check the sender and the link (Chapter 3).
  2. Notice content that makes you angry. Ask whether a feed is showing it to keep you scrolling.
  3. Separate "happening now" from "may happen." Hinton marks this himself. Keep the line clear when you repeat it.
  4. Notice what he admits he doesn't know. He says he has no simple recipe.
  5. Read the other views too. The next pages show Amodei and Hassabis, who stress different things.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "Hinton says AI is bad." He also expects big gains, if they're shared fairly.
  • "Hinton says we'll lose control." He says we have no idea whether we can stay in control. That's uncertainty, not a prediction of loss.
  • "Everyone who signed the statement agrees on what to do." It's one sentence about priority. How to act is left open.

docs.text:

  • Geoffrey Hinton, Banquet speech, NobelPrize.org, 2024-12-10. Read in full on 2026-11-09.
  • Geoffrey Hinton, Interview (phone interview with Adam Smith, October 2024), NobelPrize.org. We read the transcript on 2026-11-09.
  • Center for AI Safety, Statement on AI Risk. The page shows no date; press links on the page are from May 30 to 31, 2023. We checked the signer list (partly shown) on 2026-11-09.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
