docs.title: How Andrej Karpathy sees it ★
docs.text:
Ch. 22 · 22.1 · DeeperAbout 8 min read2026-11-09

How to read this page

This page shares views and predictions from one person's writing. They're not facts. Most of what follows comes from posts on his own blog. We couldn't pull YouTube transcripts directly, so we checked parts of his video lectures only against unofficial, auto-generated transcripts and chapters on a third-party site (Rosetta), which may contain errors. Those notes are kept separate, in section 5. We kept quotes to a minimum and put the rest in our own words.

What you'll learn on this page

  • In 2022, Karpathy guessed what AI would look like in 2055: much the same in its basic shape, just far bigger.
  • He saw people moving away from building a new model for each job. Instead, they start from one big model and tweak it.
  • In 2019, he warned that training these models looks easy, but it isn't plug and play

docs.title: Whose writing, and which?
docs.text:
Andrej Karpathy, whose video lectures have come up since Chapter 1, writes posts on his blog (karpathy.github.io). We read these:

Post Date About Deep Neural Nets: 33 years ago and 33 years from now 2022-03-14 Rebuilds a 1989 paper and predicts 33 years ahead A Recipe for Training Neural Networks 2019-04-25 A process for avoiding mistakes when training neural networks microgpt 2026-02-12 We checked only its one-line description in the blog list

docs.title: The 2022 post: 33 years back, 33 years ahead
docs.text:
Karpathy rebuilt a 1989 paper by Yann LeCun and others on reading handwritten zip codes. To his knowledge, he wrote, it was the earliest real-world use of a neural network trained end to end with backpropagation. Only the data (7,291 handwritten digits) and the network (just 1,000 neurons) were small. The paper was surprisingly modern, so he used it as a case study of how deep learning has progressed.

At the end, he makes predictions about 2055. Here they are in our own words:

  • Same at a high level, but far bigger. Neural networks in 2055 will look much like 2022's at the big-picture level, only bigger. People then will see today's data and models as a joke. Both, he says, will be about 10 million times larger.
  • Today's best model in a minute. In 2055, you could train a 2022 state-of-the-art model on a personal computer in about a minute.
  • Training from scratch is going out of style. Building a network from scratch for each task is quickly becoming outdated, thanks to fine-tuning and foundation models like GPT. A few institutions with huge computing power train the foundation models. Most uses then just lightly adjust part of one, write prompts, or distill it into a small special-purpose model.
  • The most extreme prediction: if this trend continues and grows, people won't want to train neural networks at all. In 2055, you'll ask a "megabrain" 10 million times bigger to do things, by speaking (or thinking) in English, and if you ask nicely, it will. He ends roughly with: yes, you could train a neural net too, but why would you?

docs.title: The 2019 post: the illusion of easy
docs.text: A Recipe for Training Neural Networks starts by saying that neural network training is a "leaky abstraction". Libraries show off "30-line miracle snippets" that give the false impression it's plug and play. Unlike tidy interfaces in regular software, neural networks stop being an off-the-shelf tool the moment you step slightly away from the standard case. So instead of listing mistakes, the post lays out a process for avoiding them, or fixing them fast.

docs.title: Connecting to earlier chapters
docs.text: What Karpathy says In this book Foundation models plus light tuning and prompts are the main path Chapter 2 asking tips; Chapter 9 pretraining and fine-tuning You'll give instructions in English (plain language) Chapters 2 and 15 Models will get much bigger Chapter 9 parameters; Chapter 20 scaling and the debate It looks easy, but it's not plug and play Chapter 8 checks before using AI at work; Chapter 21 testing

docs.title: From his video lectures (checked against unofficial transcripts)
docs.text:
The three videos used in earlier chapters have transcripts and chapter lists on a third-party site, Rosetta. The site says they're auto-generated and may have errors. Below is our paraphrase of what we read there. (To know exactly what he said, watch the videos.)

Video What we found (paraphrased) In this book Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT (transcript) A model with only pretraining is "not yet an assistant" but "a token autocomplete," and a probabilistic system. Even so, guessing the next token teaches it a lot about the world, stored in its parameters. Next word, Ch. 1; Pretraining, Ch. 9 Same video, chapter "hallucinations, tool use, knowledge/working memory" (01:20:32) Hallucination is the model making things up. It's a big problem that has existed since early models, and mitigations have helped somewhat. Hallucination, Ch. 1 Same video, chapter "models need tokens to think" (01:46:56) Spread computation over many tokens, have it build in-between results, and use tools whenever possible. Don't fully trust it to do everything in one go. Math, Ch. 7; Reasoning models, Ch. 20 Same video, chapter "tokenization revisited: models struggle with spelling" (02:01:11) Models see tokens, not letters, so they struggle to count letters. "How many R's in strawberry?" was a well-known example. For a long time, top models insisted on two. He says they get it right now. Tokens, Ch. 1 Let's build the GPT Tokenizer (transcript) Using a Korean example, he explains that because there's far more English data, models and tokenizers favor English, and non-English languages are at a disadvantage. Tokens, Ch. 1 Intro to Large Language Models (chapters and transcript) Chapters include "LLM dreams" (00:08:58), "Tool Use" (00:27:43), "Multimodality" (00:33:32), "LLM OS" (00:42:15), "Jailbreaks" (00:46:14), and "Prompt Injection" (00:51:30). Hallucination, Ch. 1; Kinds, Ch. 4; Templates, Ch. 2

These line up with the explanations in earlier chapters. We didn't find his views on risk or safety in these videos.

docs.title: Fact, observation, or prediction?
docs.text:
Type What it covers Stated as fact in the post The 1989 paper's data and network size; that he rebuilt it His observation That fine-tuning and foundation models are replacing training from scratch Prediction 2055's scale (10 million times), training in a minute, a megabrain you ask in English

2055 is 33 years after the post, so we have no way to check it. For context, the post was written in March 2022, before ChatGPT came out. (The post gives its own date. The ChatGPT launch date, November 30, 2022, comes from Altman's Reflections, on the Altman page in this chapter.)

★ Going deeper

  • In what we read, this post has no discussion of risk or safety. So we can't describe his views on safety from it. That's why it shouldn't simply be lined up against Hinton's or Amodei's writing.
  • "10 million times" is a rough figure for both data and models, not an exact calculation.
  • For microgpt (February 2026), we checked only the one-line description in the blog list: a GPT trainer and runner in about 200 lines of pure Python. You could read it as a habit of rebuilding ideas small to understand them, but that's our interpretation. We didn't read the post itself.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Imagine 2055. Spend 5 minutes on these:

  1. Karpathy predicted an age of "asking in English." How close is that to how you ask AI for things now?
  2. If he's right, will "asking good questions" matter more or less? Write one line explaining why.
  3. If he's wrong, how might he be wrong?

There's no right answer. It's practice in reading a prediction and forming your own view.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Read predictions as predictions. "2055" can't be checked. Be careful with confident claims tied to a year.
  2. You can already use the observation that plain-language instructions are the key tool. Practice with Chapters 2 and 15.
  3. The easier a tool looks, the more you need a checking habit. The "leaky abstraction" warning applies to people using AI tools too (Chapters 3 and 8).
  4. To learn more, read and watch his own work. We read only part of it.
  5. Don't draw conclusions about a whole field from one person. The next pages show other views.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "This prediction is the answer for 2055." It's a prediction. This book doesn't judge whether it will come true.
  • "This is what Karpathy thinks about AI risk." These posts don't discuss risk, so we can't say.
  • "People who train neural networks will soon be unnecessary." He framed it as the trend taken to an extreme, with that condition attached.

docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • Andrej Karpathy, Deep Neural Nets: 33 years ago and 33 years from now, blog, 2022-03-14. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Andrej Karpathy, A Recipe for Training Neural Networks, blog, 2019-04-25. We read the introduction. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • Andrej Karpathy, blog index. We checked only the one-line description of microgpt (2026-02-12).
  • Videos on YouTube: Intro to Large Language Models, Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT, and Let's build the GPT Tokenizer. We checked titles and IDs on YouTube, and parts of the content against Rosetta's unofficial, auto-generated transcripts. We couldn't watch the videos ourselves.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: Our summaries of his posts are paraphrases and should be compared with the originals. The video content was checked only in part, against unofficial auto-generated transcripts. We didn't check his more recent views on risk or safety (talks and interviews). The tables and comparisons are ours.

docs.title: Comparing views: where they differ ★
docs.text:
Ch. 22 · 22.1 · DeeperAbout 9 min read2026-11-09

How to read this page

This page compares only what we read on the last five pages. Things we didn't read, like videos and newer talks, aren't included. We don't judge who is right. In the tables, "Not found" means "not in what we read." It doesn't mean the person disagrees.

What you'll learn on this page

  • Experts in the same field differ on speed, which risks matter most, fixes, and their own interests.
  • Even so, four of them signed the same one-sentence statement about the risk of extinction from AI.
  • You'll learn eight questions for reading what any expert says.

docs.title: Same statement, different stories
docs.text:
In 2023, the Center for AI Safety (CAIS) put out a one-sentence statement. Its point, in our words: lowering the risk of human extinction from AI should be a world priority, next to other society-wide risks like pandemics and nuclear war.

Four people from this chapter are on its signer list: Geoffrey Hinton (listed as emeritus professor, University of Toronto), Demis Hassabis (CEO, Google DeepMind), Sam Altman (CEO, OpenAI), and Dario Amodei (CEO, Anthropic). Yoshua Bengio and Ilya Sutskever are on it too. We didn't find Karpathy's name in the part of the list we could see.

It's one sentence. Signing it doesn't mean they agree on the details. As you'll see below, they don't.

docs.title: Side by side
docs.text: Hinton Altman Amodei Hassabis Karpathy What we read Nobel speech and phone interview (2024) 3 blog posts (2025) 2 essays (Oct 2024, Apr 2025) 2 Nobel interviews (Oct and Dec 2024) Blog posts (2019, 2022; a 2026 listing) Role Emeritus professor OpenAI CEO Anthropic CEO Google DeepMind CEO No title checked by us The upside More productivity in almost every industry, if shared fairly Big leaps in science; intelligence and energy become plentiful A huge upside most people underrate The ultimate tool for scientists; cures, climate help Big shared models you instruct in plain English The risks Now: echo chambers, surveillance, phishing. Later: weapons, viruses, losing control Safety must be solved; a small flaw times hundreds of millions of users Not seeing inside AI is the root of many risks; lying or power-seeking could appear Bad actors misusing AI; keeping control as AI acts more on its own Not found The fix Governments make big companies spend more on safety research Solve alignment, then spread AI widely; society sets the limits Speed up interpretability research to win the race Society decides together what AI is for and how to share it No policy ideas in what we read Timing Next few years are a turning point 2026 insights, 2027 robots, 2030s abundance Powerful AI as soon as 2026 or 2027; "MRI for AI" in 5 to 10 years "For the foreseeable future," AI is a tool 2055: same basic shape, far bigger

docs.title: Where they split
docs.text:
1. Where the weight of risk falls

  • Hinton talks about risks already happening and possible loss of control later. He admits he has no simple recipe.
  • Altman admits safety problems, but his posts lean toward abundance and gentle change. His path is to solve alignment, then spread AI widely.
  • Amodei sees both a big upside and big risks. He puts weight on one technical fix: interpretability.
  • Hassabis names misuse by bad actors and control of more independent AI. He calls the technology itself fairly neutral.

2. Who should act, and how

  • Hinton: governments force big companies to put more into safety research.
  • Altman: society sets broad limits, and no one person, company, or country holds too much.
  • Amodei: researchers, companies, and governments all push interpretability. He suggests light-touch rules and asks other companies to do more.
  • Hassabis: society decides together, with builders talking to governments, schools, businesses, and the public.

3. How sure they are about speed

  • Altman and Amodei name 2026 and 2027. (Altman: new insights and robots. Amodei: a "country of geniuses.")
  • Karpathy's prediction is for 2055 (written in 2022). Hassabis says only "the foreseeable future." Hinton says "the next few years," but about the need to find answers, not about what AI will do.
  • They're predicting different things (what AI can do, how society changes, how big models get). So you can't line them up directly.

4. Does AI "understand"?

  • Hinton says large language models really do understand, and the linguists who say they don't are wrong. He also says it's still hotly debated.
  • We didn't find a clear position on this from the other four in what we read.

docs.title: Who's speaking?
docs.text:
Person Kind of source Keep in mind Hinton Prize speech and interview In what we read, he doesn't speak for a company Altman A CEO's blog He has a direct stake in AI going well Amodei A CEO's essays He runs Anthropic. The AI that helped write this book was made by Anthropic Hassabis Prize interviews A CEO speaking; he defends his company's research setup Karpathy A personal blog No title checked by us (we didn't watch his videos)

Having a stake doesn't make someone wrong. It means you read the same words a little differently, depending on who says them.

docs.title: Eight questions for reading any expert
docs.text:
1. Who said it? What's their job, and who do they work for?
  2. When? Views can change.
  3. Where? A speech, a blog, an interview, and a paper are different things.
  4. Is it a fact, a view, or a prediction? Mark each one.
  5. What's the evidence? A study, or one person's judgment?
  6. Who gains? Does anyone benefit if you believe it?
  7. Did they admit limits? Look for where they say "we don't know."
  8. What do others say? Don't decide from one side.

★ Going deeper

  • This comparison rests on one or two sources per person. It doesn't stand for everything each of them has said.
  • Interviews and talks can be edited or quoted out of context. Read the full text when you can.
  • Many voices aren't here. Many researchers weigh AI's risks and upside differently from these five. We didn't check their work, so we don't summarize it.
  • The table cells are our short summaries. Go back to each person's page for the details and sources.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Add a sixth column.

  1. Pick one person this book didn't cover, a researcher or a business leader.
  2. Find something they wrote or said in full. Not a news summary; the original.
  3. Fill in the rows: what you read, role, upside, risks, fix, timing. Write "Not found" where you don't know.
  4. Run the eight questions on it.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. When you see a bold claim, make a quick table. Who, when, what, and based on what. That alone cuts through hype.
  2. Signing the same statement isn't the same as agreeing. Separate a one-line "yes" from detailed views.
  3. Write down dated predictions and check them later. 2026 and 2027 are passing now.
  4. Respect "we don't know." Sometimes a person who admits doubt is more trustworthy than one who sounds sure.
  5. Look for people who disagree. This chapter shows only a few voices.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "AI experts all say the same thing." They differ on speed, which risks matter, and fixes.
  • "A famous person said it, so it's true." Most of it is views and predictions.
  • "All warnings about AI are hype" or "all of them are true." Check the evidence before you pick a side.

docs.text:
Sources (we read these and explain the ideas in our own words)

  • The earlier pages in this chapter: Karpathy, Altman, Hinton, Amodei, Hassabis. See each page for its sources.
  • Date checked: 2026-11-09
  • Status: First draft
  • Note: "Not found" in the tables doesn't mean they hold no such view. The comparison frame and the eight questions are ours. Everything here is limited to what this book read.

docs.text:
Where the principles you learned turn into everyday habits. Four reasons why "it works like this, so use it like this."

docs.title: What fills up its memory space?
docs.text:
Ch. 23 · 23.1About 7 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • The context window from Part III is Claude's working memory. It holds everything Claude can see in this conversation.
  • It's not just what you typed. It also holds things loaded at the start, files Claude read, and tool results.
  • With /context, you can see for yourself what's filling your conversation's memory.

docs.title: It only sees what's on the desk
docs.text: In Part III, you learned that AI forgets everything when a chat ends. All it can see is what's on its desk (the context window). So if you know what's on the desk, you can see why the AI acts the way it does. A full desk leaves no room for new papers. A messy desk makes the important ones hard to find.

docs.title: What lands on the desk
docs.text:
The official docs list what goes into Claude Code's context window:

When What lands there Before you type anything CLAUDE.md, auto memory, MCP tool names, and skill descriptions While Claude works Each file it reads, rules that load with matching files, and hook output When a helper (subagent) does the research Big file reads happen on the helper's own desk. Only a summary comes back to yours

So the more skills and MCP servers you add (Chapter 17), the fuller the desk is before you say a word. Only names and descriptions load at the start, so each is small. But unused tools add up. That's why the plugin page in Chapter 18 said to check the context cost before you install.

docs.title: Look at your own desk
docs.text: Type /context. It shows how much of the desk each kind of thing takes up, as colored blocks, with ideas for what to trim. It also shows which CLAUDE.md and auto memory files were loaded. To edit those memory files, use /memory.

docs.title: Even with a bigger desk
docs.text:
The docs say many current models support a 1 million token window. With a desk that big, you'll rarely run out of room. But big doesn't mean you can skip tidying. The docs say /clear between tasks is still worth doing, because a focused context gives better answers and costs less.

Here's why it costs more. Every message sends the whole conversation again. So if one chat holds three unrelated tasks, the fourth task pays to re-read all three, every turn.

In 10-year-old words

AI can only see what's on its desk. A big desk is nice, but if it's messy, it can't find things.

★ Going deeper

  • When the desk gets close to full, Claude Code compacts the chat on its own: it swaps the conversation for a summary and keeps going. The next page shows what survives that.
  • The point where this kicks in depends on the model and settings. The docs keep a table of default limits. We don't copy the numbers here because they change.
  • The docs also say subagents are no longer mainly for saving room. They're still good for parallel work, keeping noisy output out of your way, and fresh reviews. But each one costs extra tokens.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Open Claude Code and type /context before you say anything. You'll see part of the desk is already full.
  2. Ask Claude to read one file. Type /context again and see which block grew.
  3. If you made skills or MCP connections in Chapter 17, find how much of the desk they take at the start.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. If answers get fuzzy or the same mistake repeats, check /context first.
  2. Turn off or remove skills, MCP servers, and plugins you don't use.
  3. Use /clear when you switch to an unrelated task. It costs nothing.
  4. Hand big reading jobs to a helper when it fits. Just remember helpers cost tokens too.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "With a big desk, I can keep one chat going forever." Longer chats cost more on every message and can lose focus.
  • "Only what I typed is on the desk." No. Some things load before you type a word.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
• Version checked: Claude Code 2.1.319, checked on 2026-11-09. Which models have a 1M window, and when compacting starts, depend on the model and settings.
  • Source of facts: Official docs: Explore the context window and Best practices. Read on 2026-11-09.
  • This page builds on Part III (context windows and tokens).

docs.title: Habits that save memory space
docs.text:
Ch. 23 · 23.1About 7 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • There are four tools for tidying the desk: /clear (start fresh), /compact (summarize), partial summaries, and helpers (read elsewhere).
  • When a chat is summarized, some things survive and some get lost. Put important rules where they survive.
  • The goal isn't to save space for its own sake. It's to keep Claude focused.

docs.title: Four tidying tools
docs.text:
Tool When What it does /clear You're moving to a totally different task Clears the desk. The old chat won't get in the way of the next task /compact plus what to focus on Same task, but the chat got long Swaps the chat for a summary. You say what to keep /rewind, then a summarize option The early part matters, but the later part is messy (or the other way around) Summarizes only the part before or after the message you pick A helper (subagent) Research that means reading a lot The reading happens elsewhere; you get back a summary

You can steer /compact. The docs' example is "focus on the auth bug fix." Then the summary keeps what you chose, instead of what the automatic pass guesses is important.

/compact keep the decisions for the page I'm writing and the links I haven't checked yet

One catch: on a long chat, /compact is itself a big request, because it reads the whole conversation to summarize it.

docs.title: What survives a summary
docs.text:
Here's the docs' table, in plain words:

After the summary How CLAUDE.md at the top of the project Read again from the file Auto memory Read again from the file Skill descriptions Rebuilt from your current skills Files Claude read or changed Up to 5 are read again, newest changes first. A file over 5,000 tokens comes back as just its path Skills Claude already used Put back, up to 5,000 tokens each and 25,000 in total. The oldest drop first Instructions you only gave in chat Can get lost in the summary

That leads to a rule: if Claude must keep following a rule, don't just say it in chat. Write it in the CLAUDE.md at the top of your project. The docs warn that CLAUDE.md files in subfolders, and rules tied to certain files, can get summarized away too. If a rule must last, move it to the top-level CLAUDE.md.

Long skills get cut to fit, and the cut keeps the start. So put the most important instructions near the top of SKILL.md.

docs.title: Drop the old advice
docs.text:
People used to say "manage your context window aggressively." The official best practices now say that's outdated. Most current models have a big window and summarize on their own, so running out is rare. But /clear between tasks is still worth it.

So keep these habits light. Not "save every scrap," but "clear when the task changes, and keep rules in the right place."

The docs add one more tip. If you've corrected the same thing twice and it's still wrong, don't try a third time. The chat now holds two failed tries that Claude keeps re-reading. Run /clear and write one better prompt that includes what you learned.

In 10-year-old words

When you switch tasks, wipe the whiteboard. Rules you must always follow go on the wall poster (CLAUDE.md), not the whiteboard.

★ Going deeper

  • /autocompact lets you set how full the desk gets before the automatic summary runs.
  • A SessionStart hook can add text back in right after a summary. If a note must come back every time, use a hook. It's the same idea as the hooks page in Chapter 17: a promise that doesn't depend on the AI's judgment.
  • /clear oauth-migration gives the chat you're leaving a name, so you can come back to it later.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. In the middle of a chat, check /context. Then run /compact keep only the decisions for what I'm working on.
  2. Check /context again to see how much room you got back.
  3. Pick one rule you only said in chat. Does Claude still follow it after the summary? If not, move it into CLAUDE.md.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. New task: /clear. Same task, too long: /compact plus what to keep.
  2. Put lasting rules in the top-level CLAUDE.md, not in chat.
  3. Put the most important lines at the top of each skill.
  4. After two failed corrections, start fresh with a better prompt.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "A summary keeps everything." Summaries shrink things, so details can get lost.
  • "/clear erases CLAUDE.md too." No. A new chat reads CLAUDE.md again.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
• Version checked: Claude Code 2.1.319, checked on 2026-11-09. Rebuilding skill descriptions after a summary needs v2.1.304 or later. The token limits may change when the docs change.
  • Source of facts: Official docs: Context window, what survives compaction, Best practices (including "What you can stop doing"), and Checkpointing. Read on 2026-11-09.

docs.title: How do you choose a model?
docs.text:
Ch. 23 · 23.3About 7 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Choosing a model is a trade between power, speed, and cost. The default is enough for most work.
  • Pick by alias (a short nickname), not by exact name. Then you keep up when models change.
  • A simple rule: everyday work, the default. Light jobs, a small model. The hardest and longest jobs, the biggest model.

docs.title: Bike, car, or plane
docs.text: You bike to the corner shop, drive to the next town, and fly to another country. A plane isn't always best. Flying to the corner shop would cost a lot and take more time. AI models are like that too. Big models handle hard jobs well but are slower and cost more. Small models are quick and cheap.

docs.title: Choose by alias
docs.text:
Here are the aliases the official docs list. The right-hand column is what they pointed to on the Anthropic API, as of 2026-11-09.

Alias What it's for On this date default Go back to your account's default Depends on your plan sonnet Everyday coding Sonnet 5.5 opus Complex reasoning Opus 5.5 haiku Quick, simple jobs Haiku 5.5 fable Your hardest, longest-running jobs Fable 5.1 (never the default; you pick it yourself) best The top model you can use Same as fable if you have it, otherwise opus opusplan Opus while planning, Sonnet while doing Goes with plan mode (Chapter 18)

What an alias points to can differ by provider. On some cloud providers, sonnet and haiku point to older versions. So instead of memorizing model names, use aliases and check with /model.

docs.title: How to choose
docs.text:
Here's the official best practices advice, in plain words:

  • The default model handles most coding well. You don't need to change it at first. (On most plans, that's Opus 5.5 at medium effort.)
  • Sonnet costs less on routine work.
  • Haiku fits helpers (subagents) doing simple jobs, like a researcher helper from Chapter 17.
  • Fable is for jobs too big for one sitting. The docs say Fable models keep working on their own for a long time, look into things before acting, and check their own work more often.

For a video channel, that might look like this: a researcher that checks page links runs on Haiku or Sonnet, a scriptwriter uses the default, and a plan to restructure the whole book uses opusplan or Fable. That's our suggestion, not a rule. Test it against your own work and budget.

docs.title: How to switch
docs.text:
• In a chat: type /model sonnet. That also saves it as your default. To change it for this chat only, open the picker with /model and press s on the model's row. (Enter in the picker saves it as your default.)
  • When starting: claude --model sonnet
  • For a helper: the model: field in its file (Chapter 17)

In 10-year-old words

Bike for short trips, plane for long ones. Pick the model that fits the job.

★ Going deeper

  • The docs describe automatic fallback: if a model is busy or a safety check flags a request, Claude Code can switch to another model.
  • Admins can limit which models people in their organization can pick. If your /model list differs from this page, that may be why.
  • Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 need fairly recent versions of Claude Code. If one fails, run claude update.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Open /model and check which model you're on and what else you can choose.
  2. Give the same small job (like summarizing a page) to haiku and to the default. Use s so it only changes for this chat. Compare the results and how long each took.
  3. Check /usage to see how your usage changed.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Small model for light, repeated jobs. Big model for big, tricky ones.
  2. Use aliases, not exact model names, and check with /model.
  3. Compare for yourself: same job, two models. Other people's rankings may not fit your work (Chapter 21).

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "The most expensive model is always best." For some jobs, it's a waste.
  • "An alias always means the same model." Aliases point to the latest version, so they change over time. That's why this page has a date.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
• Version checked: Claude Code 2.1.319, checked on 2026-11-09. Model names and what aliases point to go out of date faster than anything else in this book.
  • Source of facts: Official docs: Model configuration and Best practices: Change the model and effort. Read on 2026-11-09.

docs.title: Adjust its thinking time (effort level)
docs.text:
Ch. 23 · 23.3About 6 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • The effort level is the main dial for how long Claude thinks. It replaces "think hard" in your prompt.
  • The levels are low, medium, high, xhigh, and max. The default depends on the model.
  • Higher levels take more time and tokens. Turn it up only when you need to.

docs.title: Time on a test
docs.text: Spending ages on an easy question wastes time. Rushing a hard one leads to mistakes. The effort level is a dial for that kind of thinking time. The official docs call it the main control for how long Claude thinks. At a higher level, Claude tests more edge cases and checks more of its work before it answers. That costs more time and tokens.

docs.title: Levels and defaults
docs.text:
You change it with /effort. Which levels you get depends on the model. As of 2026-11-09, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 support low, medium, high, xhigh, and max, and start at medium. If you pick a level the model doesn't support, it drops to the highest one it does support below that.

Level When (the official advice, in short) low Quick back-and-forth where you check every result: brainstorming, a first draft, renaming things medium Everyday work with a clear scope (the default on these models) high or xhigh When it's easy to miss a case: a bug in code you didn't write, a test that sometimes fails, a change where every place that uses something must be found max A very hard problem you want Claude to work on without you, like hunting for a security hole. On ordinary jobs it tends to overthink, so you may pay more for an answer no better than high

To go deeper for just one message, put ultrathink in that message. Your setting stays the same.

The docs add a note: each model has its own effort scale. So medium on one model doesn't mean the same as medium on another.

docs.title: Wording doesn't turn the dial
docs.text: "Think hard" and "be thorough" aren't magic words. The docs say they're ordinary text. They may nudge Claude a little, but they can't lift it past its effort setting. So if the thinking seems shallow, don't write a longer plea. Try turning up /effort.

docs.title: How long a change lasts
docs.text:
• /effort then Enter (or typing a level, like /effort high): saves it as your default for later chats.
  • /effort then s: this chat only (Claude Code 2.1.257 or later).
  • max applies to this chat only, unless you set it with an environment variable.

In 10-year-old words

Easy question, answer fast. Hard question, take your time. The thinking-time dial is /effort.

★ Going deeper

  • Effort has an order of priority: environment variable first, then what you pick in the chat, then --effort at launch, then your settings, then the model's default.
  • Skills and helpers can have their own effort: field. A research helper can run low and a review helper high (Chapter 17).
  • In the terminal, ultrathink can also raise that one turn to xhigh. When it does, the word shows in rainbow colors (Claude Code 2.1.311 or later).
  • We describe effort the way the docs do: the model decides how much to think at each step. We didn't check how it works inside.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Type /effort to see your current level.
  2. Give a hard job, like "Find every claim on this page that isn't in its source," once at low and once at high. Use s so it only changes for this chat.
  3. Write down each result's length, how many it found, and how long it took. Compare.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Quick back-and-forth: low. A review that must be right: high.
  2. Save max for rare, very hard problems.
  3. Just one deep answer: put ultrathink in that message.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "Higher is always more accurate." On ordinary jobs, it may only add time and cost.
  • "Writing 'try harder' does the same thing." The docs say it doesn't.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
• Version checked: Claude Code 2.1.319, checked on 2026-11-09. Supported levels and defaults change by model and over time.
  • Source of facts: Official docs: Model configuration, Adjust effort level and Best practices: Change the model and effort; What you can stop doing. Read on 2026-11-09.

docs.title: How is handing off a job different?
docs.text:
Ch. 23 · 23.2About 7 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Asking a question and handing off a job are different. You need to tell Claude what it can't learn from the files.
  • A good handoff says where to look, what's wrong, and what "done" looks like.
  • Don't describe what you have. Hand it over: the file, the screenshot, the command output.

docs.title: What AI can't see when you hand off a job
docs.text: Claude Code can read the files in your folder. It can't read your mind. The official best practices say current models are very good at reading code. What they can't find is information that was never in the folder: a decision your team made in a meeting, or steps that live only in one person's head. Without it, Claude guesses. As Part I showed, guesses can sound right and still be wrong.

docs.title: Vague and clear requests
docs.text:
Here's the docs' idea, reworked for a video channel:

Vague Clear "Make a video script." "Write a 60-second shorts script based on docs-en/part1/ch01/tokens.md. Don't add anything that's not in the page. Mark any numbers as examples. Save it to video/shorts-en/002-tokens/script.md." "Fix the page." "On page 16.2, check whether the 3 links in 'Sources and date checked' open. Just list the ones that don't. Don't change anything."

A clear request has three parts:

  1. Where to look: the file name or folder
  2. What's wrong, and what "done" looks like: the problem and how you'll know it's fixed
  3. What not to do: things it must not touch

The docs add one more: if you prefer one of two reasonable ways, say so up front. Claude can't read your preference from the code.

docs.title: Hand over what you have
docs.text:
Handing it over is more exact than describing it.

  • A file: type @ and the path to put its contents in your message.
  • A screen: paste a screenshot.
  • Command output: pipe it in, like cat error.log | claude -p "what's going on here" (Chapter 16).

docs.title: You set the size of the job
docs.text:
The docs explain something interesting. Claude tends to read a request carefully and build the smallest thing that fits, because it can't tell how much you were hoping for. If you want more, say so. One phrase the docs say still helps is be ambitious. For example:

Expand the "Try it yourself" section on this page. Be ambitious: add help for 3 places beginners might get stuck, and a way to check if they got it wrong.

This isn't asking Claude to think harder. It's telling it how big the job is.

docs.title: When researching: "read first, then answer"
docs.text:
To cut down on made-up answers about code, Anthropic's guide suggests telling Claude never to guess about files it hasn't opened. If you name a file, it should read it before answering. You can write it like this:

Before you answer, open and read any file I mention. If you haven't opened something, say you don't know.

In 10-year-old words

When you hand off a job, say where to look, what done looks like, and what not to touch. AI can't see inside your head.

★ Going deeper

  • Not every request needs to be exact. The docs say a loose question like "What would you improve in this file?" is fine when you're exploring. You'll just correct a bit more along the way.
  • Before you write something down for Claude, the docs suggest two questions: could it find this by reading the code, and would it actually look? If both are yes, leave it out.
  • Requests you make again and again can become a skill (Chapter 17). Facts it always needs can go in CLAUDE.md (Chapter 16). Then you don't have to write them every time.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Pick one job you recently gave an AI.
  2. Check it for the three parts: where, what done looks like, what not to do.
  3. Fill in what was missing, ask again, and compare with the first result.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Write three lines when you hand off a job: where, what done looks like, what not to do.
  2. Hand things over with @file or a screenshot instead of describing them.
  3. If the size of the result matters, give a number. For example, "help for 3 places."

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "A longer request is a better request." Length doesn't matter. What matters is whether it has the information the AI can't get.
  • "The AI already knows the whole folder." It can learn the layout by reading. But your rules, your preferences, and what "done" means have to come from you.

docs.title: Why do context, examples, and format work?
docs.text:
Ch. 23 · 23.2About 7 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • The asking tips from Part I (context, examples, format) come from how AI works. It guesses the next words from the text in front of it.
  • Anthropic's official guide points the same way: be clear, give reasons, show examples.
  • Some old tips aren't needed anymore. Once you know the reason behind the tips, you can tell which.

docs.title: The idea in one line
docs.text: In Part I (1.1.1), you learned that a chatbot looks at the text in front of it and picks what comes next. So if the text in front changes, the likely next words change too. Context, examples, and format are all ways to put better text in front of it.

docs.title: Four reasons the tips work
docs.text:
1. Be clear and direct. Anthropic's guide says to treat Claude like a brilliant new employee who doesn't know your team's ways yet. Its test is simple. Show your request to a coworker who knows little about the task. If they'd be confused, Claude will be too. Gaps tend to get filled with guesses (that's how made-up answers happen). The clearer you are, the less room there is to guess.

2. Give the reason. The guide's example, in short: "never use ellipses" works less well than explaining that the text will be read aloud by a voice program, which won't know how to say them. Once Claude knows why, it can apply the idea to similar cases on its own.

3. Show examples. The guide calls examples one of the most reliable ways to set format, tone, and structure. It says examples should be relevant (close to your real use), varied, and set apart with tags. It suggests 3 to 5. They need to vary because if they're all alike, Claude may copy patterns you didn't mean, like they all being the same length.

4. Mark the parts. If a long request mixes instructions, material, examples, and input, wrap each part in its own tag. The guide's examples use tags like <instructions> and <context>. Clear, consistent names are what matter.

<instructions>Summarize the material below in 3 lines. Use only what's in it.</instructions>
<material>
(paste here)
</material>

docs.title: Tips you can drop
docs.text:
The official best practices keep a list of advice that was good once but isn't needed now, because models got better:

  • ALL CAPS and "IMPORTANT!!" Current models follow a plain line. Too much emphasis makes Claude apply the rule too widely. A rule that must never bend should be a hook (Chapter 17) or a deny rule, not shouting.
  • "Think hard" or "be thorough." These aren't magic words. They're ordinary text. How deeply Claude thinks is set by the effort level (the second page of 23.3).
  • "Keep going, don't be lazy." Current models usually carry on without being told. Lines like that can lead to over-work.

The docs say one thing is still worth adding: a way to check whether the job is done. That's section 23.4.

In 10-year-old words

AI guesses what comes next from the words in front of it. Put good words in front (context, examples, format), and you get better answers.

★ Going deeper

The guide warns that when a tip was measured on one model, you should test it on your own tasks before using it on another. Prompt tips can stop working when the model changes. Treat this page's tips as dated too (2026-11-09).

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Ask for the same thing twice and compare.

  1. First, ask briefly: "Summarize page 1.1.2."
  2. Then ask like this, and see how the two results differ:
This summary will be used as video captions, so each sentence must be 8 words or fewer. Write it like this example.
<example>Tokens are small pieces of text.</example>
<material>(paste the page 1.1.2 text)</material>

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Add one sentence of reason to each request: where the result will be used.
  2. If format matters, show 2 or 3 examples instead of describing it.
  3. Write one plain, clear line instead of shouting. If it still isn't followed, make it a hook.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "Prompts have secret magic words." It's about giving more information, not spells.
  • "Examples always help." With only one example, it copies that one shape. Give a variety.

docs.text:

docs.title: Hands-on: this channel's checking loop
docs.text:
Ch. 23 · 23.4About 8 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • You'll put three layers of checks on the flow for making a video script: a format check (hook), a build check (Stop hook), and a content review (reviewer helper).
  • The checks become gatekeepers that decide when "done" is allowed. But you need a safety switch so it can't loop forever.
  • Test each check on its own first, with both a failing case and a passing case.

docs.title: Three gatekeepers
docs.text:
Layer What it checks When Tool 1. Format Does the page have a "Sources and date checked" section? Every time a file changes PostToolUse hook (check-page-en.sh from Chapter 17) 2. Build Does the site build with no warnings (broken links included)? When Claude tries to finish Stop hook 3. Content Does it say anything the original doesn't? After the script is saved reviewer helper (Chapter 17)

You already made 1 and 3. On this page, you'll make 2.

docs.title: The build check script
docs.text:
Save this as .claude/hooks/check-build-en.sh:

#!/bin/bash
# When Claude tries to finish, check that the site builds with no warnings.
INPUT=$(cat)

# If this hook already sent Claude back once, let it stop this time (no endless loop)
if [ "$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.stop_hook_active')" = "true" ]; then
  exit 0
fi

cd "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR" || exit 0
mkdocs build --strict 1>&2 || exit 2
exit 0

chmod +x .claude/hooks/check-build-en.sh

Three things matter here:

  • --strict counts any warning as a failure. Broken links are warnings, so they get caught.
  • Don't add -q (quiet). We ran into this while writing this book. With mkdocs build --strict -q, a site with a broken link still gave exit code 0, so the check looked like it passed. Without -q, the same site gave exit code 1. Make sure a tool's quiet mode doesn't hide its warnings.
  • stop_hook_active is true if this hook already sent Claude back. Then the script lets it stop. The docs say Claude Code steps in after a Stop hook blocks eight times in a row, and they tell you to check this value.

docs.title: Test it on its own first
docs.text:
Try both cases with fake input, from your site's folder:

export CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR=$PWD
echo '{"stop_hook_active": false}' | .claude/hooks/check-build-en.sh; echo "exit code: $?"
echo '{"stop_hook_active": true}'  | .claude/hooks/check-build-en.sh; echo "exit code: $?"
  • With a broken link, the first should give 2 (block) and the second 0 (let it stop).
  • With no problems, both give 0.

We tested this on a small practice site with one broken link. We got 2, then 0, and 0 again after fixing the link. On the same site, --strict -q gave 0 and --strict alone gave 1.

docs.title: Register it
docs.text:
In .claude/settings.json:

{
  "hooks": {
    "Stop": [
      {
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "\"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/.claude/hooks/check-build-en.sh" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

A build can take a few seconds or much longer. A Stop hook runs every time Claude tries to finish, so it can slow you down. If that bothers you, turn the hook off and step down to strength 1: add "Before you finish, run mkdocs build --strict and show me the output" to your request.

In 10-year-old words

Put a gatekeeper at the door: "You can't say you're done until the check passes." And make sure the gatekeeper only sends you back once, so it doesn't repeat itself forever.

★ Going deeper

  • Hooks run with your computer's permissions, so the safety rules from Chapter 17 still apply. This script only runs mkdocs. Avoid passing outside input straight into a hook script.
  • To use the same loop in one-shot claude -p runs (Chapter 18), first check how hooks behave in that mode.
  • If your check really needs more than eight rounds, the docs say you can raise the limit with CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Make the script and test both cases on their own. Add a broken link on purpose, then remove it.
  2. Register it, then ask Claude: "Make test.md in docs and put the link [x](nope.md) in it."
  3. Watch whether Claude gets the build error and fixes the link. If it can't, check that it stops the second time.
  4. When you're done, delete test.md and decide whether to keep the hook.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Check once that a tool's quiet option (-q) doesn't hide failures.
  2. Test every new check with a failing case and a passing case before you register it.
  3. Add a loop guard to any hook that sends Claude back.

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "If the build passes, the content is right." The build only checks format and links. The content is for the reviewer (layer 3) and your own eyes.
  • "More checks means more safety." If they get slow and annoying, people turn them off. Two or three important layers are better.

docs.title: Sources and date checked
docs.text:
• Version checked: Claude Code 2.1.319 and MkDocs 1.6.1, checked on 2026-11-09. We checked check-build-en.sh's exit codes (2 and 0) on a practice site ourselves, and the -q problem (exit code 0 versus 1) too. We didn't check Claude actually being sent back. Try that in your own setup.
  • The practice file is in the repository at examples/claude-code/check-build-en.sh (the Korean edition's version is check-build.sh). The README there says how it was checked.
  • Source of facts: Claude Code best practices: enforce the check with a Stop hook and Hooks guide: Stop hook block limit. Read on 2026-11-09.

docs.title: Give it a test it can check itself against
docs.text:
Ch. 23 · 23.4About 7 min read2026-11-09

What you'll learn on this page

  • Claude stops when the job looks done. Without a way to check, "looks done" is all it has to go on.
  • The fix is to give it a check that answers pass or fail. Then a loop runs: make it, check it, fix it.
  • Checks come in four strengths. And always ask for evidence.

docs.title: Grading your own homework
docs.text: If you do your homework and never check the answers, you hand it in with mistakes. With an answer key, you can grade it, fix it, and hand it in right. In Part I (1.1.3), you learned that AI can say things that sound right but are wrong. So a job should end on a signal you can check, not on "sounds right." The official best practices say the same. Without a check, you become the tester, and mistakes stay until you notice them.

docs.title: Four strengths of check
docs.text:
The docs list these, from loosest to strictest:

Strength How Who decides it's done 1. In the request "Run the tests after, and keep going until they pass" Claude decides when it's satisfied 2. As a goal /goal plus a condition A separate model checks the condition after every turn 3. A Stop hook The Stop hook from Chapter 17 Claude Code itself enforces it. The turn can't end until the check passes (up to a limit) 4. Someone else reviews /code-review, or a reviewer helper Eyes that never saw your chat

A check can be almost anything, as long as Claude can read the result:

  • A test file, a build's exit code, or a linter (a style-checking tool)
  • A script that compares the output to an expected file
  • A screenshot set next to the design

The docs add: if your project already has a check like this, the most useful line in your CLAUDE.md is the command that runs it.

docs.title: Always ask for evidence
docs.text:
"All tests pass," on its own, tells you very little. The docs say to ask for evidence: the command Claude ran and its output, or a screenshot. For a chat you weren't watching, that's the only evidence you have. And reading the output is faster than running the check again yourself.

Before you say you're done, show me the check command and its full output.

docs.title: Tell reviewers to skip style
docs.text:
One tip for the review step. If you ask a reviewer to find problems, it will always find something. If you fix every finding, you end up with extra layers and tests for cases that can't happen. The best practices say to narrow the job, like "report gaps that affect correctness, and skip style." That's why the reviewer helper in Chapter 17 says "If there are no problems, just say 'No problems.'"

In 10-year-old words

You grade homework with an answer key. Give the AI an answer key (a check), so it can grade and fix its own work.

★ Going deeper

  • After Claude says it's done, the docs suggest running /verify. Claude builds and runs your app and looks at the result. That catches problems tests and type checks miss.
  • A Stop hook can't block forever. If it blocks eight times in a row with no tool use in between, Claude Code steps in and ends the turn. Your hook should check stop_hook_active to see if it already sent Claude back (next page).
  • /goal matters most for long runs nobody is watching. In a normal chat, you rarely need it.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
1. Think of a recent job where an AI said "Done!"
  2. Write down whether there was a pass-or-fail check that showed it was really done. If not, what check could there have been?
  3. Next time, end the request with "Show me the check command and its output," and compare.

docs.title: Use it today
docs.text:
1. Write "done" as pass or fail: for example, "zero warnings from the link check."
  2. Narrow the reviewer's job: "correctness only, skip style."
  3. Ask for the command and its output with every "done."

docs.title: Common mix-ups
docs.text:
• "It passed the check, so it's perfect." A check can't catch what it doesn't test. A link can open and the content can still be wrong.
  • "Having the AI review its own work is enough." A reviewer that never saw your chat looks without that bias (Chapter 17). Self-review alone may not be enough.
